div.head: BRWSEY WARD. THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD.
div.p: BRWSEY WARD. THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD.
LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,-

Having been requested by an influential body of ratepayers In your ward to allow myself to be nominated as a candidate to contest the seat becoming vacant on Ist November,! now offer my services and will be glad of your votes and support on that cceasion. Jam, as you all know, a ratepayer in the borough, and I also represent the largest F firm of ratepayers in Warrington. I think these facts will be a sufficient guarantee to your interests as ratepayers. Any improvements required in the ward which may be brought under my notice will have icy special care and attention. Soliciting your vote and favour, Believe me Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, JOHN BAIRD.

I ama determined advocate of economy in the spending of Public Moneys, and am of an opinion that every step ponible ehould be taken to reduce the exorbitant Rate,' that we at present have to pay. By so doing we considerably increase the pessiblity of New Works and Industries sptinging up in our midst rendered so probable by the early opening of the Ship Canal,
I Nvill be it very important one. financially

The coming year far Warrington. Already a scheme is prepared Involvlug the expenditure of some tterty or forty thousand pomade. This, scheme requires very careful watching, as I consider tte present time a very inopportune one for spending so much money, and any part of it that can well be postponed ought to be. .

_ There are many other important public matters about which I could wish to express my opinions and I hope to hare the pleasure of doing so in public meeting at an early date, if you will be kind enough to honor me with your pre- sence thereat. I promise you. if electei, that everything that may be brought forward for the goal and well-being of this, our Town. and of Orford Ward in particular, shall hare my cordial anti emphatic support. _ _
Believe me to be, Ladies and Gentlemen, Faithfully yours, WM. P. SKELTON.

Ilorsemarket-st., Warrington, 19th October, 1893. MUN IC IPA L EL ;C.,T.1 ON, 1893. - . TO THE ELECTORS OF THE FAIRFIELD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— At the request of numerous friends and ratepayers. of different political opinions, I have consented to place my services at your disposal, as one of the representatives of the Ward In the Town Council.

As a resident in the ward, an emp,over of labour, and a large ratepayer, lam more likely to understand the require- ments of this ward in particular, anl the town in general, than a non-resident in the borough. lam aware that there arc several important matters affecting this ward especially, which require immediate attention. I refer to ~he sewerage of Padgate Lane district, tx" the evils arising from the present system of sewer ventilation, and to the wretched condition of the pavem,nt of School Brow, and the adjacent thorough- fares. As an owner of property it will be my endeavour to keep urn the rates, wh eh at the present time are very excessive, mid enable the working to:eases to have decent and respect- able homes at moderate and fair rents. To these and other matters pertaining to the Ward, should you do me the honour of returning me as one of your repre- sentstives in the Town Connell, I will devote my very best attention, without fear or favour, irrespective of party. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Faithfully yours, JOSEPH 2.1 OUNPIELD. 60, Manchester-road. October 20th, 1893. VST A RRI N GTO N MIUB6N3' ICI PAL ELECTIONS TO THE BURGESSES OF THE FAIRFIELD WARD. LADIES AN GENTLEMEN. Having been selected unanimously by the Conserva- tive Committees, and at the request also of numerous friends and Ratepayers In the Ward, of different political opinions. who hove promised one their Support, I have much pleasure in placing my services at your disposal, as one of your repre- sentatives in the Town Coui,cii.

It is now nearly 17 years since I Came to Warrington, and during that period I have always taken a deep interest in our Municipal affairs, and in those matters affecting the pros- perity of the Borough and the wellbeing and comisrt of its inh .bitanis. ‘• I was entirely in favour of the purchistrof the Waterworks, and the erection of the New Baths, aid -I think there are rnatly more subjects of great importanet be dealt with in the near future, particularly the Nese' ks and the Bast Coast Railway, while Sanitary affairs, '..Yectnical Education,' the Gas Works and Annuities, the excessive Rates, and other matters require attention at once. I am not unmindful of the condition of some of the very 014_ streets, in the Ward which ought at once to be ref laced with good sett pavement. I should be very pleased at this time In the town's history to enter upon Municipal life, and I think that with good management we have better times in' store, after the miser- able and deplorable Coal War is settled. - -
lam in favour of good wages and fair prices, and I eon. demo sweating In every shape and form.

, - But I think my views and principles are pretty generally known in the Ward, having already had the pleasure of speakit gto many of you on Municipal questions. I also gratefully remember receiving such kindness add substantial support at your hands la my contest three years ago, and on my election to the Board of Guardians, * If elected, I shall do my best to carry out your wishes and to safeguard your interests, which letter, as?, large Rate- payer, are identical with my own. Soliciting the favour of your Vbtes and Interest, I ant, Ladies and Geittlemett. Your Obedient Servant. HENRY JOIISSON LONOTON, 15, Ili per Bank-street, Warringt 16th October, 1693.

div.p: T 0 THE GUARDIANS OF THE POOR of the THE UNION, in the Coen•y of Chester, being the Sanitary Authority for the Rural Sanitary District of that Union And to all others whom it may concern. Whereas. by certain orders dated the 22nd day of October. 1881. the 4th uay of July, 1889. the 3rd day of January. 1890. and the 17th day of October. 1892. respectively, issued in poe- m trice of the Public Health Act. -18-5, We, the Local Government Board, invested the Guardians of the Poor of the said Runcorn Union, as such Sanitary Authority at aforesaid, with certain of the powers, rights, duties, capacities, liabili- ties and the obligations of an Urban Sanitary Authority as regards certain portions of their district, including the contri- butory pieces of Frodsham Township and Hull and Appleton; And whereas, we have received and duly considered an application under Section 276 of the Public Health Act. 1875, from the said Sanitary Authority to put in force within the said contributory places, certain provisions of such Acts as hereinafter mentioned ; Now, therefore, in pursuance of the powers given to us by ! the statutes in 'that behalf, we hereby declare emit order as ! follows : ARTICLE I.—Until we by order otherwise direct, the under- mettioned provisions of the said Act shall be in force within the said contributory places of Frodsliam Township and Hull and Appleton as h•reinafter mentioned, and the said Sanitary Authority shall be invested, as regards the said contributory places, with all the powers, rights, du les, capacities. liabili- ties, and obligations of an Urban Sanitary Authority under such rrovisions ; namely : Within the contributory places of Frodsham Township and Hull and Appleton,— The Public Health Act, 1875,— Section 25; Section 26, so far as It relates to the erection of a build- ing over a sewer' Sections 47, 153, and 155. The Towns Improvement Clauses Act, 1847,— So much thereof by Section 160 ef the said Public Health Act, 1875, incorporated with that Act, as relates to the naming ot streets and the numbering of houses. The Town Police Clauses Act, 1847. So much thereof by Section 171 of the said Public Health Act, 1875, incorporated with that Act, as relates to fires. The Public Health (Buildings In Streets) Act. 1888 (such Act being constmed as one with the said Public Health Act, 1875),— Section 3. Within the contributory place cd PrOdsham Township only,— The Public Health Act, 1875, Section 154 ; Section 172, first paragraph. Within the contributory place of Hall and Appleton only,— The Public Health Act, 1875,— Section 39; Section 42, so much as is not already In force; Sections 66, 112, 113, 114. and 115.1 ARTICLE 11.—The expenses incurred or payable by the said Sanitary Authority in the execution of the powers con- ferred upon them by Article Lot this order, or by the above- ! cited order dated the Third day oi January, One thousand eight hundred and ninety, except so far as such expenses ' may relate to the establishment and officers of the said Sanitary Authority, or may be recovered from the owners and occupiers, shall be deemed to be Special Expenses" within the meaning of the Public Health Act, 1875. and shall be charged as such upon the contributory place in respect of which they may have been incurred. ARTICLE lll.—This article shall come intooperation on the Thirteenth day of November, One thousand eight hundred and ninety-three, and the said Sanitary Authority shall muse it to be published once in some newspaper circulated within their district before that date. Given under the Seal of Office of the Local Government Board, this Tenth day of October in the year One thou- sand sigh., hundred and ninety-three. 7179 lIIINRYIB. FOWLHR, President. • S. B. PEOVIS, Assistant Secretary.

div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
HE : " Do you think it possible for a man to love two women?" She: "Not if either of them should find it out."

"I HEARD a compliment for you last night, Miriam." "What was it, Lizette ?" "Colonel Bronson said you were exceedingly preserved." M..—" Yen don't find lama wasting my time try- ing to get eirt-4114f1y enemies." "No, indeed; you are too busy trying to get ahead of your friends."

"DON'T you think that Mr. Gibler'a voice has a very metallic ring in it?" " Very naturally so, my dear; all his teeth are crowned with gold." A CLERGYMAN once spoke of seeing a young lady "with the pearl-drops of affection hanging and glistening on her cheek." He meant that she was crying. DOCTOR, to low-headed urchin "How is your mother, Tommy ?" Tommy : "Oh, if you please, -air, shea getting very romantic in het right knee, she says.' AGED admirer—" Think of all the luxuries a rich husband like me could give yen." Mill! De Yonny—" Oh, a rich father would do just as well; marry my mother." As Irishman, eating raw eggs, bolted a live chicken. The bird chirped as it went down his throat. He cooley said—" By the powers, young friend, you spoke too late." A MAN asked another to loan him five pounds. "Why," said the other, "I don't know you." "That's why I came here, for those who know me won't loan me five shillings." A GENEROUS farmer having presented a miserly man with a barrel of cider, took it by request to his house. The recipient said "What will you pay for the barrel when it is empty?" "Now, my hearties," said a *Yankee, captain, "you've a tough battle before you. Fight like heroes till your powder's gone, Luca run. I'm a little lame, and I'll btart now."

JKANNETTE—" Does Miss Boardman get her lovely complexion from her father or her mother?" Gladys (sweetly)—" From her father, lie's in the drug business." "I CAN take a hundred words a minute," said the stenographer. "I often take more than that," said the other in sorrowful accents; "but then I have to. I'm married."

A TRAVELLER, returning from Florida, said : "It is the most fertile country in the world; the lands produce 40 bushels of frogs in the acre, and alligators enough to fence them.' Husnallo—" What a splendid dinner you have to-night." Wife (complacently)—"Yes, dear, I thought it would please you." Husband—" What kind of a dress are you thinking of getting?' YOUNG HOPEFUL—" Papa, I wish you'd buy me a bow and arrow." Papa—"lt's only an hour since I bought you a kite." Young Hopeful— " Th' kite's on top of a telegraph pole an' I want to shoot it down."

MR. HENPECK: "I can't see, my dear, what good that border of lace does round the hem of your skirt." Mrs. Henpeck: "Oh, can't you? Well, it just shows that I can afford it; so there." "A PARASTTE," said the pedagogue, "is a creature that lives on its fellow-creaures. Now, tell me what a parasite is at once !" "Please, sir," replied the lad,"a parasite is a cannibal." A MAN was aske4 by his friend when he last saw his jolly comrade --? "Oh," said he, "I called on him yesterday at his lodgings, and there I found him sittiag all round a table by himself."

SITE—" You will love me always, won't you, dear ?" He—" Always, darling." She (petulantly) —" Oh --." He—" What in the world is the matter ?" She—" Why don't you say twice as long as always ?" BUDDING Auxtrou—" What do you think of these rooms? Good way up from the street, but just see the view from the window 1" His friend —" Fine, very fine! You've got the attic; now all you want is the genius." • A FAT fellow, mounting a horse. "Heaven help you," a bystander exclaimed. By an over-balance the fat man tumbled over the other side. " Con- found your prayers," says he, "for they got me more help than I wanted." " Docrok," said the sufferer, supinely, as he dropped into the dentist's chair, • doctor, my nerve is completely gone." "Oh, no, it isn't," was the cheerful reply. " Wait till I get a firm hold, and you'll realise your mip•to.ke." LITTLE %Vies I saved four pounds to-day." Loving Ilusbaad : "Darling! How did you do it ?" Little Wife : "I saw a perfectly lovely easy chair that I knew you'd like, and I didn't buy it.' He didn't know whether to be pleased or not. "Btsfror," said a young Methodist preacher to his spiritual superior, "won't you give me some advice how to gain and keep the love of my con- gregation ?" "Yes, brother,' replied the divine. "When you marry, select a woman from some other congregation than your own, and be sure that she is not handsome or stylish in her dress."

A FRENcir A ParcAN Exr.oßzit, while still on his travels in the Dark Continent, received the news of the death of his father. Some time afterwards he arrived in Paris accompanied by a black bride. "What on earth," mked a candid friend, "in- duced you to marry a negress?" To which the explorer made answer, in cavernous tones, "I was in mourning !" WIFE, from the window at 1 a.m. to tipsy hus- band: " Well, what's your excuse for coming „home at this hour?" Husband: "Let me in, Irrial Just come from the meeting of the labour union; been considering what we'd do about the recent strike." Wife: Well, you just sit down on the doorstep and consider what you'll do about the recent lock-out."

"WILL you be mine ? " he asked, after a year's courting. "No, it can never be," was her reply. "Then why have you let me hope so long!" he said, as he went towards the door. "Because I intend never to belong to any man. You can be mine if you like." He saw the difference and stopped. Years afterwards he saw the difference stilt more clearly. "Loot( here, said a brutal English husband, 4'l suppose it would injure the new curtains awfully if I smAced in here?" " Ah, my darling husband," responded his loving English wife; "how coesiderate and thoughtful you are ! Of course it would injure the curtains dreadfully." "Then," was the reply, "have 'em taken down. I'm going to smoke." THE man who was charged with stealing chickens deolined the services of a lawyer to defend him. He said he had obtained those chickens at considerable risk, and he wanted to keep them. He didn't think there was much chance of that if he employed a lawyer. He know something, did that man. It is announced that Charlecote House is once again to be tenantless, Colonel and Lady Mary Lloyd baying left the beautiful Elizabethan home of the Lucys, whose punning coat-of-arms, the three lines cr fishes, have adorned the great iron gates of the mansion ever since, and,indeed, long betore,the days a hen, so 'tis said, the Lucy of Shakespeare's days was the original of Justice Shallow. Local traditions concerning celebrities mu-t, of course, al- ways be accepted with a very large pinch of salt, and the tales told round Stratford-on-Avon of young Will Shakespeare? poaching expeditions have never Teceived absolute credence. But though no docu- bentary evidence exists concerning the bard's ex- ploits, the fat deer still roam over the Cbarlecote House estate as in the days when, if gossip be true, the village lads, led by the youngdramatist,excited the ire of the local J P., one of the Lucy family, who till within our own time have occupied Charle- cote.

Lord Rosebery, who was at Newmarket, was seen walking with the Prince of Wales one or two morn- ings. This will furnish the lovers of conjecture with food. We shall be told shortly that Lord Rosebery is about to marry one of the young Princesses, or, rather, the story will be revived by the aid of this new fuel.

Silly tongues are suggesting that, the absence of the Duke of York trom his bride for ten days is too long, as they were only married four months ago. The duchess is at White Lodge and the Duke is at Saudringnam.

Mr. Herbert Spencer, who in latter years his constantly been more or less of an invalid, now spends his time almost equally in London and Brighton,and always enloys markedly better health at the sesside resort, he is a martyr to insomnia —that nemesis of brain-workers, and a gentlercan who a little while ago travelled some distance with him by rail;discribes the elaborate and ingenious arrangements that have been devised by Mr. Spencer to render him oblivious to the outer world when seeking the sleep that is even inure necessary to the mental worker than to the toiler with his hands.

With broken health and advancing years—be is 73 his intimate friends say that he now almost despairs of completing the vast fabric of which he laid the groundwork 30, years ago, and known to the world as '4A system of bynthetic Philosophy." The concluding portion, dealing with 'the ."Prin- ciples of Ethics," he published,out of its order,early in the year, to avoid the possibility of the division, to which he considers all the -others, subsidiary, failing to see the ligkt. The filling of the hiatus will depend upon Mr. Spencer's power of work: r but, even if he shouid fail to complete his sell= appointed task, the volumes that bear his name will remain the most magnificent monument of philosophic genius that the 19th centuary has seen.

Lady Gorst, who with her daughter and Sir John. has just started for New Zealand—Sir John, how- ever, leaving his family when he reaches Teneriffe —is paying a visit home, since she comes from "down under,' her father, the Rev. Lorenzo Moore having long been a well-known figure in Christ- church society. Sir John Gorst some 30 years ago, at the time of his marriage, played a somewhat important part in the stormy days of New Zealand history when the Aborigines, and the Maoris were still a source of much anxiety to the whits settlers. The " Sun" some weeks since referred to a charac- teristic scene in which Sir John, who edited a local newspaper written in the Maori tongue, was one of the chief actors at the time of the uprising of the natives. The volume which he wrote on his exper- iences offers a most interesting picture of a noble race now almost completely extinct, or, as some might more forcibly term it, killed off.

Sensitive as is the. Pope on. the subject of his , succession being a matter for open discussion, His ' Holiness is clearly prepared for possible eventuali- ties, and those in his confidence have Leen lately made aware, I learn from Rome, that the Holy Father has for some time past been preparing what can best been referred to as' his political. testament, a concise statement of the situation of the Holy ee at the present moment and since the death of Pio ;Norio. Realising that the Papacy is passing through critical days,Pope Leo is anxious that the results of his shrewd observation of the signs of the tim.4 and their need shall not be lost upon his succeszor, whogyerhe may be. The document it can be unaer- stood; ii essentially not of a public nature, and its !contents, therefore can scarcely be made know to ' the world. It is primarily addressed to the present Pontiff's successor in the chair of St. Peter.

The subject of the condition of George gliot's grave 18 again troubling the minds of her worship- pers. It is not kept in the state that her disciples would like. How George Henry Lewes and George Eliot came to consort is a question which has puzzled all who were acquainted with them. Their temperaments are wholly dissimilar. Lewis was a mountebank ; George Eliot was the persontication of solemnity and gravity. She rarely spoke, and when he did it was not upon frivolous topics ; he was never happy unless he was monopolising the conversation with the greatest twaddle. But.this

'was not all. He had an. idea that he could act, and in tile middle of a dinner he would get up out of lie chair and proceed to illustrate some ludicrous anecdote with which he had been entertaining the company. What a strange pair! On one aide of a table was the woman, stern, unbending, and severe: on the other the clown of a pantomime rehearsing his part. Yet George Henry Lewis's literary life was mainly devoted to the consideration of more or less abstruse subjects.

As is well known," George Eliot's " father, Mr. Evans, began life in a humble' rank, but gradually worked himself up to the position of agent to Mr. Newdigate, " the undertaker "as he was always termed in the House of Commons. The grandson still holds this situation on the Arbury Estate, the "Cheveley Manor "of the novelist. There is a story of " George Eliot's " father which, if true or not, is "hen trovato." It shows whence the talented lady inherited her wit. It was Mr. Evan's duty to lec- ture one of the oldest tenants, and this gentleman, annoyed at what he considered Mr. Evan's presump- tion, sneeringly remarked, " I can remember you when you carried the flag basket on your shoulder." " Yes," retorted the other, " and if my name were (mentioning the farmer's patronymic), I should be carrying it still.', There is nothing like a bit of scandal for making money—in Paris as everywhere. Mdme. Rohden —the " Baroness-tleu3. Ore," whose infuriated hus- band made her the talk of the town by mortally woundiag in the circus at Clermont-Ferrand a Danish officer who had been following the fascina- ting horsewoman wherever she went for some years past—made a triumphant debut at the Polies- Bergere, the other night. Her clever equestrian performances had already propitiated the audience in favour of the new star, but when her name— which she haa in vain tried to keep secret—became known, and was whispered from mouth to mouth, the delight of the spectators knew no bounds, and now everyone runs to see—not the brilliant rider of course, but the heroine of that. scandalous Cler- mont-Ferrant business, don't 3ou know."

div.head: SLOVENLY DRESS.
div.p: SLOVENLY DRESS.

If overdressing is chiefly a woman's weakness,slovenli- ness is oftenest a masculine one. Slovenliness in the young too often is the index of other bad habits, while it is a failing which frequently renders age, venerable in itself, repulsive. Sometimes p rsons of genius fall into this fatal mistake, and the uncleanly, untidy, barely de- cent figure forms a bitter satire on the greatness of hu- man intellect, when contrasted with the exquisite poem, the philosophical essay, or the masterly novel, the work of the clever brain, nevertheless content to inhabit such an uninviting shell. Poets who feed us with the beauti- ful, authors and authoresses who delight in describing the most enchanting scenes and people, will sometimes appear personally in repulsively negligent apparel. To name contemporaries would be invidious,but the biogra- phy of the past serves us for the present with numerous illustrations, from Dr. Johnson, with the shabbiest ot wigs, to Professor Wilson who was so careless of a hand- some person that his neglect at last became intolerable. Sir Humphrey Davy was particularly negligent in mat- ters of cleanliness, and so engrossed in ssientific dis- coveries that frequently he did not remove his clothes for days together, simply throwing on a clean shirt and stockings over his unchanged linen, in order to be pre- sentable at the dinners ot his aristocratic friends; in this manner be often had three or four suits on at a time,and those who knew him used to marvel at his rapid increase or decrease in bulk. A certain wealthy marquis of the past generation was accustomed to walk out in such dila- pitated habiliments that persons offered him alms,which, , by the way, he quietly pocketed.—" Leisure Hour." The Local Government Board forwarded copies of an order which they had issued nVesting the Rural Sani- tary Authority as regarded the contributory places of Frbdsliam township and Hull and Appleton with urban Pol/4Yers under certain sections of the Public Health Acts as with the exception of the ' first paragraph of section 18i,which by an order dated the 17th 0ct.,1892,is already in force in Hull and Appleton. -The provisions of section 18p, second and third paragraphs, and section 170 also are already by an order dated the 3rd January, 1890, in force in Hull and Appleton. SNAKE POISON AND HUMAN POISON. The bite of the rattlesnake is almost always fatal to man. Yet this snake is never affected by the injection of its own poison into its own blood, neither when enraged it bites itself nor when its venom i injected by artificial means to test the question. Speaking on the latter point Dr. S. Weir Mitchell, an expert on snake poison, says: "I have over and over tried this experi- ment, but in no case have I seen death result. Why should this be 2"

Dr. Mitchell further says : "The many noxious com- pounds man carries in his liver and gastric glands (the stomach) are fatal if they enter the blood in any large' amount. There is scarcely an organ in man's body which is not a possible source of poison to him. Small doses are constantly passing into and out of his blood. The question is whether he can get rid of it as fast as it accumulates."

Alluding to death by rheumatism, gout, and kidney disease, an eminent London physician says: Thus man is poisoned by the products of his own body." Now let us cite a passage from a man's experience as related by himself. The time extends over a period from March, 1888, to May, 1889, more that a year. He says : "My head used to whirl around, and I had frequent bouts of faintness and giddiness ; and at such times I used to fall down, no matter where I was. This would occur two or three times a day. For three weeks I was confined to my bed. I grew gradually weaker and weaker and lost a deal of sleep. I felt worse tired in the morning, than when I went to bed. After a while I became nervous, and my legs trembled and shook under me to such a degree that I feared to walk out. I had great pain in my kidneys, and the secretion which I voided from them was thick and yellow as the yolk of an egg. Month alter month passed and I failed more and more, and could hardly crawl about. " I had a doctor attending me, but his medicines did not benefit rue. He said my liver and kidneys were in a bad way, and that he never saw secretions passed in such a state. After treating me six mouths, he told me that medicine could do no more for me and advised me to go to a hospital. I went to the Peterborough Hospital, but got worse while there. The hospital doctors refused to tell me what ailed me. Having spent two months there, I got anxious and returned to my home, ult., rly disheartened. I continued to send to the hospital for medicines, which I took for three months longer. I was now so emaciated that my friends who came to see me said I would never get well.

" In this condition I continued until May, 1890, when one day an umbrella vendor called at my house, and, seeing how ill I was, said his wife had been cured of a serious illness by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. He poke so earnestly of it that I determined to try it. After taking the Syrup for ten days I felt in better spirits; my food agreed with me, and from that time I gained strength daily. Persevering with it, I was soon able to return UP my work as healthy and strong as ever. Since then I have been in the best of health. You are at liberty to publish the above facts, and I will gladly reply to any inquiries. Yours truly (Signed), READ WELFARE, Ramsey, St. Mary's, Hunts, February 18th, 1892."

_ , No brief comment can do justicti to this remark- able case. What the public needs to know and to remember is this: Mr. Welfare's whole system was poisoned by the products of a tcrpid and in- active digestion. These had entered his blood, as Dr. Mitchell describes. The nervous system was dis- ordered and half paralysed ; hence the faintness and falling fits. Rattlesnake poison kills by paralysing the nerves which actuate the lungs ; it kills by suffocation. Human poison, arising from indigestion and dyspepsia, always operates in the same direction, causing asthma in its worst forms. It then attacks the heart and kid- neys, causing the state of things Mr. Welfare mentions. Nothing more noxious, or in the end, surely fatal exists in any poisonous reptile. And yet people trifle with the disease ! and doctors seem not to understand it.

Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup cures by stimulating the kidneys, skin, and bowels, and toning the gastric glands. Who, then, is man's most deadly enemy? Careless and ignorant man himself. Use the remedy when the earliest symptoms appear.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MT DEAREST NELLIE,

The present fashions are not showing us any startling changes in the shape and cut of our gar- ments, the most noticeable being, perhaps, the basqued bodices, which are obtaining some popularity. A notable change, however, is the amount of trimming used, and amongst these ribbon promised to be greatly used this season. The designs recently shown me were most elaborate, and our manufacturers appear to have this yeat excelled themselves in this particular branch. Brocaded and shot ribbons, as well as the better known striped satins and silks, all appear in equal demand, so we may expect to see the ball gowns of coming winter elaborately trimmed with bows and bands of the kind.

I do not believe that the millinery was ever prettier than it is at the present moment; it is not exaggerated, yet it can hardly be voted simple, while its materials are all of the very best, and let me tell you you may meet it under its most favourable conditions at any establishment. Some hats and bonnets are wonderfully effective. It will be quite a relief to the dull, dark costumes of winter if we continue to bestow our favour on the cream and white felt hats to which we are at present devoting ourselves. A stylish little bonnet is made in bright scarlet velvet edged with jet and a couple of jet wings slanting in butterfly fashion towards the front.

Day by day new developments appear in the making of our skirts. The latest idea is to have the opening in front, a little to one side, in place of baying it in the centre of the back. Sometimes the opening is merely defined with braid, either of a contrasting colour or exactly matching the dress. A stylish finish is to have three rather large buttons placed where the opening comes. The buttons should, of course," harmonise in colour with the gown or its trimmings. Sometimes a corresponding row of buttons is placed at the opposite side to match the opening. This side opening has decided advantages in the way of tidiness and comfort. We have all witnessed the untidy spectacle of a large expanse of white appearing at the placquet hole behind. Nothing of the kind can ever occur at the side opening; it is so entirely under the control of both our eyes and fingers.

The first and most important rule of keeping the feet warm is never to be tightly shod. Boots or shoes that fit closely prevent the free circulation of the blood by pressure; but when they do not embrace the foot too firmly, the space left between the shoe and the stocking has a good supply of warm air. The second rule is never to sit in damp shoes. It is often supposed that unless shoes are positively wet it is unnecessary to change them while the feet are at rest. This is a great fallacy, for when the least dampness is absorbed into the sole in its evaporation, it absorbs the heat from the foot, and thus perspiration is dangerously checked.

There are several novelties in hair dressiog this season and in one of the prettiest the hair is slightly waved and drawn back, leaving only tho fringe, which is kept close and rather fiat by the aid of iv fringe net. One has a large roll made on a. frizette, or one of tbe larger pin curls may be used, and the own hair for the twists round it. If the natural hair is of medium length, it may be kept in one tress and pinned at the difierent parts to form the three loops surrounding the roll or curl.

The most fashionable kind of cape is three- quarthr length and very full, and 19 out of 20 have one or two shoulder capes. A useful type of cloak is of black ribbed cloth edged with a scanty gathered frill of black and green shot velvet, headed by a band of black far, above which again are three very narrow strips of velvet. The shoulder capes are double, the under one being of velvet, and the upper one of cloth edged with fur. This mantle would look well in almost any oolonring, or could be all black with a trimming of coq feathers. For every-day wear capes of smooth-faced cloth in black or dark colours, trimmed round the hem, and on pelerine and collar, with close-set rows of narrow braid, are smart-looking as well as eerviceable—navy•blhe, braided with bleak and lined with red, being par- tioularly stylish.

The Russian type of coat has found favour with many, and a very original model, suitable for autumn wear is in the fashionable brown serge, trimmed with a darker braid, or in navy blue, trimmed black. The lining is usually faced to represent the yoke or underpart, and if a contrast is desired, this looks well in tan-coloured cloth or In white serge. It is also possible to make the top In one, and simulate the opening by trimming the front and adding the full shoulder frill. The separate yoke piece is, however, very effective in a lighter colour, or in white, with closely set lines of the dark braid running across—not lengthways; or flannel, with broad coloured stripes, may be used in the same style with blue serge.
Yours lovingly, JENNIE.

The Duchess of Connaught equals the great Cardinal Richelieu in her attachment for cats. Her favourite is a beautiful Persian puss. The Princess of Wales numbers among her many vir- tues the crowning one of being what is known in naafis- tocratic circles as "a good hand" with babies. Mrs. Everett, the wife or a master drayman in New Orleans, is one of the best veterinary surgeons in the city. She does her work entirely out of love for animals, and takes no pay for it. The King of Siam has exactly 500 wives, many of whom have, however, to act in a strictly domestic capa- city, no less than four, for instance, being employed in taking care of his Maksty's boots. Rosa Bonheur, the well-known artist, has several pretty pet dogs, but her chief favourite is her monkey, which is allowed to run about at will. It is very much attached to its mistress, and accompanies her on her country rambles, when it will gambol about with the dogs, climb trees, and so forth; but when danger threatens, it very promptly seeks ref ‘rge upon her shoulder.

div.head: To Restore Scorched Linen.
div.p: To Restore Scorched Linen.

Peel and slice sort; onions, pound and squeeze them to extract the juice, and add to the juice one half ounce of white soap cut fine, two ounces ot fuller's-earth, and a halt-pint of vinegar; boil all together. When it is cool, it should be poured on the scorched linen, and loft to dry. Then wash the goods as usual, boiling well.
Lamb Cutlets.

Try some lamb cutlets done like this: Cut the best end of a neck of house lamb into cutlets ; trim each one neatly, free from fit. Put 2oz. of butter, a tablespoon- ful of chopped parsley, one shallot, the leaves of a sprig of thyme, and the juice of a lemon in a stewpan. When the butter has thoroughly melted, put in the cutlets,and let them cook till nearly done, then take them up, brush over with the beaten yolk of an egg, sprinkle with grated bread crumbs, and lay on a grid over a clear fire ill each side is slightly browned ; drain on a hot paper for a moment, then arrange on a hot dish, and pour the following sauce over them—Take the liquor in which the cutlets have been cooked, strain it through a sieve intria clean enamelled saucepan,add a gill of good stock, thicken with a little cornflour ; when it boils throw in, a couple of small gherkins, cut into little dice-shaped pieces. Garnish with watercress.—" Truth."
The Mouth as a Catch-all.

There are a multitude of people who, in additioTi to the natural and proper uses of the mouth, seem to re- gard it as a sort of handy receptacle, into which any small object may be thrust for safe keeping tilt wanteu.' This trait is not confined to either sex, or to any age. Many a fond mother will cry out in alarm at the sight of her child running about with a plaything in its mouth, yet the chances are that if this same mother should an hour later have occasion to pay her lare on a public con- veyance, she would fish out, from some ridiculous re- ceptacle called a purse, a small coin, which she would hold between her lips till ready to make some other dis- position Of it—and this regardless of the fact that on an average the coin ha S been travelling about the country' for from 15 tO2O years, during which time it had been in all sorts of places and amid all kinds of surroundings. This observation is true of many otifer things than small coins,and• of fathers as well as of mothers: Some of the most painful instances possible have recently illustrated the danger of this habit.

div.head: GERMAN'S SUNDAY FROM AN AMERICAN POINT OF VIEW.
div.p: THE GERMAN'S SUNDAY FROM AN AMERICAN POINT OF VIEW.

The German's idea of Sunday is anything but Purit- anic. It is the very opposite. It is for ,them a day of amusement. It is no unusual thing to be asked by a German on Monday morning, " Well, how did you amuse yourself yesterday ?" There are those among the Germans, of course, who respect and keep the Sabbath; but then there are always enough of them who do not ; and to judge by .the numbers in which they frequent their places of amusement oa Sunday—the parks, beer gardens' and public halls—a stranger might possibly be ' tempted to inquire whether the Germans had any idea of ialabbath. Men, women, and children. old men with their wives, and younger ones • with their 'sWeithearts; throng these places every Sunday, and enjoy themselves careless of what impression they make on their fellow- citizens of American origin; to whom the sound of brass instruments on the Sabbath air is anything but welcome or edifying. In the cold days of winter, when the parks and beer-gardens are dreary and shorn of their beauty, the German seeks amusement in some hall instead. Here he treats himself to a compound of rather hetero- geneous elements—to music,beer and smoke ; and to all of them at once. Any Sunday afternoon, in the cold of winter, you may find him, with his wife or child,or both, in some large hall, one of a hundred or five hundred, smoking his meerschaum or his cigar, sipping his beer, , wine, or coffee, and listening to a selection from Meyer- beer or Beethoven. Were it summer, he would add the odour of roses to the fumes of his tobacco and the Smell of his beer; for he is as fond of flowers as he is of any of these, and is never happier then when the air, trembl- ing to the notes of the orchestra, is redolent With tobacco smoke, the pertume of the rose, heliotrope, and hop, and 11. e is himself in the midst ot them all.—Atlantic

PARTED BY FATE;
OR THE MYSTERY OF BLACK-TOR LIGHTHOUSE.
'B Y LAURA JEAN LIBBEY,
Author of "lone, the Pride of the Mill," ete., dco:'
CHAPTER VI. A RIVAL'S TREACIIERY.

Verlie looked up into Uldene's eyes, that glowed like burned coals behind her mask, With a slightly puzzled expression. "Of course, it shall be as you say," she replied.; "bat it is so near midnight it will scarcely be worth while. Why, how white you are, Uldene 1" she cried, when they found themselves alone, and her sister had thrown off her mask. " Why, you look as though you had seen a ghost." Uldene made no reply.

They both stood clreseed at last. Verlie was just about moving toward the door, when Uldene suddenly caught her hand. "There is something wanting in your appear- ance," she said. "You lack colour. You must wear this red rose in your corsage." "No, no,'" laughed.Verlie. "I will not wear it. I detest blood-red roses; pure white ones are best suited to me. I will wear that other one you brought up in your hand—the white rose." " Will you wear the red one, to please me? whispered Uldene, hoarsely. "Remember, it will please me more than I can tell you. Oh, Verlie, you must, you meet wear it."

, " Seeing you have set your heart upon it I sup- pose I shall have to," pouted Verlie. With trembling hands, Uldene fastened the blood- red rose in her bodice ; hot 'even rig 010 44 so, the dreroping petals seems almost to scorch the white, guilty hands. Together Verlie and Uldene descended to the ball-room.

The great clock in the hallway chimed the mid- night hour as they passed down the grand stair- way ; a silver bell rang shrilly, and the band struck a lively air. That was the signal for general un- masking. The hour that had passed since Rut- ledge Chester had left the conservatory and tbe lovely, drooping figure seated by the fountain was Indeed a long one to him. fie had mingled with the gorgeous, grotesque throng, but he hardly saw the people around him. The strains of soul-enlivening music fell upon deaf ears.
He looked eagerly around at length, but he saw no signs of the fairy bride. Was Verlie still by the fountain, taking no heed of time ?" he asked him- self.

He heard the clock chime, the silver bell tap, and the music strike up. There was rippling laughter and amusing exclamations. The moment for unma,king had come. But where was Verlie? One moment of suspense ; then he saw Uldene, and behind her he caught a gleam of a white satin dress and floating veil. His face flushed with delight; his pulse thrilled; his heart beat. With hurried steps he crossed over to where she stood. Another instant, and, mask in hand, he stool I,efore her. Verlie raised her eyes, a little cry escaped her lips, and a great, burning flush swept over her lovely face, as Bhe recognised in the unmasked plumed knight who had followed her about so per- sistently—il.utledge Chester. In that fatal glance Rutledge had seen the fatal red rose in her bodice—the rose which was to be the silent signal for his dit.toirtal. His face grew white as death. His strong hands trembled. Ah ! he had been NO sure that deep down in her coy little heart Vorlie oared for him I But it had been a delusion—the maddest kind of a fancy—he told himself. It was a moment of intense suspplute to the trembling, guilty girl who watched them, scarcely breathing in horrible fear lest her treachery vronld be exposed then and there. But no ! Fate, cruel fate, aided her. Rutledge Chester offered one arm to her, the other to Verlie ; but she caught the startling words as he bent over that golden head: "Alas I I am answered." To Verlie the words seemed meaningless enough. She never gave them a second thought. She looked up into his white, haggard face with a blush and a smile, remarking sweetly that this had been one of the happiest evenings of her life. Rutledge Chester turned and looked at her sharply. "Great heavens! had she no heart?" he asked himself, in bitter wonder. There was no veil& sarcasm in her voice. It sounded sweet and girlishly innocent. There was but one construction to put upon her words. His unhappiness had not troubled her. All Rutledge Chester's manly spirit rose to his aid at once. He bowed his dark, handsome head stiffly. His set, white face did not reveal the keen pain at his heart. The ball was a farce after that. He was heartily glad when it was all over. The ride home was not as pleasant as it might have been. Rutledge Chester had taken a seat beside Uldene. He was courteous and polite to Verlie—nothing more. " What strange change is this which has come over Mr. Chester ?" poor' innocent Verlie vaguely wondered. "Could it be that I have been so unfortunate as to offend him in any way? I can- not call to mind the slightest occasion for it." They parted in the corridor, Mr. Chester going to the library, the young ladies going up to the boadoir they occupied jointly. "What do you think is the matter with Mr. Chester? He seemed so cold and strange coming home," said Verlie, thoughtf.ally, as she prooeeded to throw oh her furlined wraps. "Don't talk to me to night, ' cried Uldene. "I am tired, and I—l want to rest." Verlie gazed at her in amazement. Was it only her fancy, or did gay, brilliant Uldene seem out of sorts, toe? She lied quite expected Uldene's busy tongue would clatter until broad daylight about the wonderful Mask ball.

Long after Verfie's golden head sank on the pillow, and her quiet breathing denoted that she slept, Uldeue stood motionless before the satin. draped window, staring out upon the snow- shrouded earth, and out into the inky blackness of the night. "I do not see my way out of it," she muttered, pantingly. "Soon* or later I shall be fottrid out. I am too dazed and bewildered to think." lhe sun was shining brightly into the room the next morning when Verlie opened her blue eyes. Uldene was already ap. For the first time since they had been guests at Senator Chester's home they missed meeting the son at the breakfast table; nor was he at luncheon.

All that day Rutledge Chester paced the library, lost in bitter thought. To meet Verlie after this, live undPr the same roof with her, meet her daily, would be an impossibility for him, he told himself. It would be better to go away, it mattered little where.

Suddenly, like a flash, a wonderful idea occurred to him. Pahaw 1 how foolish he had been 1 Be remembered now that he had heard that young girls liked to be coaxed, and that a peraistent wooer often changes their " No " to "Yea "—the demure, coy darlings "How stupid I have been " cried Rutledge Chester, his handsome, gloomy face brightening up, a pleased smile curving his moustached lips. "I should have been mad to have gone away with- out another effort to win sweet little Verne." Sittip4 &mil 12212 M hilt With,/ &fix& lag Iw --

div.p: riedly penned these few words :

- - "Dean LITTLE VERLIE—MISS SEFTON : I cannot teach my heart that you meant to wilfully and deliberately discard me. Consent to be my bride, or by this time to-morrow afternoon I shall be speeding away as fast as steam can take me to Europe. It is impossible to remain near you and be nothing to you. Let my deep love plead for me, little Verlie. If you send me away it will be sending me into the darkodeeP abyss of the bitterest despair. Grant me bat one moment in the conservatory at eight to-night. I mils see you, Verlie. Yours devotedly, for over, " RUTLEDGE CHICSTEE.- Ringing for a servant, he hastily dispatched the missive to Vei lie's room. Both girls were together when tho maid tipped at the door, and handed Verlie the note. ,

Uldenaspraing to her feet, white with terror. A note for Perlin! What if it should be from Rutledge (hester I An instant later Verlie confirmed her horrible • suspicion., "Oh, Ulclene, it is from Mr. Cheater!" she cried in dismay, her face turning from red to white as she glanced over it, "and—oh, Uldene, do look at it and see what he says! Am I mad or do I dream, Uldene ? Look at this and tell me is Mr. Cheilter—asking me to—to marry him? How odd and brusque the note is." The whiteness of death overspread Uldene's dark, brilliant face, and it horrible darkness en- folded her. The sword had fallen—her doom had civet taken her. •
Like a flash she tore it from Verlie's hands; the worde seemed stamped in fire upon the white part and every line to burn deep down into her heart sz she read.
" Will you go dowu to the c-nservatory as he. wishes? Anwer mo —will you go?" "Yes," Ladd Verlie, thoughtfully, but in evident embarrassment.

"Do you love him? Do you wish to marrY him ?" panted Uldene. "I —I should not mind, sister," replied Verlie, faintly, "if— papa and mamma—will consent. , Of course, he must ask them,;" and the sweet blue eyes drooped shyly under her sister's steady gaze. " Let us come out on the street • we will talk it over there. I must get air; theihrtat of this house it gifting." , Only too pleased to humour any caprice of her fr 'beautiful, wi!ful sister, Verlie threw on her wraps at once and accompanied (Wane out on the crowded thoroughfare. Taking a car, they rode to the end of the route ; then they left it, walking together along one of the isolated paths that led out of the city limits; ( turning an abrupt curve in the path and passing ' through an open gate, they found themselves in a churchyard. The church itself had long since fallen into dis- use. Its walls had crumbled and fallen in, and where the snow lay thick now ivy grew in the summer time and birds came there to build their nests in the branches of the willows that droopect over old time graves. "Let us turn back, Uldene," said Verlie in & ' fright. "I have such a terror of grave-Yards and monuments! It is almost dusk." r:
I
"I am tired," said Uldene. "Let us sit dovin and rest a moment. You need not be afraid but) what you will be back before eight," she added, with a bitter sneer.

Verlie looked at her with startled eyes. "Uldene,' she said, perplexedly, "I cannotunder• stand whether you are pleased that Mr. Chester has asked me to be his bride or not. leg me—are you, dear ?" - " Why should I care if your baby face and babY ways have won Senator Chester's heir or not?" All the pride and fire ot her nature seemed te flash in her face. Her eyes rained scorn; her lipe curled in direst contempt. "Uldene, do sou care for Rutledge Chester Verlie's sweet young voice rang out piteonelY• "Oh, my sister has fate been so cruel to us that we were both destined to love the same maul" In her great excitement Verlie had sprung to her feet and taken a step backward. "Oh 1 fatal step! Her foot had caught in the tangled brambles that had grown over a faller) tombstone, and she was precipitated headlong °Pen the cold marble.

The sudden wrench had sprained Verlie's ankle. In an irisLatiti Uldene was kneeling beside her. One glance at the face.upturned to the gathering dusk, and she saw that Verlie had fainted. Her first impulse was to cry aloud for. hell); but, on second thought, she knew it would be useless. Her yoke could never penetrate beyond the Walls of that lonely, isolated grave-yard. No help or assistance could reach Verlie in that silent "City of the dead" unless she herself summoned it. Suddenly a dark, horrible • thought came to Uldene—a thought so wicked that she shrank from it at first in horror too great for words.. A monv.:ilt she pondered on the terrible idea -- and that was the darkest moment of Uldene's life-- a moment in which a temptation, the cruellest that could ever drift across mortal brain came to her. Verlie, the golden-haired girl vdiom Rutledge Chester loved, lay wounded, crippled, helpless, and unconscious at her feet. Should she sumral'u help and save her, or turn and walk swiftly away, leaving her helpless rival alone and to her fate? She raised her white face to the starlit sky and to the fair moon rising behind the dark, waving trees. Never did good and evil fight for a human heart?
'I

DA they struggled then and iere for the heart of beautiful, guilty Uldene. If she saved her, it would be giving her to love and happiness with Rutledge Cheater, she cried out to the night winds; and all the fire, the pasel°l4 and recklessness in her nature rose up bitterlY against that. "Oh, if she were only to die l" she cried out, hoarsely. All she would have to do would be to turn .0.3 hurry away, and her sinful wish would be realised. "Save her l" commanded God and the watching angels in the blue sky. " Leave her to her fate !" cried the tempter. One awful moment more—then. Heaven forgive heal Mamie turned and fled, without daring te look back, lest her resolution should forsake heel at that beautiful pallid, upturned face. Yes, else fled, leaving Verlie to her piteous fate. Over the white-crusted snow Uldene sped witll winged feet, never stopping until she had Pie° her own boudoir. As she drew the curtalns? shutting out the blackness of night outside, she saw the snow had commenced to fall. With startled cry ehe shrank back. She knew it w•- falling on those polished marble shafts, on the tve; and on the white, upturned face lying among old graves in the churchyard. eah All through • the long, horrible night she pac, the floor of tier boudoir. How could she sleep wt the picture of that upturned face in the graveye ;. upon which the snow was falling, burning into ,r brain? la She must shut It out from her mind or she We'l go mad—yes, mad. How the winds shrieked and moaned as the se descended. r obb Oh, that long, horrible night! Would da9:l;ge never dawn? And when the grey morning would Verlie be found with the snow wraPr" around her like a shroud? le% At length, weak and exhausted, she Batik to s —for evett the guilty can sleep, yes, even thro" the appalling dreams that confront them. A It was morning when she opened her eyes' oh ' voice awoke her, and she sprang from her onti . and listened with dilated eyes. tbe "Bless me," the old senator was saying corrider outside, "this is the Worst snow 5t0r'7...0 have seen for years. In some places the drifts r quite three feet deep, and the snow still falling; ' Uldene crept to the window and looked ._uor. The snow seemed to bury the whole world in _not rible, ghastly whiteness, and she knew Ill' have long since covered that white, upturned lying among the graves. (To be continued).

RUNCORN BOARD OF COWAIigSIONERS.

A special meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday morning. Mr. S. Taylor presided and there were present Messrs. P. Speak- man J.P.C.C., E. W. Humphreys, W. Collier, W. Handley, W. Hankinsou, E. Imison, W. Leach, D. Bisbrown, R. Abel,T. Lea. J. Pritchard, Dr., Mangan, P. A. Lake (law clerk) E. Marshall (secretary), Mr Barber survey or. 'GRATUITY TO THE SECRETARY.—INTERESTING DISCUSSION. The Finance Committee -submitted the following recommendations "That the Seal of the Board be affixed Ito the mortgage with the Rev. Robert Fisher for the loan of £BOO. That the tender of Mr. William Nickson for alterations to offices at the Town Hall for the sum of £5B 103., be accepted, and that the Seal of the Board be affixed to the contract. That application be made to Ithe Local Government Board for their sanction to' the 'payment of £5O to the Secretary and Accountant for extra services rendered by him in connection with the negotiations for, and the purchase of, the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks undertaking, and with the raising of the loan for the purchase of the under- taking and -the transfer of the undertaking; and to the payment of -such sum under section 30 of the Runcorn Commissioners Act, 1893, and to the borrowing of the money for such period as the Leal Government Board may determine." Mr. Humphreys moved the adoption of the minutes, and referring to the proposed payment to the secretary, said those who had been connected with the business of the purchase of the Waterworks would realise the amount of extra service and labour which had devolved upon Mr. Marshall in connection with the concern. The commis- -sinners made the recommendation subject to the sanction of the Local Government Board, to the inclusion of the amount ia the costs of the undertaking which meant that ' payment of it would probably be spread over a period of ten years—that was, the ratepayers would be burdened for a period of ten years with the sum of £5 per annum. By adopting the minute unanimously the Board would do a gracious and a graceful act.—Mr. Speakman seconded the motion and said the committee were prac- tically unanimous in making the recommendation. Whatever the Board had done for Mr. Marshall in raising his salary £25 per annum that was for work yet to be done, and the £5O was for work already done. They all knew that this purchase had been steered so well by one or two, and Mr. Marshall in particular, and it would be a grabious act to unanimously vote Use urant--In reply to Mr. Collier, the Law Clerk said the Board had not yet exhausted their borrowing powers.—Mr. Collier inquired if the taxed costs would absorb what they had borrowed from Mr. Fisher. The Law Clerk replied that it would require another £Boo.—Mr. Collier said he was sorry to have to get up to oppose this proposal. No one recognised more than he did the ability of Mr. Marshall, and it was very hard to oppose him in this matter, because there could not be a better man in the place. But he was surprised that anyone, considering the state of the town, and the state of the rates, and the way the ratepayers were altogether burdened at the present time should get up and propose a bonus of £5O. He was sure Mr. Marshall had never mentioned a word about it, and no one was even more surprised than he (Mr. Marshall) was at the proposal. It was out of all reason. There I had been a lot of extra work, but just because a gentle- man with a little influence got up and proposed a sum of money like this he did not Wilds for a moment that the Finance Committee should put en the " blinkers" of one gentleman and adopt his opinion as theirs without a struggle. They could not look at this matter from a prosperous coal merchant's point of view ;they must look at it from the struggling ratepayers point of view. At the present time the place was in a fearful state. The Committee had been like potteresclay in the hands of the potter. In such matters as this, sentiment ought to be put on one side, and the.' members ought to have the moral courage to look at the question fair and square. But there seeraed to he an influence that prevented this. He did not know whether it was" Old Commissioner hypnotism " or not—(laugh- ter)—but it seemed to get over the members and stifle discussion. He considered the proposed'grant excessive ; he would willingly go in for a sum of £lo.—Mr. Lea said he was sorry he could not support this recommenda- tion. He would go in for a smaller sum. This amount was far too large for the amount of• work done.—Mr. Abel said he was of the same opinion. If Mr. Marshall was not paid for his labour,they had bert (r get somebody te help him, and instead of raising wages,use the money to pay somebody else. They would never have done borrowing money if they threw it away in this fashion. —Mr. Bisbrown said he could not be charged with ex- travagence, but he could not ignore Mr. Marshall's ser- vices in this matter, and in his opinion he deserved well of the Board. Mr. Marshall had worked pot only by day but by night. He had attended 32 special meetings of the Board, that had mostly been held at night, and this work had been going on for eighteen months. It was the first time any application had been made for an allowance to Mr. Marshall since he became an official of the Board. He was deservinu of liberal consideration. —Mr. Hankinson said the Committee who had conducted the business, knew the value of Mr. Marshall's ser- vices, and he was prepared to accept their opinion. The speakers who had opposed the grant acknowledged that Mr. Marshall deserved something. The question novo was how much.—The Chairman saia they were all agreed that Mr. Marshall deserved some rem ineration for his extra services, and the question we. a, te the amount. He did not think many of them knew the amount of work which Mr. Marshall had had since the water question was first I:m:sight forward. He knew that at times Mr. Marshall had worked exceedingly late hours in dais matter; and work which some of the members had no knowledge of. Sup- posing Mr. Marshall when asked to carry through thist work had replied that his time was fully occupied with the ordinary work of the Board, what would it have cost the Board had they had to engage someone to do the work. But Mr. Marshall did not dissent from taking the work and he should support the proposal.—Mr. Pritchard said Mr. Marshall had had to devote a vast amount of labour in carrying out the purchase. He bad worked, by day and by night and in his own time in the preparation of the necessary statistics that had had from time to time to be laid before the Committee. There would be a great want of justice on the part of the Committee, if they, knowing the extent of Mr. Marshall's labours, had not made this preposal.—Mr. Leach said since he had been a member of the Board he had always found M. Marshall a gentleman, and it was not often they found tlist quali- fication in an official. The work he had done must have been enormous, and if it were a fact that this grant would be paid out of the revenue of the Waterworks, and not come as a direct charge on the rates he should vote for it. He would give it out of his own pocket if he could afford.—Mr.Handley Said Mr. Marshall richly deserved recognition for the great amount of work done. He believed the payment would not come out of water revenue for he looked forward to the certain fact that the water undertaking would be a charge upon the rates to a certain extent. Whether it would be a charge upon the revenue or upon the rates it was a deserved charge and as such he in, tended to vote for it.—Mr. Lake said it would be charged in the first instance on the water rates ; and jf the water rates were not sufficient then it wOuld ulti- mately come out of the district rates.—Mr. Irnison Said he was the one dissentient at the committee, but he felt that the gentlemen who had had experience of the tine and trouble Mr. Marshall had given were far better qua- lified than he was to express an opinion upon tit- value of his services. He could assure Mr. Collier that the gla- mour of a successful coal merchant was not upon him. Be bad approached the question with the distinct inten- tion to do what be conceived to be his duty to the rate- payers. He did not allow himself to be influenced by any personalityan by any other influence than aindciostminmctit(tleev- sire to do what seemed to be just and right. Messrs. Collier. Abel, and Lea voted against.—Mr. Lea said if Mr. Collier had moved £25 he would have sup- ported him.—Mr. Speakman said the words uttered by Mr. Collier had not the slightest effect upon him. He hoped that Mr. Collier's career on that Board would be as free from spot or blemish as his (Mr. Speakman's) had been.—Mr. Collier Faid he meant no reflections. NEW BYE-LAWS. On the proposition of the Bye Laws Committee it was resolved to have the new bye-laws printed and circu- lated. IMPROVEMENT OF GREENWAY-ROAD BRIDGE. The Highways Committee recommended that the Seal of the Board be affixed to an, agreement with the Lon- don and North-VVestern Railway Company for the set- ting back of the walls of the Railway Bridge, Greenwaya road, the making and adoption of the road over the said bridge, and the contribution by the Board of the private street expensas apportioned against the Railway Com- pany, hi respect of Norman-road from Greenway-road to Cawley-street.
