div.head: BOOTLE MIRACLE.
div.p: A BOOTLE MIRACLE.
A CUNARD BO'SDN'S STORY.

From the "Bootle Times," September 2,1893. In that thickly populated neighbourhood which skirts the great thoroughfares leading to the Bootle docks con- siderable interest has been aroused,recently through the marvellous. experiences of a sea-faring man. Struck with what seemed to be an incredible story, a re-present- ative set before him the task of enquiring thoroughly into the mystery. With this object in view he succeeded in ascertaining the name and address of the man, and with him he first of all secured an interview. He was directed to a cottage of humble pretentious in Matthew- st., in the very heart of the busiest portion of Bootle, occupied by people who depend upon the docks arid shipping for their livelihood. On the reporter request- ing to see Mr. Scott,he was shown into a neatly-furnished apartment, where that gentleman was seated by a table near the window. After a few words, conversation turned upon the subject of Mr. Scott's experience. " Oh," be said, " I caught my illness at sea; my nerves were all as if they were numb. I have been go- ing to sea since I was a boy, and I think my complaint was caused by wet and exposure, and perhaps with sleeping in damp beds." "Now, Mr. Scott, I am beginning to feel an interest in your case; how long is it since you had the firsic symptoms of numbness ? " . "it happened three years ago last November, on my' return from Boston. I was bo'sun of the ship, and in the Cunard service. I had suffered 41, good deal from bad Weather during the voyage, and when we get back to Liverpoel, as we were waiting to get into dock,. I went into the fo'csle to see about getting a drink of coffee for the men, as they had been working half the • night, when something struck me across the shin, as if I might have stepped upon a piece of hoop iron. It struck ' me like the shot of a gun and shook me all over at the time, but I felt nothing more until the next day. Well, the following day I found it was just as much as I could do to walk home; I could scarcely put one foot before the other, and when I got up the next morning one leg was under the other and I could not walk at all, so I went down in a cab and aelivered up the keys of the ship. Eventually I went to the hospital, but got very little better, and I told them I might as well go out."

" And did you do so ? " " Yes ; but after about four weeks I had a relapse through having bad weather and perspiring under my oilskins, and I was fourteen weeks in the Llomceopathic Hospital in Liverpool. Some time after that I began to take Dr. William's Pink Pills for Pale Poople." "flow came you to try this remedy? "

" Well," said Mr. Scott, " I saw an advertisement in the newspaper, and I thought if they cured one man of paralysis they would cure me." "And have they done you good 2" asked the reporter. "Oh, yes, sir,i can walk about now ; they thoroughly cleared my body and did me all the good in the wcrld." " Well, I suppose you were a little surprised at the result after being a cripple for over three years ? " "I was, sir; for everybody wanted to make me be- lieve my complaint was chronic. But that's all rub- bish." '
"How long do you think it is since you began to take Dr. Williams' Pink Pills ? "

"I should think it is three months ago, but I have dis- continued taking them now this six or seven weeks." "Now, what was your condition when you began with the medicine, Mr. Scott ? " ‘• I could not walk at all without the aid of a stick," was the reply. I never want a stick now ; but I carry one when I walk in the public street." "Really, this is quite an interesting case," remarked our representative. "Do you recollect, now, how soon latter taking these pills you experienced relief?" Oh, in a few days afterwards I could feel my limbs I gradually getting slack." "Just so ; and I suppose your suddenly improved health has been the c ause of much astonishment among your friends." • "It has, indeed, sir ; you see I work now in the rig- ger's loft of the Cunard Company, and I have shown the boxes of Dr. Williams' Pills to the men employed there." " I suppose you procured Dr. Williams' Pink Pills from some local chemist ? " " Yes, sir, I got them from Messrs. Bndden and Co., 193, Derby Road." " Very well, Mr. Scott," said his visitor, and he ter- minated the interview, after expressing his thanks for the information he had received, with a hearty adieu. ‘• This is rather a miraculous cure," mused the re- porter as he retraced his steps; " I wonder what the chemist would say to me." Messrs. Budden's premises were close by, he strolled into them, and finding the manager exceedingly courteous, he soon got into con- versation resp ecting Mr. Scott's case. " Oh, yes," said the manager in reply to a query. "I remember Mr. Scott coming here, leaning on his daugh- t.r's arm, and I sold him several boxes of Dr. Williams, Pink Pills for Pale People. They have made a wonder- ful change in him." "So I find ; and my object in drawing you into this conversation was to learn from you whether the story, as told to me, was in any way exaggerated. This does not appear to be the case, so I am satisfied." Well," returned the chemist, " I knew before he took the pills he bad very great difficulty in getting about even with the aid of a stick, but he can walk as well as anyone now."

The representative then withdrew and turned again into the busy street, and as he proceeded homewards formcl a determination to pursue his investigation still further or the morrow. The next morning, therefore, he set out to pay a visit to the riggers' loft belonging to the Cunard Steamship Company and situated at the West side of the Huskisson Dock, where he understood Mr. Scott was employed. With the aid of a few directions courteously given by the employes of this great firm,the reporter had little difficulty in finding his way to the loft, and opening the door at the head of a winding staircase he entered a spacious room stored with all kinds of ships' rope-tackle where a number of men.were busily at work. In a corner of this room he discovered Mr. Scott at work with two others. After a few minutes' conversation with him ,the newspaper man got about amongst the workmen and found many of them willing to converse. " I dropped in to see Mr. Sc..ott," said the reporter, "and find he is a good deal better." " Oh yes, sir, he's wonderfully better the last few weeks ; Dr. Williams' Pink Pills have set him up," said one old man, whilst a younger employo spoke of the medicine haying been shown to him by Mr. Scott, and all were willing to testify to the efficacy of the remark- able Pills which had set their comrade on his feet again. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills are a positive and unfailing cure for all diseases arising from an impoverished state of the blood, such as Ansemia, Pale and Sallow Complexion, Green Sickness, General Muscular Weakness, Depression of Spirits. Loss of Appetite, Palpitation of the Heart, Shortness of f3reath, Pain in the Back, Nervous Head- ache, Dizziness, Loss of Memory, Early Decay, all forms of Female Weakness, Hysteria, Paralysis, Locomotor Ataxy, Rheumatism and Sciatica; also for all diseases arising from Vitiated Humours in the Blood, which cause Scrofula, Rickets, Hip-joint Diseases, Chronic I Erysipelas, Consumption of the Bowels and Lungs, and that they Invigorate the Blood and System when broken down by overwork, worry, diseases, excesses and indis- cretion a living. These Pills are not a Purgative Medi- cine. They contain nothing that could injure the most delicate system. They act directly on the blood,supply- ing to the latter its life-giving qualities, by. assisting it to absorb oxygen, that great supporter of all organic life. In this way, the blood, becoming " built up," and being supplied with its lacking constituents, becomes rich and red, nourishes' the various organs, stimulating them to activity in the performance of their functions, and thus eliminating diseases from the system. These Pills are manufactured by the Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, of 46, Holborn Viaduct, London, England (and of Brockville, Ontario, Canada, and Schenectady, New York),and are sold only in boxes bears ing the fl.m's trade mark and wrappers at 2,. 9d. a box, or six boxes for 13s. 9d. Pamphlet free by post on application. Bear in mind that Dr. WiUiams' Pink Pills
' for Pale People are never 'sold in bnik, or by the dozen or hundred, and any de.ler who offers suhstitutes in this form is tr; big to defraud you, and should be avoided.

Dr. Williams' Pink rills may be had of all chemists, or direct by post from Dr. Williams' Medicine Company from the above address. The price at which these. pills are sold makes a course of treatment comparatively inexpensive as c,4npared with other remedies or medical treatment.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION BOWLING
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION BOWLING
ASSOCIATION.
PRESENTATION oF THE LEGIT CHALLENGE
CUP.

At the Legh Arms Hotel, Newton, on Saturday evening, the Hon. T. W. Legh, .M.P.,preseeited to the winning teem in the Legh challenge competition, the cup offered at the beginning of the season. Prior to the presentation, three members from each I club in the Newton division, met on the green of the Newton-le-Willows bowling club to play a friendly game. One side was captained by alr. J. Robinson of Golborne, and the other by Mr. T. Paireleugh in the absence of Mr. J. Liptrott. After a pleasant game, Mr. Pairelough's side won by 154 points for 112. At the close the company adjourned to the Legh Arms Hotel, where 74 sat dcwn to an excel- lently served knife and fork tea, which they thoroughly enjoyed. After the cloth had been removed, Mr. J. Robinson was voted to the chair, and he was supported by the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., Dr. Street, Dr Dobb, 'Messrs. J. Crompton, J. Bodmer, Sankey, Leycock, and Crompton, (secretary). After the toast of the " Queen' had been duly honoured, the Chairman gave the toast of " The president, the lion. T. W. Legh." In doing so he said he thought he might explain why they were met there that night. They were met to celebrate their first annual meeting of the Newton Division Bowl- ing Association, and he thought he ought to state how that association had its origin. It was a very singular thing, but the origin of the Association had its founda- tion from the very place where the cup was going to that night, North Ashton. (Applause.) He considered the credit was very largely due to them for what had turned out to be a very happy association, and the hearty man- ner in which they should drink the toast would show Mr. Legh that the giving of the cup had been a very great blessing to the working men in the district. (Hear. hear.) He thought the idea originated trom the members of the North Ashton club and Haydock, and the gentlemen who put the thing in shape was Mr. James Crompton jun. (Hear, bear.) Through his efforts, the association had been put into shape, and he thought it was one of the most successful associations in the county. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Crompton was successful in finding a gentle- man who was very ready to help forward any good movement, supported by workingmen and the best guarantee that they could give Mr. Legla, that he had done something good, was to show him that night that he had done something that they should be pleased to ask him to repeat on a later occasion. (Applause.) He thought he was right in saying that the North Ashton team had proved themselves heroes in the matter ; there had been a tremendous struggle to wrest the cup from them, but without success. He thought it was well understood that the association consisted of those clubs which were purely 'recreation clubs, purely self supporting, and not in csnnection with any public house. There were a good many bowl- ing clubs, which would have been glad to have the pleasure of entering the competition, but the Com- mittee had been obliged to debar them, and lift up bowl- ing socially. (Hear, hear.) One remarkable thing which had been brought out, and which would show Mr. Legh, that they were in earnest, and that was the growth of the members since the formation of the Association. He thought he was right in stating that there had been an increase of re embership in all the clubs of an average of 50 per cent., and that must show to Mr. Legh that the clubs had appreciated his generosity iii presenting the cup. (Applause.) He could speak for his own club at G'olborne which had increased something like 20. (Hear, hear.) The toast was then drunk with musical honours. The Hon. T. W. Legh, in responding to the toast, expressed his thanks for the kind mariner in which they had received the toast of his health. ' He desired to express his satisfaction at being there that night and at the same time, the pleasure, not unmingled with surprise with which he observed the success which had attended the some- what insignificant trophy. it only showed the healthy condition in which the game was, from which there was no pecuniary reward. He was glad to see that the curse of professionalism had not invaded the game of bowls. (Hear, hear.) Without knowing anything about the game, he thought he could take upon himself to assert that it was an excellent game; on account of its anti- quity he could take upon himself to assert that it was a conservative game. The game had existed for many centuries, but not only had it existed for a long time,but so far as he knew, it was played in meat portions of the earth, it was played in the old world and the new, and now that he thought of it, he was, only a short time ago, in a place where the inhabitants were so devoted to the game that they used to play bowls with the decapitated heads of their enemies. In this country we pride our- selves upon being more especially, the sportsmen of the whole universe. We claim that we are the greatest authority upon games of any nation on the face of the earth. The names of celebrated cricketers were, so to speak, household words in this country, people studied their exploits with an interest which in other countries was bestowed upon the public funds. He understood in this country in particular, prominent and skilful foot- ball players were regarded as demi-gods ; their utter- ances were treated with profound respect, and all round they received a great amount of reverence from people who were not acquainted with them. Even the doings of prize fighters were recorded with minuteness. He was quite sure of this fact, that there were many people in this country who would be more affected by the news that a Derby favou- rite had broken down, than that a distinguished Cabinet Minister had been seized with a fit of gout. (Laughter.) That kind of feeling might be carried too far, but there was an amount of good in it. Very few people in this life were fortunateenough to excel in anything, and the vast majority of us were obliged to put up with mediocrity. But supposing they did excel, and were experts in any game,there came a time when a man was obliged to give way to younger persons than himself. ghat being the case people as they got on in life tbey were obliged to give up those games which attracted the greatest amount of attention in this country. They Mild not go on 'playing football of' cricket for the best I port on of their life, they must give it up sooner or later, and must Iltid a satisfactory substitute, and the game of bowls was as good as any he knew of. (Hear, hear.) One of the best known statesmen in this country, said he strongly advised nobody to give up anything in the way of games he was advised it was a good thing to go on Playing games,as long as they could do it. Ha believed men were better for it. One thing was quite certain,if a man desired to be popular in this country he had to excel in games, and although he did not offer sugges- tions, he could not help thinking tkat a person who was distinguished in the athletic world, would stand a much better chance of being returned for many constituences I than people who were better informed in other matters. I (Laughter.) He would now proceed to discharge the duty for which he rose, to present the cup to the winning team. He would re-echo the congratulations of Mr. Robinson upon the fact that the cup had found its way into the possession of those who were responsible for the starting of the idea. He congratulated them upon the idea, and he trusted in future years, the same interest would be taken in the competition. (Applause.) He then handed thecup to Mr. Crompton, president of the North Ashton club. The cup bore the following inscrip- tion," Challenge Cup presented to the Recreation bowl- ing clubs in the Newton Division by the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., 1892." Mr. Crompton in accepting the cup said they had a vast amount of pleasure in receiving from their president that most valuable and beautiful cup, which had been honourably and deservedly won by his team, North Ashton. He believed every other member of every club in the division admitted that they had won ie honestly and fairly.. He could say that every mem- ber of their club had done his utmost to achieve that object, and their work had not been in vain. (Hear, hear.) By strict perseverance and steady practice they , were able to overcome all the various clubs in the dis- trict, and secure a greater number of marks than any I other club. As president of the North A.hton club, he felt as delighted that they had won it, as any member of the teats, and he hoped next year they would be able to rise to the same position as they now held. (Applause) Mr. Legh then presented a silver medal, to each member of the winning team, viz.,--Messrs. Welsby (captain), J. Welsby, T. Shaw sen., T. Shaw jun., 'l'. Taylor, G. Davies' G. Shaw; J. Arkwright, E. Ilazleden, J. Lewe, John Lowe, James Shaw, Wm. Shaw, John Shaw jun., Wm. Shaw jun., T. Adamson. The other toasts which' were appropriately honoured, were "The vice-presi- dents,"." The chairman of the committee" "'File win- ning team," and "The Secretary." Several songs Rsc., were given during the evening and at the close a vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Legh for his presence.

The Railway Workers' Conference at Derby decided on Wednesday to empower any branch to establish a benevolent fund for the exclusive advantage of its members. A suggested new clause in the rules provid- ing for arbitration was rejected.

THE COAL TRADE CRISIS.
MEETING AT fIAYDOCK.

About 4,000 miners attended a meeting held on the Hay dock football field on Monday, to consider the pro- posal of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. fora 15 per cent. reduction. Mr. E. Briscoe presided. Mr. John Norcross proposed, and Mr. Bailey seconded, the following resolution, which was unanimously car- ried :—" That this meeting is of opinion that our wages previous to our being locked out were quite low enough, and we hereby pledge ourselves to remain out on strike until our employers allow us to return to work at the old rate of wages. Also we tender our unabated confidence in our leaders' action during the struggle." Mr. E. Walkden, district secretary of the Ashton and Haydock district, who was the principle speaker, said during the past nine or ten days there had been a remark- able change in public opinion. At the Garswood Hall Collieries the proprietors said the men could resume woik at 10 per cent, reduction, and at Messrs. Richard Evans they could resume work at 15 per cent, reduction, but the men must honestly understa•od that it only meant 10 per cent. He would like to ask the employers whether the last 10 per cent, advance was a 15 per cent. (laugh- ter), and how they made a 10 and a 5 per cent, into only alO per cent. reduction. The employers thought the Havdock miners were fools, but he was inclined to think they were mistaken, (a Voice: "They are.") He would mention an incident of a remarkable deputation that waited on Messrs. Evans on Friday. Notes were taken of the deliberations by one from the masters and one from the men. He took them on the men's side._ Pra.c-

tically nothing came of the interview, hut Mr. Grimke Drayton (the managing director) made statements which were incorrect, or he would have allowed them to be put before the public. At the dose of the interview, Mr. Drayton asked that his (Mr. Walken's) notes should be torn up, and this was done providing that the employers' man tore his notes up. Why, he asked, were not the deliberations made public? In conclusion he argued that the mines and railways should be nationalised.
THE SURFACE COAL-GETTING AT ST. HELENS.

div.head: POLICE INTERFERENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTERFERENCE.

An extraordinary scene was witnessed in connection with the surface coal-getting on Ilardshaw Fields, St. Helens, on Monday afternoon. Many shafts had been gunk to depths varying from twenty to fifty feet, and colliers have sent up large quantities of coal, which have been sold and carried away. The agent of the estate• visited the place on Monday,and had a long conversation with Chief Constable Wood,the result being that at four o'clock Mr. IVood and half a dozen officers in uniform appeared on the fields and warned every man that if lie was found getting any more coal he would be locked up. Thousands of men, women, and children were on the ground,and swarmed nkund the police so that their pro- gress was rendered difficult. We understand that vigo- rous proceedings will be taken if this coal-getting is not discontinued. Mr. Thos. Glover, .T.P., miners' agent, visited the place, and counselled the coal-getters to dis- continue the practice. RIO rING AT ST. HELENS.

The coal strike at St. Helens culminated in rioting on Tuesday afternoon, in the course of .which considerable damage was done and several persons received serious injuries. A mass meeting of miners was held at Ashton Green, near the collieries of Messrs. Bromilow, Foster, and Co. It was stated that several men were working down the pit, but Mr. Thomas Glover, the miners' agent, said there were only eight men and two boys engaged clearing out water from the pit. Ile earnestly appealed to the men to refrain from committing a breach of the peace, and a resolution was unanimously carried to remain out on strike unless the masters conceded the old rate of wages. Riotous scenes followed the meeting. A crowd invaded the colliery yard, and swarmed over the pit brows and thronged the top of the shalt. They yelled and hooted, and the first man who stepped from the cage received a gash on the head, and blood flowed profusely. Four other men were battered with sticks and stones about the head. A desperate effort was made to throw two of them into the colliery reservoir, but a force of twenty-five constables under Chief Const.ble Wood ap- peared on the scene and prevented this being done. The under manager, named Briscoe, oncoming up the shaft was beaten about the head and body with bludgeons, and kicked through the colliery yard. The police at- tempted to rescue him, but the crowd turned on the officers, who drew their staves and charged the mob. At this time the mob crowded on the banks lining the road- way and delivered a tremendous.shower of bricks and heavy stones at the officers below. The policemen were scattered, and were all mote or less injured. They were utterly powerless to cope with their assailants, and several of the officers fell to the ground severely injured. Two of the constables, named Rigby and Wilkes, were carried away unconscious with severe wounds on their heads, and Police Constable Mercer was removed with his left leg badly smashed. On the police making an effort to march back towards the town they were again assailed with bricks and stones, and had to fly. Police Constable Wilkes had 1-ieen removed to the colliery offices, ad the crowd riddled the windows of the build- ings with bricks and stenes. The constables were ulti- mately driven to seek refuge in the White Lion public- house, and the mob surrounded this place and smashed some of the windows. The neighbourhood was greatly excited, and renewed disturbances were feared. The colliery proprietors and their officials emphatically deny that any men were engaged in coal getting, and state that they had only a dozen men in two pits clearing out water which was flooding the workings. ,

div.head: SOME COALOWNERS STILL OBDURATE.
div.p: SOME COALOWNERS STILL OBDURATE.

The members of the Coal owners'Federation met in Man- chester on Wednesday to decide upon further action with regard to the coal stoppage. l'ilr.A.M.Chambers presided at the conference, which was private. The decision of the men not to return to work except at the old rate of wages was discussed, and the coalowners passed a series of re- solutions. They were willing to meet the men to en- deavour to find a reasonable method of bringing the dis- pute to a close' but could not entertain the proposal of the miners that the pits sh .uld be re-opened at the old rate of wages. They confirmed the resolution that the men might go into the workings at a reduction of 15 per cent, of the advance given. They were also prepared to agree that the reduction should not be taken on either side as a final settlement, and to submit the whole ques- tion of reduction er no reduction to a committee formed of owners' and miners' delegates, with an independent chairman.
SERIOUS RIOTING- AT HAYDOCK.
CONFLICT BETWEEN MINERS AND POLICE.

- - - - At Haydock, where Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. have a large number of pits,serious 'intim, took place on Wednesday afternoon. the scenes,whicewere exciting, occurred round the Wood pit, in which a disastrous ex- plosion took place fifteen years ago. For Same time past it has been freely rumoured that a large number of " knobsticks" were engaged in the pit,and that, coal waa being wound to the surface during the night. Frequent I visits have been paid to the shaft by colliers for the pur- pose of ascertaining whether this was true or net,but in spite of the repeated assertions of the offiCials that no men were engaged,the colliers still seemed to think they were being deceived. On Monday notices were posted that the men could resume work at a reduction of 15 per cent., but the men refused to accept these terms. Later in the day it was rumoured that abuut eighty men had gone to work at the reduction, and this so exasperated the miners that they threatened the" knobsticks. ' Seve- ral men who were engaged in the pit were warned, but they took no notice and continued to descend the work- ings. The help of the rioters at Ashton's Green was soli- cited, and upwards of 500 men marched in a body from Parr to Haydock during the afternoon. This force was augmented by an equal number from Haydock and the surrounding district. The colliery officials,however,had been informed of the impending attack, and they sought the aid of the police. A large force was immediately drafted into the district, and by two o'clock there were 150 foot police and 15 mounted men armed with sabres. The officers in charge of this force were Inspector Smith, of Manchester ; Inspector Pickering. Wootton ; and In- spector Kelly, EarlestOwn ; with Superintendent fliggin- bottom, of Leigh. Tne police were all drawn up in the colliery yard out of sight, and about fifty were held in reserve in a building close by. The colliery officials pre- sent were Mr. E. J. George (secretary), Mr. J. Robinson (manager), Mr. Lathein traffic manager), Mr. Stewart, and Mr. Bell. The detachment of colliers from Parr, arriving near the private line of the firm, surrounded some houses abutting on the line in search of a "knob- stick," and not finding their man they wrecked the house in which he lodged. The police interfered, but were powerless against such a crowd. The mob then made their way over the fields in the. direction of the Wood pit, at which a large crowd had al- ready gathered. On arriving there the police advised the men to go away, but they refused, and demanded that the men employed below should be brought up to the surface. rhey then swarmed up the banks and round ' the workings, and Mr. George, addressing them, said there were no men down except officials of the firm and firemen. This statement was received with a groan of disapproval, and the mob asked that a deputation of six men be allowed to decend the shaft to satisfy themselves upon the point. This Mr. George refused to allow, and his refusal was received with groans. Two waggonette- leads ot police now drove up to the pit, and their approach was the signal for an outbreak of hostilities. The mob who swarmed on each side of the road show- ered stones upon the officers, and when they alighted a perfect hail of missiles assailed them. Many of the police were struck. The attack became so lan that they had to retaliate, and they turned and charged the mob with their batons. They could not make much headway and the mounted men were called out. The latter charged the mob at the gallop, scattering them in all directions, but those behind the hedges stoned the officers as they passed, one constable being badly wounded with a stone. The police cleared the road,and the crowd climbed the fences into the fields. Those assembled about the workings now received the atten- tion of the police, and the order being given to clear the banks, the police charged, mad with the assistance of the horsemen chased the mob in all directions, and a very large number received some nasty blows from the batons. Several had their heads cracked, and one or two were knocked insensible. The police after chasing the rioters a distance of a quarter of a mile returned to the pit. The mob reassembled at Newton Common, and

threatened, With the aid of reinforcement. to renew the I disturbances on Thursday. The police, however, are in such strong force that it is not expected they will revisit workings. A MINERS' HOUSE WRECKED AT EILACKBROOK. Another serious disturbance took place at Haydock on Wednesday. Some hundreds of men, after being dis- persed at the Wood pit, made their way to Blackbrook, a subrub of Flaydock, where Robert Day,one of the engine- men working atWood pit, resides with his wife and six children. His house was surrounded and showers of stones rained upc,n it. Every window in the building, back and front, was smashed, and stones were thrown into the house, damaging furniture and fittings. The police were summoned, and fifty constables on foot and a force of niounted officers, cleared the street with diffi- culty. Some stones were thrown at the officers who re- mained in the neighbourhosd. When the main body of officers marched back to their stat:on the crowd again surrounded the house and resumed stone-throwing. At the time of telegraphing, some thousands of people sur- round the house, which is practically a wreck, and as the stones crash through the window-spaces into tho room loud cheers are raised. The few police present are utterly unable to quell the disturbance. It is stated that Day and his family are inside the building hiding from the attack.
CHARGE AGAINST BURTONWOOD COLLIERS. A SCRUPULOUS MAGISTRATE.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day before Messrs. G. Comber (chairman), and J. is Sleekly, Wm- Swan, John Quinn, and Matthew Weir,all colliers, of Collins Green, were charged with committing damage in Burtonw )od, on the 28th Sept., to a cart, the property of Wm. Prescot tof Burtonwood. The case had evidently aroused great interest among the colliers in the Burtonwood and Collins Green district, as the court room was crowded with them. Mr. P. Davies appeared for Mr. Prescott, and the Collins Green Colliery Co., and Mr. H. L. Riley for the defendant. Mr. Davies said that as everyone knew, the colliers were now on strike, the Collins Green men of course among the rest. At about six o'clock on the evening of September 28th, William Prescott's boy who was about 15 years of age, was engaged taking some coal from the Collins Green colliery to SOMA brick works. He was met on the high road by the three defendants who without speaking a word,went to the cart, and Swan deliberately pulled the " kecker " out of the cart. The other men then lifted up the cart, the body of which tell to the ground. The horse was going at the time, and the consequence was that the back of the cart was broken in two places: The hinges were also broken as also were the sides of the cart. Under the Act of Parliament, they were not allowed to ask for a penalty of more than £5, although the damage to the cart was .£l2 10s. In addition to this damage,the bit in the horses mouth was pulled tight owing to the fall of the cb.rt, and its tongue was cut through, the result being that it could eat nothing for a week.—Mr. Blackly here interrupted and said that he was a director of the colliery, and as this rase involved the question of the colliers strike, his impartiality might be impugned He thought therefore that this case might with fair rea- son be adjourned,unless it covld be postponed for an hour to see if another magistrate cauld be procured. Had he - known that the case was coming on, he would have taken objection before.—Mr. Davies thought it a proper course to take.—Mr. Riley said that the intimation came to him as a surprise as he was quite ignorant that his worship had had any connection with any colliery com- pany. He however, did not think that it should pre- vent the case going on.—The magistrates retired and on returning they said they had decided to adjourn the case until that day fortnight. REOPENING OF PITS ON THE OLD TERMS.

It is announced that the Sirley Pt a of the Sheffield Coal Company were re-opened on Thursday morning on the old terms. These collieries employ 2,300 men,and are among the most', important in South Yorkshire. Alderman Gainsford, the managing director, in an inter- view on Wednesday night, said that in his opinion the owners made a fatal *mistake at Derby in not accepting the Mayors' compromise. He believes the best plan now is for the owners to accept the proposals of the Miners' Federation, and immeniately after the resumption of work establish a board of conciliation, which might be made exceedingly valuable. A LONDON SYMPATHISER.

Mr. S. Woods, M.P., has received a letter from Mr. Ralph 1 hicknesse, of Abchurch-lane, London. who writes: —I have been following with intense and painful interest the long struggle which you are conducting so ably on behalf of the miners,and sent you a telegram on Thursday congratulating you, on the collapse of the owners in the Midlands, and what I believe to be the coming victory of the men all round. I fully recognise, however, that the struggle is not yet over, and I shall be glad to send you tel. per week until the men of the Wigan distric' are hack at work again. I enclose £5 for the first five weeks from to-day, whether a settlement is come to or not in the meanwhile. Please use that money exactly as you think best. lam very glad that so many people are coming forward to help the women and children,but with me it is a matter of principle,and I feel with all my heart for the men who are fighting in a righteous cause. I should be glad if the money were used in the way you think hest to secure victory. Ido cot envy those owners who ha,vo made a profit or who have hoped to make a profit out of this business. If the ring leaders could be compelled to keep their pits idle six months after everybody else had been working I should be delighted. DURHAM MEN REFUSING TO FILL YORKSHIRE TRUCKS. The fillers an other off-hand men of the Usworth Colliery Company,Durham have refused to fill Yorkshire trucks with coals, and in consequence work at the pit has been stopped.

div.head: ILLNESS OF MR. T. GLOVER.
div.p: ILLNESS OF MR. T. GLOVER.

On Tuesday afternoon, while addressing the meeting at Ashton's Green, St. Helens, Mr. T. Glover, J.P., miners; agent, contracted a cold, and by order of Dr. Fourquemin, who was called in on Wednesday night, he was confined to the house yesterday. Last night Mr. Glover's condition hid improved, and he hopes to resume his duties in a d ty or two. THE BAMFURLONG PITS.

The Press Association's Golborne correspondent tele- graphs that contrary to- expec'ation the directors of Messrs. Cross, ToVey, and C0.,0f Bamfurlong, on Thurs- day eveninz filially decided to re-open their collieries at the old rate of wages. The decision has caused great rejoicing, the firm employing 2,001 men. Other firms are expected to follow. MR. S. WOODS, M.P., AND TIIE RIOTING AT HAY DOCK.

1 ' Mr. S. Woods, M.P., miners' agent for the Ashton and Hayclock district, who is confined to his house under medical orders, on Thursday, sent the following tele- gram to Mr. John Turner, miners' secretary, at flay. dock :—" Deeply regret rioting on Thursday at Wood pit. Do tell them from me they are damaging our cause. Employers are responsible by opening their pits and encouraging knobsticks. This contemptible move of theirs ought to receive the condemnation of every respectable citizen. Ask the men from me to be peace- able in the face of this inhuman treatment at the hands of the coalowners. Our best interests are being served by being peaceable.—Sam Woods."

div.head: KILLING OF YORKSHIRE MINERS.
div.p: THE KILLING OF YORKSHIRE MINERS.

The Commission appointed by the Home Secretary to inquire into the,recent colliery riot at Featherstone, in the course of which two men were fatally wounded by the military, was begun at Wakefield on Thursday. Lord Bowen, the preshient, indicated the scope of the inquiry and stated that while they were glad to see counsel pre- sent, the Commissioners proposed to. reserve to them- selves, as a rule, the entire examination .of witnesses. Subsequently. Lord Bowen and his fellow-commissioners, Mr. Haldane, Q.C., M.P., and Sir Albert RoRR, M.P., visited the locality of the riot.
GOLBORNE.-TFIREATENED ATTACK ON A MANAGER'S MANSION.

Owing to the disturbance on the previous day no work was carried on on Thursday in the Edge Green and Gol- borne Collieries belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and CO. During the day a large number of colliers were standing in the streets, and a resolute determination was expressed by the men not; to resume work at a reduction in the wages. The police received information in the course of the afternoon that. a mob was on its way to Golborne Park, the residence of the managing director of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Limited. This gentleman is away on business ist the present time, and on receipt of the information at flaydock, Inspector Pickering at once left for Golhorne Park with between I thirty and forty constables. On arriving at time park the officers found that about 1,000 colliers were in the grounds marching t-mwards the house. The police went ihrough the drive to the house,and finding all safe there ordered the men to leave the park. Many of the men on seeing the police retired of their own accord, and the remainder were driven out of the place by the cons- tables. Once outside the park the mob began to gradu- ally disperse,and finding everything very quiet the police returned to Ilaydock at half-past five o'clock.

SEQUEL TO A "BACK CaRDEN PARTY" AT NEWTON.
A SCENE BY CANDLELIGHT.

A case which attracted to the court a large num- ber of interested persons was heard at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday. A young man named John Brown was charged with assaulting William iluest, of Bridge-street. Newton, on the 9th inst. Prosecutor, a little, aged man, was asked by the clerk if his name was Brown, to which he indig- nantly replied' Nay, nay, my friend, there's starry a Brown abart me." He was then asked to state his ease. Be did so. He said about a quarter past eleven at night he heard a noise in his back garden, so begot up and lighted a candle and then, he said "I went to Harry, the young man that lives with me. I said Wakken up; there's a boggart in the yard. Harry said.—The Clerk: You must not tell us what he said."—Prosecutor, not understanding: "Harry said—he said, oh ! what did he say ! He said—." The 'Clerk : "You must only tell us what you did in consequence of what he said." Prosecutor then continued and said he and the young man went down into the back garden with the candle. They saw %own. Be said to Hurst "Do you say I planted your timber ?" be- cause the prosecutor had-complained about his timber being stolen. " No," the prosecutor replied. " I never said you took the timber—but its gooing all the same, and you live next to it." Then Brown, to use Ilurst's expressive words " Met me with his fist and copped 01113 in the face, and knocked me hack'ards flying." Defen- dant and prosecutor now harangued as to the timber which defendant was alleged to have been in the act of taking. Defendant said it was simply 'a stump which formed part of the fence between his garden and the prosecutor's. Upon being asked to explain this, prose— cutor entered upon a narration about a pony he once had, which some one described as having a stump tail, like banana, a glide in one eye, and a rambling disposition, which caused it to be constantly taking nocturnal walks from the stable. Owing to this latter proclivity fOrr wandering, the prosecutor had erected a post in the garden, to which he tethered the animal, and which in its lucid moments, frequently stood by for I shelter. He alleged that defendant was in the act of stealing this stump, when the astault was committed. Another harangue took place now, and the prosecutor to emphasise his utterances, punctuated each word with a "cut at the air " with the testament upon which he had been swearing. The Book frequently hovered over the Clerk's head, like a" descending sword of retribution," but the Clerk did not like the classical position of a Nemesis' victim, so after a considerable amount of trouble theyrosecutor was persuaded to give up the Book. The defendant stated that he did not strike the prosecutor. He said they were both struggling for the stump, each pulling against the other. The defendant released his hold suddenly with the result that the stump "hanged " against prosecutor's face, and knocked him down. Defendant called his witnesses. Our ot ',hem had seen the occurrence as described by Brown, but he was outside the garden and had seen everything by the light of the candle. Another nitness, when called promptly said "I don't know anything about it "and left,whilst another ingenuous person, who came to swear that defendant did not commit the assault was dis- suaded from his purpose, because he said "I'm pretty sure he didn't do it. I seed him about half an hour be- the row, and he didn't seem up te anything." The Bench thought defendant had errnmittPd a cowardly as- sault on an old man, and fined him £1 and costs.

div.head: EXPLOSION' IN A BF. HELENS COLLIE ItY, EIGHT MEN TNAIRED.
div.p: EXPLOSION' IN A BF. HELENS COLLIE ItY, EIGHT MEN TNAIRED.

About four o'clock on Saturday morning an ex- plosion occurred in a new shaft which is being sunk at the Lea Green and Sutton Heath Collieries. St. Helens. During the sinking operations the men passed through a seam of coal, which is sup- posed to have given off a small quantity of gas. Eight men were at work on a platform a few yards above the coal bricking round the shaft, when an explosion occurred, burning the whole of them severely about the arms and face. As quickly as, possible the men were drawn to the top, where' Sergeant Small, three constables and others rendered • first aid, and the men were sent in cabs to the Cot- tage Hospital, where Dr. Jackson attended thee. It is supposed that the gas from the seam of coal came up the shaft, and was fired a'.; the lighteby I which the men were working. The names of the eight injured men are Henry Francis married, inspector of the work, employed by the colliery company, and the others, employed by Mr. Piggott, con- tractor, are James Rigby, married, 'Matto Heath; James. Riley, of Billinge, single ; Joseph Ediv, ef Swansea. married ; Dennis Dowd, ingle, 'Matto Heath ; Michael Flynn, single, Brook-street, St. lielen. ; Evan Jones. widower, Sutton ; and William James, married, Thatto J3eath. rue pit tahltft has been sunk 420 yards, and the

, platform was twenty yards from the bottom. Dr. Jackson states that the men are all badly burnt on the arms, hands, faces and necks, the parts which were ex- posed while working, their bodies being protected by the woollen shirts and other clothing they were wearing. Each man has similar injuries. and although Dr. Jackson does not anticipate fatal results, the injuries are very serious. Our correspondent visited the St. Helens Cottage Hospital, and found that the influx of eight patients had caused consiaerable inconvenience and re-arrange- ment of other patients in their beds. The statement made by several of the men sutnmarises it as follows: We descended the shaft at ten o'clock, and should in the ordinary way have finished at six on Saturday inorniue. We ascended at 2.20 for a snap of something to eat, and went down again at 2 50. ,We were working round the shaft breaking up, At four o'clock we heard a loud re- port which s4ook our scaffolding and knocked us down. We were immediately enveloped in flames, and in a few seconds afterwards another smaller report took place,and more fire ascended. We were among the fire for abou: a minute and then it disfppeared up the shaft. Half a dozen men were working at the top, and they were very much shaken by the explosion. The timekeeper, William Lloyd, came down in the hoppet, and we were brought to the surface. We were working with naked candles on the scaffold. We had gone through a seam of coal eft. thick in sinking. It further transpires that William Lloyd hail a narrow escape of being injured, he having just ascimded before the explosion took place. The men were stupified by the effects of the afterdamp, and one or two of them appearod to be in a dying state. Whether the gas came up and caught the naked lights or whether one of the candles fell into the gas is not yet known. The force of the explosion was so great that a hoppet of mortar was overturned at the trp, but none of the men were injured by it.

div.head: GAMBLE INbTITUTE, ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE GAMBLE INbTITUTE, ST. HELENS.

On Wednesday the plans tor the new Gamble In.- stute, St.. Ilelens,were placed in the Assembly-room at the Town Hall, for public inspection. The first prize of £l.OO had been awarded to a set of designs by Messrs. Willoughby and Wood Miuse,of Manches- ter. They show a building of four storeys • with basement and tower. The main entrance to the public library is under the tower at the corner of Ilardshaw-st., and Corporation-st., while the main entrance to the technical schools is in liardshaw- st., and near flickerstaffo-st. In the basement there are library stores, plumbers' room, builders' room, metallurgical room and storeroom. On the ground floor there are entrance halls,a general reading-room 89ft. by 313! t., ladies' reading-room 3131 t. by 221 t-. boys' reading-room Mr. by 23Ft., and reference library and reading-room. Workingmen THE greatest hypocrisy in the and the politics of the present day is the Veto Bill, cry raised by the Tory party in regard to the" workingman's beer." As a matter of fact the cry that is raised in this connection is

not on behalf of those who buy beer but on behalf of those who sell it. It is raised by and for the benefit of men who are making great fortunes out. of a huge and injurious monopoly. These chair' pions of the big brewers have been particularlY loud in their denunciations since the Veto Bill was brought in by the present Government. Their seal in defending what they are pleased to call the "liberties of the workingman " would have been admirable were it not inspired by motives 10°1 are purely selfish. Fortunately workingrnea are sufficiently articulate in these days to make lonsvn themselves what are their real wants and feelingg The declaration which has been issued on theit behalf this week with regard to the Local Veto is in the highest degree interesting and vaiii/ibletlJla. MCDONALD, Thar WOODS, M.P., and Joszrsi ARCH, M.P. - following passage should be read and pondered bf - every workingman : the " The present Parliament is unquestionahlY most democratic Parliament that has ever elected, and the present Government in bring 7, in the Liquor Traffic (Local Control) Bill, is eiraPof endeavouring to bring about a further extensioniao popular rights. Tho control of the liquor rra!'ill, (a matter closely concerning the domestic, financial, and political well-being of the w°/1/IrTs classes), has hitherto been in the hands of to classes. The Government propose to ineke,drol masses the masters of the situation. The o°- rr of the liquor traffic by the classes has hitherto of sulted in the impoverishment and degradation .1,, the working people and the enrichment cf the;r, ready rich property owners and great liquor ea° bo polists. So long 8:01 as the days of Queen Elizabeth,the licensing under the control of a class, was seen by ene,7l as of popular power to be capable of being 80,1:1S-vvete to impoverish, debase, and weaken those Nvu° er then called the " meaner sort." Thus,in the tic MSS. of Elizabeth's reign (vol. i., AD. found a letter from a certain nobleman to the !nog Cecil, Secretary ot State, from which the follot ig is an extract :—" The wealth of the meaner s°'bor the very summit of rebellion, the occasion insolence, of the contempt of the nobility. Ir '-wers be cured by providing, as it were, of some Be-riey or channels to draw or suck from them their by subtle and indirect means, to be handled Wor. sibly." The latter describes with wonderful anafr acy the actual effects of the traffic as carried 00 to day. The rls, is absolutely and completely in their own he°, We. therefore, being strongly convinced 037,9 0,. theL Veto Bill would confer on the industrial cie9;,-,orl this country a measure of legitimate and neee'ri itr power to deal with a matter which directlY•an urge titnately concerns their own dearest interestet„ndo every working man and all true and earnest fig:loV of the working classes in the country to gire" warm and energetic support to this bill, aucl_; ,"",,ory mand that the Legislature stiall,without delay r it into law."

WIDNES LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of this cornimite was held on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. J. Morrison presiding, Mere were also present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Councillors H. li. Shores and O'Donnell, Messrs. J. H. Lee and W. Sadler. The librarian reported that the attendance in the reading room for September was 15,730, daily average 605, against an average of 509 in the corresponding montn of 1892. During the same period 5,392 books had been con- sulted, being an increase of 623 in the lending depart- ment, and 40 in the reference department. If you want your WATCH EIPAIRED by skilled workmen take it to PRITCHARD'S. Adel. ALLEGED WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court on Monday, William Hallam, Manchester, was brought up under a warrant, charged with failing to keep up payments for the maintenance of ' his wife, under an order made under the Married Women's Maintenance Act. —Defendant admitted the debt, but said be could not pay, as he had been out of work for ten weeks.—The police had found that this statement was correct. —The case was adjmirned until November 25th, in order to allow defendant to pay the arrears if possible. Defendant was allowed out on his own recognizances of LS. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTPI. The usual monthly meeting was held on Tuesday even- ing, Mr. William Handley in the chair. There were aim present Messrs. Sowerby, Grice, Taylor and Riley. The Librarian reported that during the month of Septet-lila-a% 1,820 books had been issued, being an increase of 19 en the corresponding month last year, being 20 theology, 11 philosophy,7s science and art, 96 history,bioeraphy and travel, 11 poetry, 1,389 prose fiction, and 218 miscellane- ous literature, h was recommended that the new ladies' magazine" The Woman at Home," and the "Strand Magazine" be taken for the reading room. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN. The series of " people's services" which were SO Suc- cessful last winter, are to be repeated during the present teason. The first was held on Sunday evening, when there was a large congregation in the sacred edifice and heartily joined in the singing. The choir sang the an- them " 0 taste and see," and Mr. C. Le Couteur. the organist. played " Gloria" with much effect. A solo entitled " Where is the Nazerene," tl,.e words of which are composed by a member of the church and the music by Mr. Le Couteur was ably rendered by Miss Heatherington. The words and music were much sp- , predated. The Rev. J. Simpson delivered a brief ad- dress on Hire's song '• A man's a man for a' that." EXTRAORDINARY ACCIDENT TO A SHIP CANAL MAIL TRAIN. An accident which might have been attended by serious logs of life occurred on the Manchester Ship Canal rail- way on Wednesday morning, The mail train which con- veys workmen from Runcorn to Acton Grange, started as usual shortly before six o'clock from the Old Quay, with between 200 and 300 men. After proceeding along the lino about a mile it was found that a pair of points which ought to have been closed were open. The men in charge of the train exerted all their power and resources to bring the train to a standstill. The trucks were also disconnected from the engine and the wheels spraggecl. The engine however could not be brought up, and ran off the rails attire points and almost went down the embankment into the Canal cutting ; and it was clear.that but for the prompt measures taken,tbat many of the numerous passengers must have met with an un- timely end. SHOCKING FATALITY TO A WIDNES WORKMAN. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner held an inquest at Widnes Police Court on Monday afternoon touching the dPath of Richard Henry Evans aged 52 years, of Princess-street, , which occurred in the Accident Hospital on Friday. It appeared that the deceased was a slater employed at flutchinson's Works of the United Alkali Company and on Monday morning the 9th inst,he was removing a bad slate from the roof of the mortar mill house. He was standing with one foot on the ladder and another on the spout, and was attempting to dislodge the slate with his hammer, when the latter slipped and he fell backwards to the ground below, a distance of 16 feet. He was seriously injured. In conversati•a with his son Mr George Evans, the deceased had said he attached no blame to anyone.—The jury returned a verdict of "acci- dental death."—Mr. W. L. div.p: THE EN MINE?, SATURDAY. OCTOBER '2l. 1893.

WIDNES RELIEF Commirrait. The weekly meeting of the committee for the relief of the distress in Widnes caused through the colliers' dispute, was held at Whines Town Hall, on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. Frei Neil. The Chairman announced that the Widnes Subscription Band and Mr. Ed. Grime were giving a concert in aid of the fund in the Alexandra Theatre on Sunday night, and Mr. Keddie was allowing the use of the theatre free. The thanks of the committee were lecorded. The chairman further stated that the ' total income for the present week was £l7O, and the expenditure £220. There was still a balance of £220 in the bank, and 'under present ciremnstances this would he sufficient for another month. He was glad to see that the catering co mniittee, without diminishing the relief, had rediuiad the expenditure during the past week by nearly £2O. It was reported that some of the works which had stopped their subscriptions last week through a mistaken idea that the affair would be at an end, had resumed their payments, The family of Mrs. Deacon : had doubled their subscription, and Mr.H. Wade-Deacon had increased his contribution ft om £1 to £4 per week; and Messrs. Greenall had doubled their subscription of £5. The fund was considered in a satisfactory position, and it was decided to continue the relief as usual. UNION OF LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE INSTITUTES. A- meeting of delegates of this union was held at North wich on Tuesday under the presidency of Dr. (Alderman) Hewitt. The delegates from War- rington were Mr. C. Madeley, chairman, and Coun- cillor J. Shaw Green.

FATAL ACCIDENT. A labourer at IV ilderapool Brewery, named William Collins, 43 years of age, and residing at 7, Gas-street, died at the Warrington Infirmary at 11 o'clock on Tuesday morning. It appears that on Monday the deceased went to his sister-in-law at 69, Bank-street, and whilst crossing the kitchen floor, he caught his clog in a loose tile, which threw him to the ground, breaking his leg above the ankle. He was taken to the Infirmary shortly afterwards, and attended to by Dr. Bowden, The deceased had been a heavy drinker, and after his admittance to the Infirmary, he suffered from delirium tremens and inflammati‘m of the lungs. An inquest was held at the Infirmary yesterday morning, touching the death of the deceased,by Mr. Jones, deputy coroner. Evidence was given by Nurse Roberts, Mrs. Mary Collins. and Mrs. Burke, bearing out the above account. A verdict in ac- cordance with the medical evidence " that the deceased died from delirium tremens and inflamma- tion of the lungs" was returned.. BILICK-ST. MISSION BAND OF HOPE SOCIETY. The first of the winter series of entertainments was held in the Mission Room, Crossley-st., on Tuesday evening,under the presidency of Miss Bessie Dutton, who, in the course of a stirring and feeling address, strongly advocated the principles of total abstin- ence. There was a very large attendance. The pro- gramme (which was provided by the female mem- bers) proved to be a very enjoyable one; and re- flected great credit on their catering. Recitations were given by Misses E. Grundy, L. Jackson, 11. Shaw, P. Massey, L. Lewis, A. llill, and Messrs. P. Massey, S. Gallop, and J. Shaw. A reading was given by Miss B. Dutton which was very much ap- preciated. Solos were sung by Misses E. Gallop, A. Warburton, and A. Holt. The following dialogues were ably_ gone through, viz., "Ten Band of Hope Boys," 'rile Woman's Rights Association," and "One good turn deserves another." The rieibilit les of the audience were roused by the rendering of a sketch, Entitled, " Call John,' by Misses M. Atherton, A. Warburton, and Messrs. 11. Lightfoot and William Barton. A vote of thanks was tendered to Miss Dutton, and ably responded to. The singing of the doxology brought a pleasant evening to a close. The juvenile section of the society now numbers 180 members. An adult temperance society has also been formed, and already 70 members have been enrolled,

div.head: "WILLIAM OF WYKEHAM."
div.p: "WILLIAM OF WYKEHAM."

- At the first meeting, in the Museum bec.ure Room ou Monday, of the session of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Soc'ety, the president (Rev. L. J. T. Darwell) re - d a paper on " William of Wykeham " Mr. Robert Davies occupied the chair. The essayist gave a short biographical sketch of W ykeham, wtio was born in 13'24, at Wickham in Hampshire, and by his boyish cleverness soon attracted the notice of the lord of the manor, who educated him. Alter going through the University he first became secre- tary to his patron, and afterwards chaplain to Edward 111. At one time he acted as surveyor to the King, and he advised several changes at Windsor Castle. He came in time to be keeper of the Privy Seal and King's secretary. The black death was decimating the clergy, and as fast as vacancies occurred at cathedrals or collegiate churches where the King had the presentation they were filled by Wykeham's appointmeni to them. And over and above all, he was made Archdeacon of Lincoln. On the death of Bishop Bdington of Winchester. Wykellam was appointed to the see, and set about restoring the cathedral. The essayist alluded to Wykeham,s work in the restoration of the cathedral, and in founding colleges at Oxford ard Winchester for the practical 'efficiency of the church, which his wealth enabled him to carry out, A vote of thanks was passed to the Rev. L. T. T. Darwell for his paper, on the motion of Mr. Edel- sten, seconded by Mr. A. J. Jolley.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.

ST. EDWARDS CATHOLIC CHURCH, RUNCORN. The services at this church on Sunday had a threefold purpo,e. In the first place to celebrate the feast of St. Edward, secondly, to offer thanksgiving for the bounti- ful harvest, and thirdly to help the funds of the day school, and large congregations assembled at both the morning and evening service. The sacred edifice had b,en beautifully decorated for the occasion by fruits, flowers, and cereals, aud excited much admiration. In the morning high mass was celebrated by priests from Ditton College, Dr. Gastaldi, the na.tor,acting as Master cf Ceremonies. The Rev. Father Kelly, of Congleton preached an eloquent sermon, during which he made an earnest appeal on behalf of the day schools connected with the mission. He remarked upon the strenuous efforts made by Dr. Ga staldi to provide secular education for his flock, and spoke of the great improvements the pastor had effected in the school. He had not only greatly increased the accommodation,but had augmented the regular attendance. The preacher mentioned the difficulties that denominational schools experienced, and showed that although assistance was afforded by Govern- ment grants, they were not sufficient to meet all the expenses. Under these circumstances managers had to ask help from other quarters' and therefore those present would be asked to reappnd liberally to the request of their resident pastor. a the evening the Rev. Father Kelly based his discourse upon the life of our lady. He showed the reasonableness of Catholic devotion to St. Mary, inasmuch as she was the mother of Christ, and consequently all Christians must acknowledge her to ne worthy of honour. He stated that the life of all was one of suffering, like that of those who had been called to higher sanctity ; and remarked that this should enable them to be more satisfied with the lot God had marked out for them. This life was simply a preparation for the one to come. During the Benediction the To Deum was sung in an effective manner. The choir, which was augmented, gave an excellent rendering of their portion of the service. The collections realised £7 7s. A VIOLENT HUSBAND AT RUNCORN. div.head: BT AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. ----
div.p: BT AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. ----

The Runcorn Tonic Sol fa Choir is a living monu- ment to the perseverance and teaching ability of Mr. John Ilolford, the founder and conductor, and is also a ciedit to the town. There are, I should think few places of similar size that can boast two such numerous and efficient choirs as those of the Sol Fa and the Musical Society. Healthy and good hum- oured rivalry in any undertaking produces better and more finished work, and it is a cause for con- gratulation that our two local societies can each maintain a separate and successful existence. The concert of the Sol fa Choir on Thursday evening was of a highly enjoyable character and their next appearance will be awaited with expectant interest.

The school fee difficulty created by the action of Runcorn Board of Guardians. has come to an end by the Guardians receding from the position they had taken up. The guardians for the township of Runcorn, with the addition of four " outsiders" will continue to grant school fees when necessary and the Board will subsequently approve of their work. Mr. Brandleth stuck to his guns to the last, and even hinted that he would lay the question of paying the fees for the last quarter before the Local Government Board., He maintains that it is not right that the fees should be paid by the Guardians. Right is scarcely the proper word to use. Had he said it was not " just" perhaps the whole of the ratepayers would have agreed with him,but the law ordains that they shall be paid and the Board of Guardians as an executive body must obey. The end to be aimed at is an alteration of the law and, as every cause must have a leader, here is a chance for Mr. Brandreth to become a champion for the removal of an unjust law.

The proposal to give Mr. Marshall, the secretary to the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, a gratuity of £5O for extra services performed by him in con- nection with the purchase of the Waterworks gave rise to an interesting discussion. That his labours in this matter had been heavy was not denied, the question at issue was as to the amount of the remuneration. Mr. Collier suggested £l5, but only Mr. Abel supported him in this proposal, and even- tually the grant was made by nine votes to three. The dissentient three were Messr.t. Collier, Abel and Lea.

div.head: WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. I GILCIIRIST LECTURES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. I GILCIIRIST LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

The usual weekly Meeting of the Widnes (T. P. O'Connor) Branch Irish National League, was held in the League Rooms, St. Paul's Chambers, Victoria- road on Sunday, Councillor Hugh O'Donnell, presi- dent, in the chair. The Chairman remarked that it was gratifying to see the large and increasing attendance at every meeting as well as the steady increase of new members. On the motion of Mr. John Campbell, seconded by Mr. J. O'l-lagan, it was agreed to send the sum of .E 5 to the Executive in London for the further supply of membership cards. After a lengthy discussion on the coming contest in Waterloo Ward the meeting pledged itself to support Mr. Carney who had given entire satisfac- tion during the past year and formed a working committee to assist him.
F RODS ELAM.
SHOCKING DISCOVERY AT MANLEY.

On Sunday morning, the body of Thomas Potter, farmer, Manley, was found in a plantation not far from his home. He went -out of the house on Saturday even- ing, and failing to return home a search party was organized on Sunday morning. The result was that his dead body was discovered in the wood. His throat was cut in a horrible manner, the windpipe being com- pletely severed. Abut 50 yards away a razor was found with blood upon it, so that evidently after inflict- ing the wound he had walked a short distance. The circumstances point to a case of suicide. The deceased had suffmci. from influenza, and had since been in a depreAsed state.

• THE PAPIPCHIAL COMMITTEES. At a meeting ef these committees, held on Friday evening, presided over by Mr. H. E. ileywood, a letter was read calling the attention of the committee to the condition of the smithy at Overton, alleging it to be a positive danger to the public health, also to the stenches which continually rose from the sewers in Frodsham, especially Chapel-lane. The writer asked that a search- ing inquiry be made without delay.—The Inspector stated that he bad been to the premises referred to, and he could not find anything which required to be remedied. The attention of the committee was directed to the fact that a stream of water flowing from the land above Mr. Bretherton's h)uses had been connected with his recently-erected property, when it was decided to ask him to disconnect the same, as the water was not fit to be used,—Colonel Ashton. read a letter received from Mr. S.Davies, secretary of the Frodsham Gas Inspectors, in reply to his letter inquiring whether the inspector would object to the committee taking over the duties and powers exercised by them in carrying out the pro- visions of the Lighting and Watching Act of 1833, to the , effect that before giving any definite reply in the matter, I the inspectors desired to know, " In the event of their relinquishing their duties, is it the intention of the corn- mittee to take. over their secretary at the same time 2" It was decided to send a copy of the letter to the Lncal Government Board. The committee strongly objected 'to such a course being followed, "to take over the secre- tary "as well as the duties.—A copy of the award of Mr. Charles E. Linaker was produced, and the contents read, from which it appeared that after going into the whole question between the committee and the Frodsham Gas and Water Company with reference to the supply of water from Frodsham, he found that the company was " neither willing nor able to supply the township of Frodsham with water proper and sufficient for all ' reasonable purposes for which it is required by the Sanitary Authority," and awarded "that the costs of the reference shall be paid by the said Sanitary Author- ity." The Clerk reported that the award had been sent to the Local Government Board, who had duly acknowledged it. It was decided not to press the Board for their sanction to the proposed scheme until their next meeting.

WAVES OF RATER AND WAVES OF LIGHT. Runcorn Public Hall was again crowded on Thursday night, on the occasion of the second of the series of lectures, under the auspices of the Gil- christ Trust. The lecturer was Mr. A. P. Laurie, M.A., F.R.S.E., F.C.S., fellow of King's College, Cam- bridge, and the subject for consideration " Waves of Water and Willies of Light.' In the unavoidable ansence of Mr. P. Speakman through domestic affliction, Mr. F. Wiswall, chairman of the Technical Instruction Committee presided. The Chairman said it would be his business to refer to the Technical Institute, which they were desirous of establishing. He was sure they would all admit that it was a great favour co Runcorn to have these lectures. (Applause.) And it was because of the proposed Technical Institute that they had got these lectures. (Hear, hear.) So he trusted they would admit their indebtedness and support that institution. At the last lecture the Rev. Canon Wood told them that it would cost £4,000 to establish the Institute. They had obtained about two thirds of that sum, and consequently they only required the remaining third to complete the matter, and put it in a safe position. The site, which belonged to the Commis- sioners, had been secured with the sanction of the Local Government Board ; arid the Board had also had plans prepared and submitted to the Cheshire County Council and to the Science and Art Department,who had approved of them. Toe it and had now only got to ask for tenders at any moment they wished. Some of the members would lute to proceed at once, but there were others more cautious, and who thought that none of the fund should be mortgaged, but secure the total amount by donations. It was believed that with the help of the townspeople they would secure the money. Some had suggested that a bazaar should be held, and he did not know why it should not. Judging from that audience it should not be a difficult matter, to raise twelve hun- dred or fifteen hundred pounds for such a grand institu- tion, which was for the benefit of the masses of the people, and if the masses of the people did not come to the front, and support it, it would be their fault if the thine drooped and perished. Surely it would never Come to such a sad end as that! (Applause.) 'Abe Le.tturer said there were two theories with regard to the phenomena of light. One was the wave theory and the other was the emission theory but the latter had been abandoned. The wave theory was that a source of light, such as a gas jet, set up a vibration, a wave, or a ripple, winch entered the eye and gave the sensation of light. The next question was, what do these ripplee consist of and through what do they pass. They knew that they did not pass through air, because if they took a glass vessel and pumped HU the air out of at, and then allowed a ray of light to fall upon it, it would pass right through the vessel. flat vessel although utterly void ,of air must still contain something which was in the air, and which could penetrate through glass, and something through which waves of light could travel. They had : been driven to the conclusion that the whole of the space is filled with something to which the name of ether had been given ; that this ether can penetrate through all solid and liquid bodies like iron, stone or glass and tilled all space between tho different suns, stars and planets. When these waves travel through the ether and strike the eye, the semation of light is produced, and only in that way did they know that ether was there. %Wowed this theory of light to a brilliant man of genius, Dr. Thomas Young. All the different facts about light can be perfectly and exactly explained by supposing light to con,l-t of little waves through this substance called ether. As an illustration of waves he would suppose they were in a boat on a lake, and while there a steamer came along. They would know of the presence of the somet in three different ways. The paddles as they turned round beat the water up in a form of waves and these came across the surface and made the boat rock. The second way was that the steamer's paddles made a noise and they would hear the waves of sound beating on the ear. The third way was that as they looked toward the steamer, they saw the light reflected 1 rom its sidsi,and so saw the vessel. These were all examples of wave motion. These were three kinds of water waves. There were waves caused by earthquakes, tidal waves, and ordinary water waves. At Lisbon, an earthquake caused the water to recede until the whole harbour was left dry ; then the water formed into a great wall forty feet high; and rushing back to the land,destroyed every thing before it. The principal cause of tidal waves was the attraction of water by the moon. The moon attrac- ted the water into a great lump, but as the earth was rapidly revolving round once in 24 hours,that lump was made to rush round the earth,aud produced the effect of a wave travelling rapidly round the whole globe. The tide was also affected by the attraction of the sun for water. Ordinary waves were to be seen on the sea shore or by throwing a pebble into a lake or stream. Water did not moVe forward with the wave, but simply moved up and down in a circular, swinging motion. Waves striking a breakwater are reflected in the same Way that light is reflected from a mirror, and the wave left the breakwater at exactly the same angle at which it struck the breakwater. The analogy between waves of water and waves of light was 1-scribed,and the effect of waves upon Each other illuetrated by experiments. To explain the phenomena of light, the lecturer said would exhaust not only one evening but many, but lie would present one or two facts. An Atlantic wave 300 feet from crest to crest travelled at the late of 27 miles an hour. Light travellef through ether at the rate of : 186,000 'odes sot an hour, but per seccnd. A I wave of light was the furty-thou•andth part of an inch from crest to crest. A wave of light occupied only the 392,000,000,000,000 th fraction of a ascend in making one vibration. They were thus dealing with enormously rapid and very minute waves. He was not going to all- swer that night how they were able to measure these minute wave lengths, moving at this enormous velocity. If they wished to find out bow these things were done, they must find out for themselves by reading. White light consists of many waves of different length travell- ing at the same time. They could separate these waves one from another by the simple process of passing light through a glass prison waves of different length were associated with impressions of different colour upon the the eye. Light, red in colour, meant that they had get light from a long wave, and violet colour meant that the-, had got light from a short wave. A red ribbon was read because it absorbed all the different wave length in white light, except the red, and only reflected the red vwaves,and so looked red. A blue ribbon absorbed all the different wave lengths except blue. And so on the invention of the spectrum, and the discoveries male through that instrument of the atmosphere of the sun and the most distant suns and stars, was now a most fascinating depatture of the wave theory of light. The colours of a soap bubble were caused from the fact that the light was reflected from the front and the back of the film. In conclusion the lecturer urged the study of this science on his auditors. In the course of time lecture a number of beautiful views were shown through the Oxy-hydrogen lantern by Mr. Garbutt, of Leeds and by the means of an experimental lantern, in charged of Mr. Alfred H. Saunders, of Brierley Hill, there were pour- trayed on the screen experiments illustrative of the lecturer's statements. Colours of the most gorgeous hue wets produced from a soap film. On the proposition of the Chairman the lecturer was accorded a hearty vote of thanks for his most beautiful, most charming and instructive lecture. In replying, he proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and to Messrs. Garbutt and Saunders • for being at the lantern. The experiments those two gentlemen had shown so success- fully were of a most delicate and difficult character. The expriments was the soap film had not been shown In lectures of that kind before. (Applause.) They were proud of that experiment and proud of being able to show it to such an audience. (Applause.) If that lecture did anything towaids raising money for the Technical Institute he should be immensely pleased. The votes were accorded and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: SUPPOSED CASE OF CHOLERA AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SUPPOSED CASE OF CHOLERA AT WARRINGTON.

A considerable amount of alarm was occasioned in town on Tuesday, by the rumoured death of a man from Asiatic cholera. The case occurred at a lodging-house. No 18. Percival's-fold. The victim was a Ship Canal man named John Jones, aged 30. He came into town on Sunday from Barton-on-Irwell,and on Monday evening complained of feeling unwell. He I was advised to seek medic:d advice, and in consequence I of this consulted Dr. Adams. The latter gentleman at I once noticed suspicious symptoms in the man's illness, and despatched him in a cab to tho infectious diseases host ital. Upon arrival at the institution Jones was in a state of total collapse, and only survived a few hours. Dr.Gornall,medical officer of hcalth,and his son,Dr.Guest Gornall, investigated the affair thoroughly, and sent on , to the Local Government Board necessary portions of the deceased body for the purposes of a bacteriolcgical examination. In the meantime all necessary sanitary precautions were taken. The lodging-house where the deceased had been stayine was placed under quarantine, under the supervision of the police, and no one was allowed either to enter or to leave the building, until it had been thoroughly cleansed and disinfected. The conveyance in which deceased was removed from Dr. Adams' surgery was also thoroughly disinfected. From latest information we understand that the case has not been definitely decided as one of Asiatic cholera.
