div.head: WARRINGToN MUNICIPAL
div.p: WARRINGToN MUNICIPAL
ELECTION S.

Nothing could better illustrate how completely the Conservative party organisation of Warrington has fallen into the hands of the publicans than the " shuffling of the cards" that has taken place this week in connection with the municipal elections. As we mentioned last week, there was something like a revolt amongst a large and intelligent Action of the party against the glaring attempt that is be- ing made by the publicans to capture the Town Council. Mr.W. P. Skelton was invited by the mal- contents to come out for the Town Hall Ward, in spite of the fact that Mr. Shillcock, " mine host " of the "Bay Horse," had been adopted as the official Tory candidate,and he accepted the invitation. But the publican is "king,' and Mr. Skelton has this week been neatly shunted into Orford Ward, there to light a hopeless battle against Mr. W. Pierpoint, the Liberal candidate. Still,we are told,and we can well believe it, there is a great deal of heartburn- ing amongst Conservatives in all parts of the town. ' Four out of nine candidates directly representing the liquor trade is too much for one gulp, even for Tories.

As we mention above, Mr. Skelton has now been transferred to Orford ward as the Conservative can- didate, Mr. Jenkins having withdrawn at an oppor- tune moment owing to indisposition. He may under the circumstances be described as a "second- hand" candidate. His natural position was the Town Ball ward in which his business is carried on, an this is the ward he was ambitious to stand for. Mr. Skelton is only seeking the suffrages of the burgesses of Orford because it did not suit the plans of the publicans that he should come out in the central ward of the town. It is to be feared the Orford voters will not appreciate this delicate compliment.

Mr. W. Pierpoint, who is championing the Liberal cause in Orford, is conducting a vigorous canvas of' the ward, and is meeting with every promise of success. In his address. which will be found in an- other column, he refers to the fact that he has received promises of support from both political parties, as be objects to the introduction of politics in municipal affairs. The declaration he makes in favour of play-grounds for crowded areas, and of the establishment of free lending libraries and newsrooms in several parts of the town ie in corn- pletlyharmony with the policy he followed during the nine years he was on the Town C.3uncil. The key-note o: Mr. Skelton's address, which will also be found in our advertising columns, appears to be economy of the cheeseparing, order He seems dis- posed to veto every scheme of public improvement, although as a rule these schemes result in ultimate benefit to the town and in the meantime put wages in the pockets of the working class.

In the neighbouring St. John's Ward Mr. Farness, the Liberal Candidate,is meeting with every indica- tion of success. Mr. Furness is lighting his battle with the intention of winning by a handsome majority, and o far his vigoroas personal canvas has resulted in something like two out of every three of the burgesses promising to support him. lie has the great advantage of being thoroughly well known in the ward, while Mr. Shaw, his op- polent, isonly an importation, or, as the Tories— who are fond of drawing these distinctions, would say--a " foreigner."

In Fairfield Ward a clear course as a Liberal can- didate has been left for Mr. Joseph Mountiehi by the decision of Councillor Dixon not to again seek re-election. In his address Mr. Mounfield points out that he is a resident in the ward, an employer ot labour, and a large ratepayer, and therefore I much more likely to understand the requirements of the ward and the town generally than a non-re- sident in the borough. Mr. Mounfield's complete acquaintance with the affairs and the requirements of the town give him a great advantage over his Conservative opponent, Mr. 11. J. Longton. In fact, in regard to Mr. Longton, the puzzle is to account for how he comes to be a can- didate for the ward at all. His personal connec- tion with the town is very slight. He comes in by a train in the morning and leaves by a train in the afternoon. He is, we believe, warmly interested in homing pigeons, a wholesome enough hobby when rlghtly conductad, but still not a conspicuous re- commendation for a seat on the Town Council. Mr. Longton was defeated in this ward three years ago, and we do not think the electors have changed their minds since then.

In Town Hall ward, Councillor Fleming is finding that the solid services which lie has rendered the town during his occupancy of a councillor's seat is not forgotten or overlooked by the ratepayers. Tie ' is fighting his battle vigorously, and so far the results of his canvas are of Ike most encouraging character. In his address Mr. Fleming reminds the burgesses of the fact that he supported the freeing of the library, the erection of new baths, and of the active part he took in advocating and completing the purchase of the waterworks all of which have resulted in great advantages to the town. Mr. Shillcock has no past services to appeal to, and, as we pointed out last week, the most notable part of his address is the declaration that he is " moderate in his views of things in general."

We understand that in Howley ward the retiring councillor, Mr. Arthur Browne, is being energetic- ally assisted in his candidature by a large number ot workers, both Liberal and Conservative. Political distinctions seem to be ignored in this ward as Mr. Browne is receiving numerous promises of support from Conservative electors, in addition to those of Liberal voters. Mr. Browne's three years service in the Council seems to have gained the approval of the electors generally, and Ohs opponent, Mr. Arthur Bennett, will find only a very small opening.

In Whitecross ward the fight is heing conducted with commendable vigour. Councillor 11. Roberts has set the pace and his opponent, Mr. IL T. Smith, is doing his best to keep up with it, though from all accounts with only a moderate amount of suc- cess. Mr. Roberts has furnished every elector in he ward with a copy of the admirable speech which we reported last week, and a perusal of it will, in itself, be sufficient to prove how poor an exchange would be make by returning Mr. IL T. Smith.

As far as Bewsey Ward is concerned there is no likelihood of Mr. Baird, the Conservative candidate, ousting Councillor Shaw Green. Mr. Green's canvass Itas,so far,been very gratifying in its results to that gentleman. We are told that some Conservatives have openly said that this ward can be " bought," and this contemptible slander upon the residents of the district has been indignantly repudiated at meetings of Liberal workers held during the week. We may gather from this how slight are the hopes of the Tories of making an impression upon this Liberal stronghold.

It is expected that before the time for nomina- tions 'closes! on Tuesday there will he Liberal can- didates in both St. Austin's and Latchford, thus making an "all-round" contest. In neither ward is the retiring Conservative councillor a strong op- ponent. As the representative of St. Austin's,Coun- cillor Hepherd has not by any means distinguished himself. He is vice-chairnaan of the Gas Commit- tee, and we do not know whether be claims any credit on the ground of either the quality or the price of the gas that is supplied to the ratepayers.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WAR RINGTON.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WAR RINGTON.

Warrington Town Council might do worse than follow an example set by the City Council of Manchester. As everyone now knows, Warrington Corporation intends to promote a Bill in the next session of Parliament in order to secure powers to do various desirable things. Why not insert what is known as a " betterment " clause in the Bill ? " Betterment" means that when a Corporation has carried out a great and expensive improvement, such as widening a street, and thereby greatly increared the value of adjacent property, a certain , part of the increased value should go to the Cor- poration towards meeting the cost of the improve- ment. At present all the cost of an improve- natnt falls upon the general body of ratepayers while a few property owners get pretty nearly all the benefit.

There would be absolutely no injustice in the operation of the "betterment" clause. Suppose, for instance, an improvement was carried out in Warrington—and there are several needed and spoken about—which increased the letting value of adjoining property by ..£lOO a year, " betterment" simply means that a portion of this .Cloo— .E• 25 or £so—would go into the exchequer of the Corporation towards meeting the costs of the improvement. Even under " betterment" as it is now understood the private landlord would still pocket the lion's share of what is really a return upon the outlay of public money. London County Council adopted the principle in a Bill that .was passed by the Ilouse of Commons but thrown out by the blouse of Lords. Manchester has now decided to beck up 1.7,nd0n by making a similar application, and Warrington should do the same.

Some of the candidates for a seat in the Town Council are rather prof use just now in their pro- mises, to economise the ratepayers' money. I think there is one direction in which even the most ingenious financial mind of the Council would find it difficult to cut down expenses any lower. I refer to the wages that are paid to the labourers in the Corporation s'one yard. I notice from a police case that one of these labourers has been charged with stealing two wooden setts—valued at threepence— and it was stated he had given seven years' service to the Corporation, and was paid the munificent sum of fifteen shillings a week. It is to be hoped that the Town Council will not, in a fit of economic zeal attempt to " dock " the wages of these labourers-0 least a demand for a twenty-five per cent. reduction, which seems to be the fashion just now, would be altogether ton much. Councillor Ashton is the only retiring member of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, which has control of the stone yard, and I think that some of the working men electors of Latchford might fairly ask hug to give his views as to how a workingman. with a wife and family,is to live on fifteen shillings a week —and coal at nearly 2s. a hundredweight.

A local cave in which three colliers are alleged to have done a considerable amount of damage to a cart used by the Collins Green Colliery Co., haa aroused considerable interest amongst the colliers of the district near Warrington. This was shown by the large number of colliers who put in an ap- pearance at the court on Wednesday when the case should have been tried. They had their trouble of coming for nothing however, as when the case was commenced and Mr. Davies got through his statement for the prosecution, one of the magis- trates, Mr. J. J. Bleckly, discovered that he was a colliery director, and declined to adjudicate. His action, I consider, is very commendable, and is in pleasing contrast with the actions of certain magis- trates in some other parts of the country. MERLIN.

div.p: WARRINGTON AND-Mg-DUCT- HOMING
SOCIETY

ANNUAL MEETING AND TEA. The annual meeting and tea of this S viety took place on Tuesday evening, when all the members together with a few friends, including Messrs. Moore (Lymm), Armstrong (Wigan), Timperley (Stockton Heath), , Edgerley (Cuerdley), Dixon (Penketh), and others; sat down to an excellent repast provided by the worthy host and hostess Mr. and Mrs. R. Anderton at their hostelry, the "Cross Kees" Hotel, Buttermaricet-st. After the good things had been "removed "the President, Mr. H. F. Gre-nough opened the proceedings by giving a report of the past : season's work. The Eon. sec. having read the report of [receipts and expenditure the diplomas were distributed to the winning members. At this point a spirited dis- cussion arose as to the advisability of a Grand National Race for the whole of England and Wales from France, Mr. 11. J. hongton, Mr. W. C. lilgore, Mr. J. Harrison, Mr. Greenough, and Mr. J. Houghton were the principal speakers. After the usual toasts had been accorded, the harmonic portion of the evening commenced. Songs were rendered by that versatile comedian " Will " Whittle, his impersonation of Chevalier, Leno, and God- frey being thoroughly enjoyed. Songs were also given by Messrs. Armstrong, Anderton, and Lamb. Every- thing passtd off in a most enjoyable manner, the party breaking up shortly before eleven o'clock. The balance sheet which was submitted during the evening, showed the total receipts for the year to be £4B is. Bd.,whilst the expenditure left a balance in hand of £ll 10s. ld. The following is a

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

BRUTAL ASSAULT I7PON A WIFE. Thomas Griffin, 23 Warburton-at.,. was charged with assaulting his wife Margaret Griffin, on July 30th.— Inspector Spinks said that complainant's sister lodged an information of assault against prisoner,and from inquir- ies, he found that complainant was in the infirmary suffering from a fractured jaw, a-nd that prisoner had inflicted the injuries. The wife could not then give evidence, and the case was adjourned. The complain- ant said she was drunk on the day of the assault, and that she struck her husband on the back of the head. Ile then pushed her down and her face struck the door- step.—lnspector Spinks here interposed and said that complainant's sister ought to have been present to give evidence but was not.—The magistrates hereupon ordered her to be sent for. When she arrived in court, she appeared to be very reluctant to say anything. But after great persuasion, she said that she saw prisoner kick his wife, and immediately afterwards she noticed that her jaw was broken. Both prisoner and his wife were drunk at the time. The magistrates considered the case a very bad one, and sentenced prisoner to coo , Month with hard labour, Alderman Harrison, however, differing from his brother magistrates on the ground that the sentence was not severe enough. A SHOWMAN'S HORSE.

9eorge Cooke,a travelling showman,was charmed with travelling a horse on Sunda'. while in an unestate.— Mr. P. Davies defended. P.C. Monks and P.C. Delahey gave evidence to s-eing the horse being led along rants- road, being very lame at the time. It was discovered that there was a corn on its foot, and Inspecter Dowty also said that it suffered from strained tendons.—Mr. Davies did not deny that the horse was walking lame, but as prisoner belonged to a travelling show, he haa taken it to a blacksmith to have a shoe made so as not to affect the corn, but the blacksmith refused because lb was Sunday.—The magistrat.s dismissed the case on con- dition that the horse was not travelled in its present con- dition.

div.head: ANCMIER SHOP DOOR THEFT.
div.p: ANCMIER SHOP DOOR THEFT.

At the Warrington Borough Court on Tuesday, a Ship Canal labourer, about 40 years of age, named John Walsh, was placed in the box, charged with stealing from the shop entrance of Mr. A, Bradbury, 106, Bridge- street, the previous evening, a pair of men's trousers, value 24. 11d. Herbert Charles linden, manager of the shop said he was told about six o'clock that a pair of trousers had been taken from the door, and had been taken In the Lion Hotel yard. He (witness) proceeded there, and found that the trousers had been tied up in a handkerchief, and the ticket on which was the words " Men's trousers, 2s. 11d, bargains," had been thrown on a shed in the Lion Hotel yard. Information was given to P.C. Rylatt, who apprehended the prisoner. Henry Bird deposed to seeing the prisoner take the trousers, and take them to the Lion Hotel yard. Prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour. A DARLIII AND HIS BANJO.

At the E4)rough Court on Tuesday morning, a coloured man, about 30 years of age, and a native of the West Indies, who gave his name as Josiah Graham, had a very long charge read out to him by the Clerk. It purported that Josiah had feloniously broken and entered the lock-up shop of Mr. Walter Boothroyd, Sanker-st., and stolen therefrom on the 14th inst. three melodians, two concert flutes, two piccolos, one banjo one musical box, about 200 violin strings, and is. id. in money, valued in all at £9 10s. 3d. The prisoner who spoke intelligible English said he pleaded guilty to stealing the articles that the police produced, wlikich were minus one piccolo, and two melndians as stated on the charge sheet. It appeared that the prisoner was an itinerant musician and had been in England about eighteen months. From the statement he made to P.C. Phillips, he said he was on the road between Warrington and St. Helens when be was set upon by three men who robbed bin; of his banjo, tin whistle, and another instrument. Be arrived in Warrington on Friday afternoon last week, and after an inspection cf Mr. Boothroyd's window, he said he was so enraged at haying been robbed, he was deter- mined to get another "stock in trade." This he did with a vengeance, between three and four o'clock on Saturday morning, by breaking a plate glass window, valued £5, with a brick. Strange to say the prisoner entered the shop, took the money from the till, and decamped with the numerous muSical instruments with- out being seen. The police were informed of the matter, and the Chief Constable telephoned to various police stations in the vicinity, and issued circu/ars,but nothing was heard of the prisoner until Monday, when a tele- phonic message was received from the Wigan police, stating that a man had been detained in a pawnshop there, when trying to pledge a flute. Superintendent O'Brien, Wigan, took the man in custody, and at the prisoner's lodgings found the bulk of the musical instru- ments produced in court, P.C. Phillips was despatched for the prisoner, and he was brr ught by train to War- rington. The magistrates allowed him to have another railway ride, at the end of which he was to undergo three months' hard labour.

div.head: MASTER AND His FOREMAN,.
div.p: A MASTER AND His FOREMAN,.

John Edward -Jefferson, Liverpool-road, was charged at the Warring.ton Borough Court, yesterday, with as- Saulting Walter Walker,of the Green Dragon Inn,Bridge- st., on thel7th inst. 'none was also a cross-summons against Walker for assaulting Jefferson Ft the same time and plaer. Mr. P. Davies represented Walker and Mr. Longland represented Jefferson.—Mr. Davies said that Jefferson was a plumber and painter and Walker, whose

wife was the licensee of the Green Dragon, was his fore- man. On Tuesday Walker was working for the defen- dant at some houses in Atherton-et. Ile arrived that morning at 8.30. Jefferson came to him and asked him if he had only just come to his work. It would not do to come at that time. Walker noticed that Jefferson was under the influence of drink and thought he had better go away and leave him. He accordingly went to an empty house where his tools were, and commenced to pick them up. Jefferson followed him and after some words had passed between them, Jefferaon gave him a blow in the eye, which caused it to be black. Walker thento defend himself, caught hold cf Jefferson and held him by the neck. Jefferson struggled and scratched Walker in the face. Walker, however, held him until he was unable to do any more injury. Walter Walker, James 'thompsoo, and James Walker, gave evidente in corroboration of Mr. Davie's statement.—Mr. Longland said that it was. rule of the trade that before a man went to do any work at some houses, that he should call at the workshno. On the morning in question, Walker did not call at the shop, and Jefferson when he saw him at work asked him why he did not do so. Walker made no reply and shortly afterwards be commenced to pack up his tools. Jefferson went to him, and after a wordy dispute, Walk-r struck him in the chest, and knocked him away. Jefferson struck back and several blows were exchanged. Jefferson denied that he was under the influence of drink, but had had some tea and rum that morning. J. E Jefferson and Wm. Sharpies corro- borated this statement. The magistrates decided to dis- miss both cases, each side to pay their own costs.
MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SAWED/LT.—Before Ms: John Burgess (chairman) and
Mr. L. Voisei.

Tnr OF WOODEN SETTS.—Martin McMahon, was charged with stealing from the Corporation stone yard, at 5.30 the previous night, two wooden setts, value 3d., the property of the Warrington Corporation. The Chief Constable stated that the defendant was a labourer em- ployed in the Corporation yard. The manager (Mr. Wm. Woods) complained to the police that he had every reason to believe that wooden paving blocks -were being taken from the yard. Sergeant Taylor and another constable were set to watch the premises, and as the men were leaving work at 5.30, the prisoner was seen carrying a bag *Mich was found to contain two wooden blocks. Wm. Woods, foreman, said during the distress they had had about 200 men at work in the yard breaking stones, but the prisoner had been employed at the yard for seven years. Be had never given him permission to take the blocks. The prisoner earned fifteen shillings per week. As it was the prisoner's first offence, the magis- trates discharged him on payment of one shilling. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Andrew 'Duffy, lodging at 13, Pinners Brow, made his tenth appearance for being drunk and disorderly, He was found lying across the pavement in Pinners Brow by P.C. Chrimes, refused to go home, and oommenced to use bad language. He was fined ss. and costs.

Mosam—Before the Mayor (chairman), Aldermen Harrison and Sutton, Major Nicholson, Messrs. F. Monks, W. Pierpoint, and S. Wright. DESERTION OF FAMILY.—Wm. Newton, was charged with running away from the borough of Warrington and leaving his wife chargeable upon the Warrington Union. Mr. Shearer who represented the Guardians said that prisoner ran away in 1891,and his wife and two children were left chargeable off and on tc the Guardians, entailing an expense of over £4. They were not now chargeable upon the Union, and the Guardians did not wish to press the case. The magistrates adjourned the case for a month to give prisoner a chance of maintaining his family. A NAVVY'S " Aiersur.DODGE."—Martin Scanlon, a Ship Canal labourer, was brought before the magistrates on the charge of stealing 4s. by means of a trick, from Mr. Lane, provision dealer. Town Hill, on the 12th inst. From the Chief Constable's statement it appeared that prisoner went to Mr. Lane saying : "Poor Jack Birmingham is blown to pieces on the Canal. He was 4s. short of his club money and if you pay it, we we can draw £lO and repay you to-morrow." Mr. Luse believing this statement, lent prisoner 4s. but hearing nothing of any such accident, he became suspicious,and informed the police, and prisoner was arrested.—Pris- oner said that he was willing to repay the money to Mr. , Lane, but the magistrates did not consider this to be , sufficient, and sent prisoner to gaol fcr 14 days. I DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Edward Crosby, Thomas Burns, John Conroy, and Bridget Kenny, were dealt with for this offence.

SLEEPERS oQT.—John Smith was charged with sleep- ing on an oat stack in Hoyle-street on Sunday morning,' and sent to gaol for 14 days.—James Thompson was charged with committing a similar offence in a stable of Charles Stewart in rurner-street, on the same date and was discharged with a caution, it being his first offence.

ALLEGED TLIFFT BOOTS.—WilliaM Thomas, James Murphy and Edward K:nnedy, all Ship Canal labourers, lodging at Daley's lodging house, Scotland-road, were each charged with stealing in concert from the shop of Messrs. Stead and Simpson, Horsemark,t-street, on Saturday night, a pair of boots valued 7s. Mr. Hunt said that on Saturday night the pair of boots in question were missed about eight o'clock, and sometime after- wards, Detective Monaghan saw Thomas and Kennedy trying to sell a pair of boots similar to those which were ' missing, in a shop in Mersey-street. He took them to the police statihn, and afterwards from a statement by Mr. Daley the lodging house keeper, Murphy was also arrested. Murphy and Kennedy both admitted that they had the shoes in their possession, but said that Thomas had asked them to sell them, but they were not aware that the boots had been stolsn. The magistrates dis- missed the case against Murphy and Kennedy and sent Thomas to gaol for 14 days. . .
A BREACH' or THE imacn.—Thomas McGuire and Clarence McNulty, both of Friars' Green, were ordered to pay the costs for fighting in Friars' Green on the 7th inst.

OBSTRI7CTION OF TEE HIGHWAY.—Thomas Smart Kent, mamager of Stead and Simpson's boot shop. florserearket- street, was charged with obstructing the free passage of the highway of Golden Square by leaving some boxes an unreasonable length of time on Saturday morning.—P.C. Bell, P.C. Forster, and P.S. Cheenev said that the boxes were in the street from 10 a m. to 11 15 a m.—Mr. Kent admitted that the boxes were there up to eleven o'clock, but said that he was unloading them during the whole of the time.—The magistrates dismissed the case, but hoped that he would not be so long in toe future in un- loading on a Saturday or Wednesday. STONE TnnowiNo.—Thomas Owen and Charles Titchett, both of Howley, were dismissed with a caution on the charge of throwing stones to the danger of pas- sengers in Napier-street on the Bth inst. TuaspaY.--Before Mr. R. Garnett (in the chair) and Dr.
Starkey Smith.,

Sciwor. ArrinmexcE C;sns.—Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, prosecuted in the following cases of irregular school attendance i—John Barnes, coffinmaker, Tanners-lane, 2s. ed. ; James Birchall, plasterer, Crossley- street, 23. 6d. ; Thomas Chrimes, forgeman, Portland- street, 53. ; John Jackson, filemaker, Arpley-walk, 5.; Thomas Jackson, publican, Dial-street. boy ordered to he birthed for truanting ; Sarah Jones, Bewsey-road, 2a. 6d. ; Joseph Kinsey, railway porter, Bank Quay, ss. ; Ellen Mellor, charwoman, Arpl,-y-walk, 23. 6d. ; John Owen, forgaman, Foundry-street, 2s. 61. ; Fre&rick Roberts, clock-mender, Keen-street, case adjrurned for a month ; George Sutcliffe, brewer, Watkin-street, 2s. 6d; , William Lythgoe, glasscutter, Portland-street, boy ordered to ship" Clio "as he was incorrigible.

A StISPiCIOUS CHARACTER.—MichaeI Prevton, a young married man living in Haydock-street, was charged with being a convicted thief, and found frequenting Owen- street, with intent to commit a felony. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. P.C. Bell said he was in company with P.C. Newey that morning. They watched the prisoner who was accompanied by another :min go to the hen-pen of Mr. Bailey, near the Farmers Arms. On seeing the police the two men ran away, but after a chase of 100 yards they managed to catch the prisoner. P.C. Newey corroborated. Prisoner was sent to gaol for fourteen days' hard labour. FRlDAT.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Messrs. Wm. Pierpoint and J. W. Hayward. • DM:MC AND DISORDERIX.—SamueI Parker, 1 Admiral- st., was fined Sc. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-et., on the previous evening .

AN ARMY lIESERVE MAN Di TROUBLE. —Richard Budden, 9,Leonard-st., was charged with stealing from the shop of James Lashford, Market-lace, on Thursday morning, a hatcher's knife, valued 2s. 6d., also with stealing shout the same time frnm Christian Bowers 21bs. of kidneys valued is. 6d., and further with assaulting Joseph Top- ham, on the same day.--Mr. Hunt said that prisoner was seen to come into the Market-place by a man named Edwin Molyneux nick up the knife from the shop of James Lashford. Molyneux drew the attention of Mr. Topham who looks after the Market-place, to the pri- soner's conduct,and Mr.Tonham took the knife from him. He then went for a constable, and while he was away, prisoner cut some of the kidneys from the shop of Chris- tian Bowers. P.C. Delahay and Topham at length found prisoner in Bank-st. and took him to the police station, at which place without any warning, he struck Topham on the temple.—A number of witnesses were called in corroboration.—Prisoner's wife said that her husband was not responsible for his actions. He had been strange for a long time. He had baen in India for a number of years in the Army, and was now on the reserve receiving a pension.—Prisoner was dismissed promising not to commit a similar offence again.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
iiEDNESDAY.—Before Me?.srs: G.. Comber (chairman);and

J. J. Bleckley. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—James Hewitt and Sarah Inn Hewitt his wife were each fined 25. 6d. for being drunk and disorderly on the 2nd inst. A POLE AND EIS WIFE IN COURT.—flannah &heliski, a Pole was summoned by her husband Antony Sobeliski on the charge of stealing a suit of clothes, a shirt, and a pair of trousers, his property, on the 4th inst. The par- ties reside in Earlestoim, and the defendant was unable to understand any English. The court was in a dilemma, but at length decided to hear what prosecutor had to say. He made a long statement in broken English, the gist of which appeared to be that his wife had bent the clothes back again, and that he did not wish her to be

punished. The magistrates accordingly decided to get 1 out of their difficulty by discharging the. defendant. When told that his wife was "let off," he cried out amid much laughter "Let her off. No! No !" They however left the court together. DAMAGE TO A RAILWAY FENCE.—John Mullin of Hay- dock, was charged with stealing one board valued 3d. from the fence of the bridge over the Liverpool, St. Helens and South Lancashire railway at Haydeck on the 6th inst. It appeared that there had been a large num- ber of the boards taken away recently and on the above date a constable shvr a number of men pulling them up. and he caught defendant who had one board in his pos- session. Derkiu was fined ss. including costs and was allowed a fortnight to pay it In.

div.head: 711 E EXA MI v-FT?, SA TTTR DAY, OCTOBER 21, 1893.
div.p: 711 E EXA MI v-FT?, SA TTTR DAY, OCTOBER 21, 1893.
RUNCORN PETTY SMSIONS.

MONDAT.—Before Mr. P. Speakman and Mr. Thomas Rig by. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—EIizabeth Barker, an Old offender, was fined £1 and costs or a month in default, for using obscene and profane language in Mersey-st.— Harriett Baxter, a woman of ill-fame, was sentenced to three months hard labour for disorderly conduct on Saturday night. This was her 28th appearance.—Ann Corcoran, Jno. Jornay, William Kenny, and John Jones were each charged with being drunk and were fined in various sums.
Sraawr OasraucrioN.—John Baguley, a hawker, was fined ss. and costs 10s. 6d. for obstructing Devonshire Place on the 7th October.

THErr or A HORSE CoLLAß.—Patrick Whelan, a middle- aged man, ple.ded guilty to stealing a horse collar, value 10s. ed.' the property of John Jeffs, farmer, of Weston Point. The prisoner who is an old offender, was sen- tenced to three months' hard labour.

div.head: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.
Sezunntor.—Before Mr. T. D. Grienke-Drayton (in the
chair), Mr. R. Stone, and Col. L. VVood.

Coat. MITS DlRT.—James Coward, coal dealer, New- ton, was charged with having on the 30th September, been guilty of selling coal at short weight, with intent to defraud. Mr. Stewart, who appeared for the defen- dant, pleaded not guilty. Inspector Spencer, who pro- secuted, stated that on the day in question, he saw the defendant in Newton driving a lurry, on which were three bags of coal for sale. Each bag was supposed to contain one cwt, of coal, but prosecutor upon having them weighed, discovered a deficiency of 201bs. in one bag an a deficiency of 7lbs. in another.—For the de- fence it was stated that Coward was hawking the coal, and previous to meeting with prosecutor he had been told by his customers that the coal was "dirty," and that they would not have it. He accordingly went back to the yard and riddled quantities of dirt from the coal, and this had caused the deficiencies complained of. Evidence was given in corroboration of this, and the case was dismissed. DEFRAUDING THB RAILWAY COMPANY.—AIfred Cald- well.clerk, Newton, was summoned for travelling be- tween Newton and Lime-st. Ststion, Liverpool. on the L. k N.W. Railway, on the 29th September, without a ticket. Mr. Fenna, solicitor to the Railway Company, conducted the prosecution. He stated, after defendant had pleaded guilty, that Caldwell had been guiltyof systematic frauds, but only two cases, one of which was to follow, had been taken up against him- In the case then under notice he would prove that the defendant travelled from Newton to Lime-at. Station, in a third class carriage, and at Lime-st. presented to the collector a ticket from Edgehill to Lime-st. This ticket he had obtained the previous day by taking a return ticket to Edgehill. A porter spoke to travelling with the defen- dant on the day in question, in consequence of sus- picions which had been aroused respecting defendant. The latter did not book, and upon arrival at Lime-st., presented a ticket from Edgebill, and refused to pay for excess fare. Further evidence was given after which, defendart admitted travelling with the Edgehill ticket, but contended that he had not been asked for the excess fare.—Ele was then further charged with travelling on the 31st Sept. ,from Lime-st. to Newton without a ticket. One of the Company's detectives who travelled in the next compartment to the defendant, proved the case.— The Bench inflicted a fine of 40s. and costs for each offence, or in default two months imprisonment. In inflicting the penalty the Chairman said that it was not the first time the defendant had been convicted of this kind of offence. ri e had evidently been carrying on a systematic fraud. He was evidently a man with suffi- cient education and brain to earn a good livelihood honestly, and therefore they felt compelled to inflict the heavy penalty that had been decided upon. Fnom DO/ERTY TO Tnnyr.—James McGrail, a collier, was charged with stealing a qnantity of coal, the pro- peas, of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., from Wood Pit yard. Defendant pleaded guilty to taking the coal from the yard, but he said it was only from the waete heaps, for other people had taken it. He said, "I had no money —and neither food nor coal in the house. I did not think of doing wrong." Mr. Stone, on behalf of the Bench, from which Mr. Grimke-Drayton had retired, expressed his sorrn v at the defendant's destitution, and said they had decided to inflict the lowest penalty, and that was to bind him over to appear for judgment when called upon. . .

MINRRS IN SEARCH or FOOD.—Four miners, who offered in extenuation of their offence,the plea that 41 they were in search of food," were charged with poaching on the land of Mr. R. Stone, J.P.,Winwick. They were respec- tively named John Whittaker, Robert Speakman, Robert Thompson,ami Demetrius Ackers. The offence was com- mitted on the 30th September. A keeper named Henry Smith, who proved the case, appeared with "a rabbit,' some "jams," and a part of a " net " in his capacious pocket. Mr. R. Stone retired from the Bench during the hearing of the case. The defandants were fined 53., in- cluding costs. ALMOST ON "ANOTHER CHARGE."—John ROthwell, a drayman, in the employ of Messrs. Greenall, Wnitley, and Co., was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of two horses and a dray,at Elaydock. A constable stated that there was in Company with the defendant another man,when the vehicle arrived opposite the Police Sta- tion. The defendant's companion fell from the dray. De- fendant di 4 not attempt to pull up his horses until one of the wheels had passed over his fallen companion. When the vehicle did stop the defendant also fell from it. Defendant was lined 10s, and costs, the Chairman re- marking that he ought to take the occurrence as a les- son,for he had evidently only just escaped being brought up on a more serious charge.

div.head: WARRINGTON FIELD CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FIELD CLUB.
AN INTERESTING EXHIBITION.

A Most interesting and instructive exhibition of the work of members of the Warrington Field Club was held in the Lecture Room of the Museum, on Saturday evening. It is five years since the club held a similar exhibition, and since that time the objects shown on Saturday have been collected. ' The object of the Field Club is the mutual improvement of the members of the society in the study of natural history, more particularly of the botany, zoology, and geology of this district. Field walks are organised in the summer menths, and meetings are held (by permission of the Museum Committee) in the Lecture Room of the Museum, in, winter. Papers are read for discussion and exhibitions of objects gathered are held. Mr. Charles Madeley is president of the club, and Mr. A. J. Jolley, the secretary. The programme for this session includes a lecture by the secretary on heredity, Mr. Newsteali (Chester) on wasps, Mr. Gillanders on entomology, and Mr. Jackson on the greenfinch. There was a large at- tendance of members and friends at the exhibition on Saturday, and a pleasant evening was spent in examin- ing the various objects shown. Light refreshments were partaken of during the evening. Mr. W. Collins and Mr. Acton exhibited a large collection of local moths and butterflies. Mr. James F. Dutton showed a number of British Beetles. Mr. Gillanders, of High Legh, had on view a number of Farm and Garden Pests, represented by specimens of 250 species of insects which may come under that denomination. Mr. Billups had a large series of beautifully mounted sheets of Pond weeds, illus- trating the variability of this group of plants. Mr. G. Mounfield exhibited a number of local specimens of birds,which are rarely found in this district. It may b, mentioned also that the whole 'collection had bee • mho and mounted by Mr. Mounfield. Messrs. W. H. Woo cock and J. A. Jackson showed by an ingenious arrange- ment, a considerable number of magic lantern slides representing geological structure in Cliffs, and other rocky exposures, ail(' also of Birds Nests, and young taken in situ. Mr. Jackson also showed specimens to illustrate his paper on the starling and sparrow. Mr. George Ellison contributed some water colour drawings, and a collection of Sea Bird Eggs made by him during a visit to Sole Skerry, a small islet, of the Orkney group. Mr. L. Greening exhibited specimens and diagrams in illustration of the evolutiwn of Air-Breathing Arthropods. , Other exhibits were by Mr. Mort, of Lymm, of Seaweeds &c. ; Mr. E. E. Lowe, a local collection of Birds Eggs made during 1892-3, including some very peculiar varieties; and Mr. G. Fryer, British Mustelidre. Mr. Joseph Smith showed acme stone weapons of early man. Mr. B. Chandley had some Larvae of lepidotera on view, and Mr. W. Mounfield ex- hibited insects found in foreign timber imported into Warrington. On behalf of the Museum Committee there was exhibited an interesting ancient canoe, hewed out of a solid log of oak, which was recently found in the bed of the river near Walton Arches, also geological specimens found in the Ship Canal at Warrington and Morley Common, and a collection of birds ergs, which was lately presented to the Museum by Mr. Henry Roberts, a member of the Field Club. A numberS of microscooes were also exhibited, under the charge of Messrs. WoodcOck and Billups.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.

Though there was not a characteristic gate of 6,000 at Wilderspool, on Saturday to witness the game,*there was a defeat inflicted by the home team which was characteristic of their old form. The Broughton en- thusiasts must have been somewhat disheartened not only because it swells the list of defeats against their team, but because Broughton claim the honour of having " taught Warrington the game." The visitors played a man short. The superiority of War- rington asserted itself throughout. Carey, the "new addition," became a general favourite by his brilliant performances. Broughton led off. However, breath- ing time had not been allowed before Turner secured from a loose scrimmage, and running strongly he scored near the corner, and by a magnificent kick landed the goal from touch. Shepherd re-started, and though the Broughton men reached half-way, it was only a flying visit, for James Bate, Taylor, and High= led the way back, and Smith saved capitally. At this early stage of the game there was no mistaking Brough- ton's inferiority, and when the home backs got work- ing, headway was generally made. Piercy and Hassan ultimately got in a good kick and run, which Boscow failed to neutralize. Carey put in a pretty run and kick along the enclosure touch ,and, although D. Roberts responded, Turner aud Nevins soon forced Broughton again on their lines. Twice did the visitors goal escape by the merest shade, and then marks fell to Evans and , Jolley, with nothing accruing. The game was carried I on at a hot pace, and Heesom was tackled in time. The I Warrington forwards screwed a scrimmage in fine style, but Smith met the opposition in the coolest manner' possible and piloted back to the half-way. Boscow was I equally safe, and although Manock got neatly away,. Hassan spoiled a chance by a hasty pass forward. Jolley dribbled ta the line, and Thornilev became a prominent feature in a struggle here, but Broughton once more got the hall out cot danger. Then ensued one of the prettiest bits of passing seen this season, for the two Bates trans- ferred to one another, and in turn Carey. Evans, Hee- som, and Potts handled the leather, but the last-named failed at the critical moment. However, a better fate awaited a pass from James Bate to his companion half- backs the skipper romping over for a good try. The oval had scarcely been dropped out and the usual ex- changes followed than Carey accepted a pass from Evans and running strongly from half-way he finally punted, over Smith's head, and in the general melee which followed succeeded in regaining posseesion and scor.cl the final try of the first half, at the close of which the homestsrs led by a goal and two tries (eleven points) to nil. On resuming Hassall had hard lines in the first minute for,taking advantage of an erratic pass,he was only nailed under the posts. After this Broughton were. never really dangerous, for after a minor had been credited to them, the ball rarely escaped the Manchester quarters. Turner attempted a number of penalty kicks with ill-success, though one from near touch on the popular side was, very near the mark. Carey delighted the onlookers with a pretty run, and was held just inside, and gradually the oval was worked to the opposite touch, where-James Bate gat away, and passing to his captain a yard from the line, that player cantered over for a clever try. Heesom doing the needful with the place.. Interest in the game lacked somewhat, and slovenly play tended to' make the game monotonous. However,, a cheer was elicited when John Bate passed across-to James Bate, and this capital player ran in strongly. Broughton had a chance when they passed the half ways but excellent work by Carey and Evasis was productive of the last- named racing in under the posts, a point which was over-ruled, owing to a plea of the Broughton touch. judge. No mistake was made when Heesom got posses- sion after clever passing by the Bites and Evans, and also landed the goal. To.) lor dribbled down the touch in tine style, and in the last minute of the match he put the finishing touch to an effort by Jolley, and no goal resulting, the final score read—Warrington three goals and four tries (27 points) to Broughton nil. Teams : Warrington: J. Boscow, full back F. Carey, F. Heesom J. W. Evans, and C. Potts, three quarter backs ; James Bate and John Bate (captain), half backs; Bair Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, J. Higliam J. Taylor, S. Buckley, J. T. Thornley, and E. Bailey;forwards. Broughton : J. Smith, full back ; G. 11. Piercy (captain), S. Hassell, and G. H. Roberts, three quarter backs; D. Roberts and S. Manock, half backs : F. Frost. J. Munro, J. E. Shep- herd, A. L. Auty, U. Hamilton, G. Tomlinson. R. Tom- linson, and J. Walton forwards. Touch-line judges, Mrs J. H. Dickson (Broughton) and Mr. ti. Ashton (Warring- ton). Referee, Mr. S. Williams, Salford. WARRINGTON A v. Beornanron A.—At Broughton. Lally started on behalf of the visitors, but the home team were the first to attack, until checked by Edleston. Mason and Lally soon get away to the centre, where a fine dribble, started by Edwards, Handles, Wilcox,,and Lawless, carried the scene of operations further intothe Broughton lines. Frost and Turner retaliated with a bout of passing, but Warrington were quickly attaaking, through some smart dribbling by Hampson, Freeth, and Phillips, and passing between the two La wlesses. With , a strung footing near the line the visitors strongly attacked, and after a disallowed try had beea, scored, Hampson crassed the line. A little later, Lally got away with a fine run and pass to Thornton, who rushed under the posts, the easy place, however, failing. Now Brough- ton got into their opponents territory. Goggins replied splendidly, and being supplemented with a fine dribble by Phillips, the hoinesters were again soon compelled to repulse their antagonists. Eventually a smart bit of work between Lally and %oral enabled Lawless to drop a goal, the whistle blowing for half-time. Upon the resumption of hostilities, some very lively play ensued, Warrington quickly forcing their opponents into their I quarters, where Handles secured from a line out and threw to Lawless, who smartly rounded his men. no drop-out was followed by free kicks to either side, mad then some quick pa:sing between Hampson, Mason, and Lawless, almost ended in a score, Lally ultimately got a try, Handles placing a splendid goal. Then Broughton had an innings, but the forward rack of Warrington soon had the leather hovering in the vicinity of the home quatter flag, and liampson, who was play- ing extra half-back, was very conspicuous by some splendid play, Mason ultimately scoring from firs pass. Handles placed another fine goal. The chief items of interest alter this were a fine dribble by Latiy, Mason, and Monks, and a splendid run by Hampson, alter which Broughton made a tying visit to the other end, but retired defeated pointless. Warrington 3-3-2 to nil. WARRINGTON 2ND V. BAINCOUGH t B nomturrosr) . —The above match took place at Warrington. Owing to a mistake in the arrangement of fixtures and an unex- pected turn up on the part ef Raincough, Warrington were unable to muster their selected team and at the last moment, had to raise a scratch team. Warrington 'started with 13 men, and the visitors were nearly over I in the first minute, Rowe saving, The visithrs pressed,

and from a passing movement, Bentley scored, the same player kicking the goal. Warrington now had a turn at attacking, and after a spell of give-and-take play Daniels secured, and running well got to the line, and passing at the right moment Foster completed the try, the kick being a failure. fialf-time arrived, with the visitors leading by one goal to one try. Resuming, the visitors pressed, and Diggle scored. Warrington now showed up, and Clare dribbling past the visitors' full back had a try at his mercy, but obstruction robbed him. The end saw the visitors winners of a pleasant game. Final—War- rington, one try three minors; Raincoagh, one goal one try one minor.

HALIFAX v. HIINCORN.—These well-known exponents of the passing game met br the second time this season at Halifax on Saturday, where the Cheshire men made their debut, and a fast, even, and interesting game en- sued. Neither club had a full representation. The only point scored during the first period was a minor to Flail- fax, the result of a drop by Keepings. The teams proved to be thoroughly well matched, and each side did capital Work both fore and aft. The second half was very ex- citing, and the play.for some reason was at times rather too keen. Halifax were fortunate enough to score a winning point, but their opponents had quite as much of the play as they.. After a dashing effort by Miles, Dick- inson claimed what appeared to be a fair try for Halifax, but it was disallowed. A little later, after a long kick by Nash, the home full-back, Morris mulled badly be- hind the Runcorn line, and Fletcher was credited with a very soft try, the legitimacy of which the visitors strongly questioned. No goal was kicked, but in spite of the determined efforts of the visitors, the majority thus gained proved all that was necessary to give Hali- fax the victory. The Halifax forwards played a better ' game than in any previous match this season. Miles greatly distinguished himself; and Brown, Knowles, Riley, Dickenson,.and Ben Mellor were all very promin- ent. The Runcorn men held their own, however, and Davis, Langley, Moores, and others did clever work. The hacks, too, were as evenly balanced as possible in every respect, and, although the afternoon was not favourable for the passing game, Abrams, Warder, Morris, and Houghton on the one side, and Rigg, Jackson, Keepings, and Cluley on the other, played finely.

ASPIILL, v. WIDNES.—The meeting of the above teams attracted about 3,000 speLtators to the Aspull enclosure on Saturday. Both clubs had their strongest teams, and altfmugh the greasy state of the ball was against accurate play, a grand game was witnessed. In the first half nothing was scored, but the kicking was ex- ceedingly line, Sharrock, Hulse, and Singleton, for As- pull, and Alford, Drummond, and Wright for Widnes, showing up well for their respective sides. In the second half the home team completely overplayed their oppon- ents,and Hogan giving a smart pass to Sharrock,enabled that player to drop a neat goal. Resuming, pretty pass- ing between Lowe, Singleton, and Smith almost ended in the last-named scoring. Brennan kicking dead in the nick of time. Play continued very fast, and Hogan, re- ceiving from, Lowe, got away, and after a tricky run dropped the ball over the bar; but it having touched Alford in transit, the goal was disallowed. A fast and pleasantly contested came ended in Aspull winning by onegnal to Widnes nothing. LOSTOCK.ALSALI v. MR. PELCOCK'S (RUNCORN) TE/ill. A Rugby football club has been formed at Lostock by the workmen of Messrs. Bowman, Thompson, and Co., and the opening game was played on Saturday, when Mr. Peacock brought up a strong team to do battle with them, his team including such well known players as Harry May, of St. Helens F.C. ; and W. H. Broady, of Runcorn, who has represented his county on several occasions. A large number of spectators wit- nessed the match,heing, attracted no doubt by the novelty of a game under tho Rugby code, which is unknown in this district. The game ended in a draw. Runcorn 1 try, 4 minors ; Lostock. 1 try, 2 minors.

STOCKTON HEATH V. WARRINGTON ST. MART'—This match took place at Stockton Heath. After several fine passing movements by the respective halves, and parti- cularly on tl e part of Woods and Longmore,the visitors got into the home half. The screwing of the home for- wards,however,gained a lot of ground.and the oval was gradually worked to the home line,Cross dropping a neat goal. At half time the homesters were leading by two goals to nit. The other part of the game was iiterest- ing, and at the close the Stockton Heath team were de- clared winners by three goals to nil.

Martin King. a collier, living at Haydoe34, was Srought up at the Occasional,Court, Warrington, on Monday moraing,before Mr. W 11. Bleckly„obarged :with having on the previous Saturday evening stabbed his. wife with a knife with the intention of "killing and murdering" her.--=-As the prosecutrix was unable- to appear, so-ae formal evidl.nce was given, and, the case was remanded until Thursday. It appears that on Saturday . morning Mrs. Kiag went to Earlestowa. As she had oat returned at four o'clock her husband went in search, of her. He found her and spent sometime in her company at Earlestown. They called at a public-house, and at half-past eight started for home. When in Vistaulane, near the Wood Pit, Hay- dock, the prisoner, it is alleged, forced his wife over rw. hedge and stabbed her vAith a' dagger-clasp knife" in, her heck. She was otherwise badly iniored. Her pit,l- - screams for help attracted the a%tention of some passers-by, and she szas removed to the house of hat sister. Medical aid T.VIS summoned. and Dr. Heywnad found the woman in a, critical condition, she having lost ' a large quantity of blood. She somewhat improved. oa Sunday and Mond:Lye, but was, of course, unable to appear to give evidence, and the case was remandsd as stated above. Bes]-des the wound ita, the neck she sat-rid from cuts on the hand as if she had grasped the hhade or raised her hand to, ward off the blows of her hi:sba.nd. Police-sergeant Page and Constables Wallbank and B9A et Blackburn at ce ourcd the district in search of- the runaway husba,nd, hut their efforts to discover him were unavailing until about nine o'clock on Sunday morning, when Constable Wailbank saw him making t.2.,wards his 'home, and ha took him into custody. fie was conveyed to the police, station at Haydock, and was charged with attempting to murder his wife, but made no reply. The husband it Itity years of age, and the is4,ured woman forty-fivo. They have been married a good many years, and have, a, family of six children. It is stated in the district that the couple had been on fairly good terms s until reae.ntly. Mrs. King has, it is said, declared her unwillingness to prosecute. On Thursday morning prisoner was brought before Mr. 27:i.ba Armitage at the Warrington Occasional Court, when ;:he police applied for a further remand to the nest Newton Petty Sessions, as the prisoner's wife would not be able to appear to give evidence until that time.

Hanby, Messrs. S. Taylor, T. Lea, D. IL Jones, S. Tarwood, -A. It. Norman, C. T. Wbitley, E. Aaron, H. B. Heywood, J. M. Williams, C. W. Davenport. J. Parkinson, S. Woodward, J. Bran- dreth,, E. TEE SCHOOL FEE QUESTION. lii accordance with notice, Mr. Williams moved that the following resolution be rescinded : " Resolved that the Pnquiry Officer for the Runcorn district be required to attend before the Guardians at their ordinary meeting, whenever applications have been made to him for the pay- ment of school fees, and lay before them his school fees application and report book, and take the orders of the Guardians thereon."—Mr. Parkinson seconded th- motion which was carried unanimously without corn- , ment,—Mr. Brandreth then said he should object to the accounts respecting the payment of these fees, as they had not been brought before the Board la the terms of the resolution on the books.—Mr: Taylor said the Inquiry Officer appeared befere the Board and the payment ot fees was then 'approved.—Mr. Brandreth argued that that would not meet the case.—Mr. Hanby said there was an easy way out of the difficsulty. He gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the resolu- tion referred to by Mr. Brandreth he rescinded.—Several members pointed out that this had just been done.—Mr. Brandreth said Mr. Hanby must-remember that he was only a new member.—Mr. Hanby t Yes, with all the latest improvements. (Laughter.)—Mr. Brandreth said he-strongly objected to the payment of these accounts, and he would write to the Lecaf Government Board if necessary. The Guardians had, no right tp Pay these fees. The School Board , of Runcorn ought to provide free education for al these children. . The Guardians had no right to pay these fees. If parents had the right to send their children where they liked ,let 'them send them and pay for them and not call upon the Gbardians to pay for them—Mr. Woodward said he , was fully in sympathy with Mr. Brandreth but the !Heard had been informed that they must pay for them end he failed to see there was any value in continuing this discussion.—Mr. Brandreth said there was no other 'place in the Union, besides Runcorn, where school fees were paid.—Mr. Norman asked were there any fee pay- ing schools outside Runcorn. If there were none it would be difficult to pay fees. He wished the whole• of the schools in Runcorn were free.—Mr. Hanby said there was one school partially tree at Balton.-7Mr. Williams then moved that it committee consisting of the ' Runcorn Guardians, together with Mr. Brandreth and Mr. Parkinson consider the,applications for school'fees • and recommend them to the Board for payment. —Mr. Aaron seconded.—Mr. Brandreth said he considered ttde whole thing illegal and refused to serve on the commit tee.—lt was ultimately decided that besides the Run- corn Guardians Messrs. Parkinson, Aaron. Stokes, ami- Williams, should form part of the Committee.

div.p: Zetter% to the ezbitor.
THE CONTEST IN BEWSEY WARD.

Sir,—The Tories are again fighting a public battle in this stronghold of Liberalism. That their chances are hopeless, is apparent, from the fact, that, the candidates they put forward get poorer on each occasion, until at last the climax has been reached. But, there is some- thing more ominous of the result than this. I was pass- ing down Dallam-lane the other day, and to and behold! I saw a blue and white placard containing the words "Mr. John Baird's Committee Room," and this room is nothing more nor less, than an undertaker's shop; and in the window, where a day or two before you could see the empty melancholy shrouds, you now see the equally empty and melancholy address of the Tory champion. In fact, Mr. Editor, the only sign of life near at hand, is to tle found nckt door, in the tap room of the Tory pub ccupied by Councillor Shaw of the present, but not of the future. I would only add that although it is boasted by the Tories that Bewsey Ward can be bought, that if they try it on they will be sold.—Yours, AN ELECTOR.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTION.-THE DRINK TRAFFIC
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTION.-THE DRINK TRAFFIC
INTEREST.

Sir,—The fact that four out of the nine wards, are to be contested in the interest of drink traffic is a char proof that those who live on trading in the chief cause of Poverty, crime, impurity and immorality, are rot satisfied with the past ruinous effects caused by them and their traffic. Can any saine minded personldisprove that drink and gambling go hand in hand, and are the most prolific causes of sin and immorality in every shade and mane in our midst ?. This being a fact, it follows that in the dearest interest of humanity and morality mere party politics ought to be set aside. It needs be in order to prevent the government of our town being in the hands of publicans and brewers. Their hold and influence already exercised in our midst is mighty for evil, and every voter who votes for such a class of men being placed in authority in our town to exercise their subtle power over the police and the Watch Committee is acceuntable in the sight of God for the wrong use of the vote cr votes so given.—Faithfully yours, A. STOREY. Oct. 20th, 1893.

div.head: COAL-GETTING BY MACHINERY.
div.p: COAL-GETTING BY MACHINERY.

Sir,—ln a recent article in the Manchester "Guardian" the writer suggested a way to fix the present rate as a " minimum wage" by better supervision, greater eco- nomy in management, and by using "mechanhal appli- ances."and thereby cheapening production. Respecting better supervision and economical management, I say I nothing, but leave that to those who understand it bet- ter, but of mechanical appliances I claim to know some- thing.Undergr.. und haulage and pumping by compreseed air engines has been tried and practised, and in most cases with success, but the mechanical collier, or "iron map," as far as my experience goes, has been a failure A colliery manager at Normanton, in Yorkshire,told me twenty years ago that he had produced a perfect machine, but I never saw it—or heard anything of its performance. I therefore condo& that it never made a figure as a coal-getting machine. With the " Grafton Jones" machine I have had some experience of its work- ing ; but it did not pay. It vt as clever and faultless an a machine ; it would strike an angle from horizontal to vertical, would uadermine or cut down the sides, was worked by compressed air, thereby giving the attendant a supply of pure, cool surface air. So far very good but it would not pay, and the cause was difficulty of lo- comotion. It wt.s carried on a " bogey,".and when set ' to work had to be propped fast down from the top to keep it steady. Alter undermining a few feet it had to I be loosened and removed along the face of the coal, propped again, and set to work. The constant removals, propping and loosening took UP the time of the attend- ant, so that when the cost came to be counted it was found to exceed that of hand labour, and was, after re- peated trials under favourable conditions, eventually ' abandoned. Another contrivance was a drilling machine, carrying a number ot drills of 21 to 3 inches dia- meter,making holes about 5 to 6 inches apart,for cutting down the sides, and worked by hand. The holes were ' drilled in about two feet,the interstices were cut through with two long narrow saws combined together one inch apait,with space between and reaching to the far end of the holes drilled into the coal. This, as well as the " Jones " machine, was patentul but neither ever could ' be got into practical use. Mr. Grafton Jo.-.es invented , an implement to supersede the use of powder in coal- mines, and, as far as I saw it tried, it acted well. It was a wrought iron cvlinder,about three feet long,three inches diameter, 1-inch bore. Emanating from this cylinder was aseries of small pistons at right angles to it, length. A hole was bored,say three feet deep in the coal the cylinder inserted with a strip of iron above and a strip below, one range of the small pistons pointing up- wards the other downwards. The cylinder was then filled with water which was acted upon by a screw, the outer end compressing the water and forcing out the pistons,one set against the roof the other set against the coal, forcing it downward in large masses. Carrett, of Leeds, too, invented a machine for coal-getting—a huge , chisel forced out the coal by hydraulic power. This fell 1 through with the others. When it comes to carrying compressed air or water through pipes underground there must of necessity be constantly at hand men to ex- tend and repair damages ; the.extensions and repairs of pipes must be frequent,causing loss of time and expense. Anything to succeed as a mechanical contrivance in coal-getting must be simple and portable ; unwieldy and intricate machines are costly and unmanageable, and more plague than profit. With these facts before me, I think the writer of the article in the "Guardian " in his reference to lessened cost of production lacks experience in underground operations and coal-getting.—l am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO.

div.head: CONSECRATION OF ST. LUKE'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.
div.p: CONSECRATION OF ST. LUKE'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.

The above church which has been erected in Liverpool-road near Sankey Bridges, was c,pened and consecrated by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Ryle) on Wednesday. There Was a very large ' congregation and among the clergy present were Archdeacon Taylor Canon Peurhyn (rural dean), Rev. F. W. Willis (rector of Warrington), Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (vicar of the parish), Rev. H. R. Wild (curate in charge), Revs. J. J. &Ingham, H. V. Pigot, Percival, etc. The prayers were read by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Canon Penrhyn read the first lesson, and Archdeacon Taylor the second lesson. The Lord Bishop took as his text Ezra 7, 27, " Blessed be the Lord God of our fathers to put such a thing as this into the king's heard to beautify the house of the Lord.' tie said that the text was an expression of thanktulness by Ezra, and this should be the feelir.p, of every churchman at every consecration. This was the thirty sixth church he had consecrated since he had been appointed bishop of the diocese thirteen years ago. He hoped that he might be spared to take part in many others. He went on to speak of the noble work a rich man could do if he used his money aright, and instanced Lord Shaftesbury. He regretted that this virtue was not more common at the ' present day.—After the service an offertory was taken. The united choirs of the Holy Trinity and St. Mary's Churches lead the singing during the afternoon.—The church is a branch from Holy Trinity Church. and will be used as a chapel of ease to the mother parish and will be under the charge of the Rev. H. R. Wild. It will not be cut off from the mother church until such time as there is sufficient endowment. The church will seat 550 ixople and has cost £5,500, of which all but £250 has been raised. The building was commenced in May, 1892, although for a number of years previously, the present site had been reserved for the purpose. The architects were Messrs. Bodlev and Garner, Gray's Inn Square, London, %4.C.. and -Mr. H. It. Franklin, Ded- dington, Oxfordshire, was the contractor. The church stands a short distance from the highroad, and the site is walled off by a stone wall. The building is erected with Runcorn and Helsby stone, with a red tiled roof, the inside being plastered. Its length is 1161 t, width 45ft, height to the eaves 16ft and height to the top of the roof 351 t. It will thus be seen that the roof is very pointed. The style is known as the " late decorative "style, and consists of an arcade of five stone pillars at each side of the nave There is only one other church in England which is I built in this style, viz., Caythorpe Church in Lincoln- shire, although there are many on the continent. The keystone of the chancel arch is in the form of an angel bearing a shield, on which are the letter's 1.F1.5. The chancel is 18ft. 61n. wide, and 36t. long. The five broad steps leading to the altar are of York stone, blue and brown set diagonally. The altar itself is a plain oak table, and the choir stalls. The rich tapestry which covers the altar has been snecially designed by Mr. Bodlev. The roof is circular, and is divided into spaces with a green hack ground, and with a floral decoration running along the centre. The following inscription is painted along the chancel roof :—" With angels and archangels and with all the company of Heaven we laud and magnify Thy glorious name, evermore praising Thee, and saying Holy, Holy, Holy." The floor is set with wood blocks and the doors are of plain oak. The site is the gift of the Hon. Fox Powys.

div.head: EXAMINER, SA TURD A Y OCTOBER 21, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TURD A Y OCTOBER 21, 1893.
N UTitB ON GAMES A., I)
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

How things change! Here we had the poor old Brough- ton team at Warrington, on Saturday, raceiving a most complete and " scorching " drubbing at the hands of a team whom they can honestly claim to have taught how to play football up-to-date. True, Warrington did play football before that, but then it was not strictly in accordance with the rules, or even ethics of the present system. It used to be played in a field in Arpley, and before the players could be stimulated to what they call football, it was necessary that there should be a free fight among them. Of course things have changed. The crude players of 10 years ago have had their " talent" put through the crucible of "cultivation," and they now appear in the light of teacher to their old tutors, which is not an unusual thing. But Broughton have had particularly bad fortune this season, and as they have not won ODO match yet I am beginning to fear that they are not going to run away with that much coveted cup.

The gime was from the first one-sided, and Warring- ton's superiority became startlingly obvious to the most uninitiated of observers, this of course had the natural effect of making many Warringtonians of an enthusias- tic character commence to do what our American cousins term " chewing the red rag." This means talking over much. In every department, Broughton were certainly out of the pale of comparison ; indeed, their position regarding the game,was like the youth's position regard- ing the boat out of which be had fallen—wasn't in it ! As a matter of fact I feel convinced that if had not been tor the splendid, almost brilliant form of Broughton's full back, the homesters would have increased the drub- bing. The four three quarters system was put into use for the first time, and the result was that several displays of passing were made which simply made people rub their eyes, while it induced one facetious gentleman near the press gallery to express his determination to give Carey, Lieesom, Evans, and Potts, the " buttered scone between them."

The mention of Carey's name, however, leads me to ejaculate " Bravo !" Can anyone say that there has been a more pleasing and skilful performance given on the field at Wilderspool this year, than the one given by this lately acquired member? What I should like to know, and what many others would receive as a piece of valuable information, is the reason why Carey was not selected to play against Wigan. Had he done so and taken with him any of Saturday's form, the day bad been ours—or as the pupil teacher more correctly said "the day had been hours."

The first try Carey obtained on Saturday was achieved in a style which was a true specimen of his talent. He picked up a ball from a dribble at half way, slipped in and got among a crowd of the visitors like a piece of greased lightning, found himself cornered opposite the quarter flag, made a dexterous kick, and then like a young antelope, sprang forward through the crush after the,ball,caug,,ht it a yard from the line,and touched down amid the most deafening applause. This was a perform- ance he showed himself capable of repeating. I thought myself that his play was not merely faultless, but simply brilliant for one who has only just issued from the ranks of an insignificant junior team.

The two Bates did not show up quite so well as usual; but then we must not always expect people to be in good form. Nevins and Turner gave splendid perform- ances. Turner especially did so ; he is rightly termed Fair the Evergreen, for his feet never seem to lose their cunning when he goes on a rapid " Sprint" ; his kicks are more vigorous than ever, while as tho balancing— or more truly, the overbalancing power—in scrimm- ages he has simply taken to himself trained weight and increased muscle. However tho team may have had cause for downheartedness so far during the season, there was certainly ample reason to draw in a little self congratulation in beating Broughton by 27 points to nil. Of course, the idea in the competition is to win the cup again. Warrington has a fourth chance, and a look at the table of statistics informs me that they still have a chance—if they will " rush in where angels fear to tread "—cf obtaining that cup. I should like to men- tion that considerable satisfaction was expressed on Saturday, with the umpire, Mr. Williams, of Salford. This was not because he gave all the points to Warring- ton, but because of his entirely impartial judgments and congenial manner. These are the results of the competi- tion :

The Warrington St. Mary's first team on Saturday had again to taste defeat. This made two defeats on two successive Saturdays. They paid a visit to the Stockton Heath ground, but the homesters were by far the best team, and at the call of time Stockton Heath ran out victors by three goals to nil. The second string of the St. Mary's had better luck on their ground when they met Stockton Heath 2nd. and beat them by one try to nil. This is a creditable victory when it is considered that several members of the first team of the Rangers, who had no match to play, helped the Stockton Heath team.

The fret of the county trial matches arranged by the County Committee was played on Wednesday afternoon, at Whalley Range, under favourable conditions, before a fair attendance of spectators. The sides were selected from a large number of clubs, and played as Stripes and Whites, under the respective captaincy of T. Bowker (Barrow) and G. H. Murray (Swinton). Of the chosen players several failed to put in an appearance, the most important of whom was W. Winterbottom, of Swinton, whose club form this season at full back has been highly spoken of. The game was fairly well contested, but in its earlier stages a lack of good combination was very evident, the passing at times—due, no doubt, to want of practice together and over-anxiety—being wild and dis- appointing. In the second half great improvement was shown in this respect, particularly by the Stripes, who in the latter part of the game quite held the upper hand of their rivals. The game ended in a win for the Stripes by one goal, three tries, to one goal and one try. J. W. Evans, of Warrington, who was playing three-quarter for the Whites, and John Bate who was playing for the Stripes were both injured unfortunately, but both made a capital show while they were at play.
