ANTECEDXNTS."

In accordance with a- W-i;il--t-I;t many of the public have expressed, I commence this week to give in these notes, under the head of " antecedents" some few de- tails of the football career of the playing members of the first team. I commence this week with a few facts about H. Ashton, who has now commenced, like others who founded thereputation of the:Warrington team,to relegate to the limbo of the past, such operations as "donning the jersey." But he is not se iering himself either from the club or the game ; indeed I think if he wished to retire on his well earned laurels, the club wouldn't allow him. They would feel uncomfortable without the familiar form of their old leader hovering around them to diffuse encouragement and see to fair play. So H. Ashton has taken to refereeing instead of playing. He has been captain of the team for seven years alt,gether, and first enterfd upon the duties of leader in 1885, when the War- ingtm team amalgamated win the Wanderers. Then it was in the following year, when Warren was captain, and had to retirethrough an injury that the subject of our "antecedents" was made captain, and led the team on to that memorable victory in the final round of the West
LancaAhire cup competition. flow well he played the game then, how well he ha's played since, and how skil- fully he has always manipulated the team as captain, is proverbial.

Mr. Harry Ashton was born at Warrington—l believe at the Bridge Inn—on the 16th October, 1860, and is consequently no chicken of a footballer. In 1876 he commenced his football career, by joining the Warring-, ton Football Club. It was the strong enthusiasm that he showed which soon made the committee select him as on official, and in 1881-2 he launched upon the secre- tarial duties, and discharged them with such satisfac- tion that the next year, in accordance with a unanimous resolution, he Was made captain. He served as captatn the next year, which followed that of the winning of the cup, and he has since served, with the exception of three years, up to the end of last season, when his retirement was the cause of much regret to the club and to the en- thusiasts of the game among the public. Though Mr. Ashton's connection with football is not one in which we can include a great many events, still his long career as a leader of the code in Warrington has been one of con centration and arduous toil for the benefit of the game and he may claim to Ue one of the best friends of Rugby, not alone in Warrington, but in Lancashire.

div.head: NEW CHURCH HOUSE FOR PADGATE.
div.p: A NEW CHURCH HOUSE FOR PADGATE.

A BAZAAR.—SPEECH BY MR. T. W. LEGH, M.P. One of the greatest deficiences in parochial fie- corn monation, in connection with the Parish Church of Padgate, has been the lack of a meeting hall. Much has been done to lessen the inconveniences caused by this deficiency, but in face of the recent growth of the parish, these endeavours have not been efficacious. Indeed,-the call for accommoda- tion for Parochial meetings increased to such a degree, that the Parochial committee and the active church workers of the parish, determined recently to accomplish the erection of what is to be called a Church House. This is to serve as a meeting hall for parochial classes, mothers' meetings, and sew- ing meetings, Sze., and will involve an expenditure of £6OO. Towards this sum £lOO has already been received, ' and a three day's bazaar, commencing on Thursday and extending to to-day (Saturday), was arranged for the purpose of raising as much as possible of tee balance. How necessary the accommodation is may be surmised from a statement made by the Rev. J. J. Langliam,vicar, to the effect that all class meetingA which had been con- vened had to be held in. his private study, whilst such a thing as a mothers' meeting had to be held in the kitchen of the rectors. The bazaar was held in the Parish rooms, and was formally opened on Thursday afternoon by Mr. T. W. Legb, M.P. Five large stalls in the charge of ladies of the parish, had been laden with a bountiful supply of miscellaneous wares—articles of clothing and needle- work, drapery and tapestry, Ses, together with bric-a- brae, and a host of such things as the earnest labours of the ladies of the congregation had been able to devise and obtain. Then in addition to this a Committee of lady and gentleman workers, "by dint of effort and original device" had arranged a programme of amusements, varied enough in its character to satisfy the most fastidious seeker after delectation. It comprised conjur- ing exhibitions by Professor Acton, of Warrington; caster songs by Mr. W. Whittle, of Warrington ; vocal enter- tainments by the school children, under the conductorship of Mr. Blackwell,schoolmaster, whilst selections of in- strumental music were performed by an admirable band under the leadership of Mr. R. H. Pearson. The per- forrnances were all given in a room which had been hand- somely decorated. The stallholders were : No 1 :—Mrs. Langham, the Vicarage; Mrs. Mortimer, Ortard House ; Mrs. Beevers, Bruche Avenue; Mrs. flodgkinson, Fearnhead ; Miss Sanders, Castle Eden ; Miss Ada Birtles, Fearnhead. No 2 :—Mrs. Royston, Paddington ; the Misses Appleton, Bruehe Hall ; Mrs. Fowles, Woolston ; the Misses Warburton, Wall Farm, Woolston; the Misses Royston, Paddington Grange; Miss Carter, Ash Villa, Padgate. No 3:—Miss Jackson, Paddington; Mrs. Grange, Fearn- head ; Miss Bennett, Pear Tree House; Miss May Hough- ton, Woolston. No 4, refreshments :—Mrs. 'turner, Fearnhead ; Mrs. George Hatton, Padgate; Mrs. Thomas Dainteth, Padgate ; Miss Wood, Fearnhead ; Miss ! Antrobus. Padgate; Miss Brimilow, and Miss Harding, Manchest-r-road, Warrington. No s:—Mrs. J. W. Houghton, Woolston ; Mrs. Hallwood, Padgate ; Mrs. Joseph Hatton, Woolston ; and Miss Earle, Worrlston.. There was also a fish pond, which was left t the man- agement of Miss Bessie Beevers. At half-past three the presence of Mr. T. W. Legh, member for the division, was called attention to by a cordial welcome of applause. Amongst those present at the time, besides the Rev. J. J. and Mrs. Langliarn (vicar), and the Rev. W. R. Hartwright (curate), were the following :—The Rev. F. W. Willis, the Rev. H. V. Rev.Pigot, the Rev. A.A. Markham, the Rev. C.E.Cook, Mrs. Bearnont, Orford ; Mrs. C. Parr, Grappenhall ; the Rev. ' E. C. E. Carleton, Warrington ; Mrs. Hanselin, Mrs. Birtles, the Misses Bennett, Lyndhurst ; and Messrs. J D. Buckton, A. J. Jenkins, Hodgkinson, F. Appleton, W. Horton and others. _ .

The Rev.' J. J. Longhorn, in calling upon Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., took the opportunity of explaining the various causes which rendered the erection of such an institution as they were going to build, absolutely neces- sary. He said a site was available and the cost for building would be £6OO towards which they had received £lOO. It had been suggested at tirst to call the house a parish room, but, in view of the proposed Parish Coun- cils Bill they wished to emphasise that it was church property and so decided to call it the Church House. (Hear, hear,) They would thus lay stress upon the fact that the place was church property, and not public property. Mr. Legh, M.P., referring to the purposes for which the proposed church house was intended, said it would confer a religious benefit upon the loadity ; it would be a place of business; and it would afford an opportunity for mental, and intellectual recreation tor persons of both sexes. There was one thing which was heard a great deal of at present, and that was the depopulation of rural districts. There was a great deal of truth in the statement that the rural population was rapidly flocking into towns. People urged various remedies. Some thought the best way to induce the country people , to remain was to increase the burdens upon the land, ' while others thought the more agreeable way would be to provide suitable rooms where the country people , might meet once a quarter to discuss the affairs of the parish. A third plan was much in favour, and that was in making things as unpleasant as pos- sible for two classes, the squires and the parsons. they thought if they could worry these people (squires and parsons), sufficiently everything would go right in the village. He ventured to think that the establishment of a church house might possibly act as an inducement to some people to abide in the place. For that reason the proposed institution should be wel- comed. There was another reason, it was one more proof of the increasing vigour and activity of the National Church, a vigour and activity which he maintained would compare favourably with that of any other denomination. This might not be so gratifying to those people who did not welcome any accession to the vigour of the ' Nacional Church. but viewed it with detes- tation. There were various methods which arose from time to time by which all clergymen might be worried and cowed and lie believed there would be some opportunity in indulging in this under the Parish Councils Bill. If he found anything in this bill which would act prejudicially upon church work and church rights, he would do his best to oppose it, and it would be opposed by everyone who had his church at heart. He was afraid the present was a very inopportune time for holding a bazaar, when landlords were receiving reduced rents,clergy man reduced stipends and the dividends of the middle classes and the wages of the working men were being wasted away in a suicidal struggle, and the industries of all were being prejudicially affected. Mr. Legh after declaring the bazaar open,was accorded a vote of thanks, and upon the proposition of Mr. Royston seconded by Mr. Fowles. The business was then proceeded with. The attten- dance was very large throughout the day, many persons visiting the bazaar from Warrington. The total receipts taken during the day amounted to £l6l 12s. The baziar was again opened yesterday afternoon by Mrs. Bea/Dont. The Itev.J. J. Langliam said at the open- ing of the bazaar the previous day, he pointed out that they wanted £5OO to complete the church house. They had already realised the satisfactory sum of £l6O, and they still required the sum of £340. They bad that day their old friend Mrs. Beamont to open the bazaar, and he felt sure he need use no w(irds by way of introduc- tion to them. The name of Beamont had been associated with everything that had beendone:in that parish for the extension of the church for the last 50 years. A short time ago he (the speaker) was looking over the list of subscribers for the building of Paigate Cnurch, and he found the name of Mr. Beamont. Mr. Beamont also as- sisted in the building of the Vicarage and the school- room, and Woolsteu and Orford owed very ' much to the munificence of Mr. and Mrs. Beamont. They welcomed Mrs. Beamont there that day as an old friend and he was quite sure there was no one who could ocen that bazaar who hod more at heart the interests of the parish. (Applause.) Mrs. Beamont said she couldn't make a speech as her voice was too weak, but she would tell them how glad she Was to be present , that day. It reminded her of old times when one better than herself was present. She then declared the bazaar open. A vote of thanks was passed to Mrs.Beamont for her presence, and the action she had taken in connection with the bazaar, on the proposition of Mr. Win. Hough- ton, seconded by Mr. George Mather.

At a special meeting on Wednesday,the Town C )uncil of Salford resolved to again urge on the Local Govern- ment Board the importance,in the interests of the public health, of holding an inquiry into the pollution of th.l waters impounded in the Manchester Ship Canal. The opinion was aiso expressed that the Mersey and'lrwell Joint Committee ought to take much more vigorous acti.in for the purpose of enforcing the law against those local authorities who continue to pollute the river before it reaches the Ship Canal.
ARBITRATION CASE AT WARRnGTON.
THE HON. MISSES WILSON-PATTEN Y. THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY.

An important arbitration case was heard at the Lion Hotel, Warrington on Tuesday and Wednesday, arising out of a claim by the Hon. Misses Ellinor and Elizabeth Wilson-Patten, against the London and North-Western Railway Company, with respect to the purchase of land. Mr. J. 11. Glutton was the umpire, and the arbitrators were Mr. John White and Mr. Charles Hall. The counsel for the claimants were Mr. Balfour Browne, Q.C., and Mr. T. G. for- ridge (instructed by Messrs. 11. B. White and Sons) ; Mr. H. D. Greene, M.P. (instructed by Mr. •C. IL Mason) appeared for the London and North-W estern ' Railway Company. Mr. Balfour Browne, in opening the case for the claim ants, said the land in question was taken under the powers of the London and North-Western Railway Act, 1890, and proceeded to describe its situation, which is between the Mersey and the Loncl,m and North-Western Railway Company at Arpley, the only means of access being from Wilson-Patten-street along Slutcher's-lane. The railway company were not entitled to stop up this road until they had provided a substitute. The principal owners of the land were the trustf,es of the late Lord Winmarleigh. Mr. Browne read the various sections of the Act bearing on the subject, some of which referred to the power which the company enjoyed directly under that Act to take land, and others, indirectly, by reason of the stopping up of access to certain property which remained in the hands of the late Lord Winmarlei,gh's trustees. In 1891 certain correspondence took place between Lord Winmarleigh's agent and Mr. Hull with a view of, if possible, getting a better road than was pro- posed to be made. The road ran along the north side of the railway, then crsssed over the main line, and after going over the land under consideration went along by the s,cle of the railway. Lord Winmarleigh's agent desired, if possible to get a road which would develop this land, and he asked Mr. Hull to make a road in such e position. Unfortunately, nothing of that sort had been arranged. Lord Winmarleigh died on the 11th July, 1892, having devised 13 acres 3 roods 18 perches to the Honourable Misses Elliaor and Elizabeth Wilson-Patten jointly in fee simple. That was all the land that lay to the west of Walton Junction line. Then after that there was some more correspondence about the road, but no result followed. On the Bth June, 1893, particulars of claim were sent in with reference to that 13a. 3r. 18p., it hav- ing been agreed that the two should be taken separately. For that 131. 3r. 18p. they now claimed £12,320, and that, although it might not be seen at first, was a reduc- tion in the price of the original claim. Practically, when Lord Winmarleigh was alive, they were claiming for this land £l,OOO an acre. The present claim of £12,320 worked out to something like £BOO an acre. A great deal of the property about there belonged to the Wilson. Patten family, and a large amount of the land in the possession of the London and North-Western Railway Company to-day at one time belonged to that family. There had been no dispute between them before. Ells clients thought that £12,320 was a figure for settlement, because it was a figure they had given before, and at a time when property was not near so valuable. Some property was sold by Lord Winmarleigh in 1871, at a time when the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany agreed to make Wilson-ratten-st., at the same price they asked to day. They first asked for it as a chief rent, and afterwards turned it into a capital sum. Referring to the value of the land, Mr. Browne said first of all it lay between two railways, and that was a matter of the very greatest importance, and it was Poked upon as being eminently suitable for w,.rks. It was only 700 yards from the Manchester Ship Canal, and river water which was eminently suitable for works, could he readily obtained. Furthermore, it was outside the municipal boundary, and so any works built thereon would escape the borough rates.

Mr. William Owen, architect, Szc., Cairo-street, War-. rington, was the first witness called. Before giving in his valuation, and in answer to questions by cross-ex- amining council, he said, in his opinion, the Ship Canal would greatly enhance the value of the land tinder con- sideration. He also thought the land was eligible for the erection of manufactories. His total valuation of it amounted to £15,174. Alderman Sutton, J.P.. who had also valued the land gave in his total valuation as £14,260. Mr. A. Selby,surveyor and land agent, Leigh, gave in his valuation at £15,375 16s. 51. The valuation of Mr. William Radford, Manchester, came to a total of £15,264. Mr. Greene, M.P., before calling the witness for Vie company, in his remarks to the Umpire con- tended that the land was not of the value claimed be- cause it was not useful for building purposes of any des- cription, and was subject to floods.—Mr. Thomas Tay- lor, Liverpool, valued the land at £3,675; Mr. C. E. Linaker, of Frodsham, gave his valuation in at £4,754 10s. id. ; and Mr. Downing, engineer and surveyor, Manchester, then spoke to the same effect. This con- cluded the evidence on this claim.—Mr. Balfour Browne then proceeded to put forward another claim on behalf of the trustees of the late Lord Winmarleigh for com- pensation with respect to a piece of land in the same neighbourhood measuring 2 acres 0 roods 3 perches, es- timated at £2,413, and which it was alleged had de- teriorated to the extent of £lOO an acre by being cut off from the new Chester-road, and for damage to access. Mr. William Owen and Mr. T. Sutton, having given evi- dence in support of the claim, the proceedings were ad- journed until Wednesday, when evidence was given in support of the claim, and valuations submitted in its favour, estimating the acreage at a general value of £l,OOO The valuation against the claim stated the acre- age value at about £3OO.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCEIES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCEIES-WARRINGTON.
THE P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH.

The chairman at the P.S.A. meeting in Wycliffe Church, on Sunday afternoon was the Rev. G.H. Brown, of Settle, Yorkshire. He said that was the third P.S.A. meeting he had attended, and he was the more convinced of the usefulness of them. He congratulated those present on the success of the movement in Warrington, and hoped they would still turther increase their mem- bership. Mr. Jesse Bryant, of Manchester, was the speaker for the afternoon, and he spoke on the question, as tn whether a man was called upon to support women and children who might be wanting the necessaries of life, because their husbands refused to work for the wages offered. The speaker dealt with the subject from a Christian standpoint, remarking that christianity said they must render help to those who were suffering, and as an illustration, he pointed to the parable of the good Samaritan. Mr. Bryant also spoke on the importance of building up a good character. Mr.W. H. Wallington, and Miss Coubrough, each contributed a solo during the service. The secretary, Mr. T. Wallington, and Mr. H. Pendlebury also took part in the meeting. Mr. W. H. Payton, the organist, accompanied. The meeting was very largely attended, and the membership now exceeds 950. A St. John Ambulance class has been formed in connection with the brotherhood.

CARVED FIGURES AT ST. MARY'S, R.C. In one of the recesses in the interior of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, another small group of figures in carved stone•bas lately been placed. The subject re- presented is "Jesus is made to carry the Cross." It is the work of Messrs. Boulton and Sons, sculptors,Chelten- ham, and is in keepinz with the other splendid carved work in the church which was executed by the same firm. Nine recesses are now filled, leaving five more to be completed. BANK QUAY MISSION.

The anniversary and harvest thanksgiving services at Bank Quay Workingmen's Mission were held on Sunday and were attended by very large congregations. The building was tastefully decorated by members of the congregation. In the morning and evening, sermons were preached by Mr. Stafford, of Leigh. In the after- noon a service of song entitled " Joyful Harvesters," was rendered by the song, Mr. W. Hickman giving the connective readings. Mr. J. Mills conducted at each service, Mr. F. Atkinson presiding at the organ. Col- loctions cvere tiken which amounted to £4 3s. sid.,with ! a donation of £5 from Mr. Crosfield. WESLEYAN MISSIONARY WORK AT PADGATE. Sermons were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday by the Rev. J. Chamberlain,of Didsbury College, on behalf of fcreign missions. On Tuesday evening the annual missionary meeting was held. Dr. Starkey Smith, of Warrington, presided. The Secretary (the G. D. Mason) read the report of the past year. Amongst the items regarding l'adgate were—Subscriptions, £4 14s. ed. ; Master Percy Bennett's box, £1 Is. ; Miss Lon- don's box, 7s. ; Select Class, Boys, £1 lie. 10d. ; Young Women's Class, £l. ss. ; and public collections, £lO 193. 4d. Mr. Collier said that education,however eleva- ting, would not save the world, and the only thing that would raise heaven to earth was religion. The Rev. Owen Watkins (pioneer missionary, Central Africa), ad- dressed the meeting mt missionary work in Africa, and said that in the Transvaal thirteen years ago, there were in that district three ministers, no native agent,and two native churches. To-day there are 25 missionaries and assistants,33 paid native agents,s3B unpaid native agents (who devoted their whole time to the work of G0d),3,539 members, 14,091 membkra on trial, 25,303 worshipping in Wesleyan Churches, and the Gospel was preached in Ve different languages and innumerable dialects. A collection was taken in aid of the mission. ST. GEORGE'S MISSION.

The annual harvest f'stival In connection with the above mission was commenced on Sunday evening,when there was a Large congregation. The mission room had been exquis!tely decorated for the occasion by the ladies. The musical portion of the service was rendered in a highly creditable manner by a slightly augmented choir. Spinney's anthem, " He watereth the Hill," was given with great taste. The Rev, C. E. Jackson, curate in charge of the mission. preached an excellent sermon from the words "For they have sown the wind and they shall reap the whirlwind, Hosea flc, 7v. The festival was continued on Tuesday being especially intended for the Sunday School children to whom the rev, gentleman delivered an eloquent address on flowers. The offertories at both services were in aid of the mission bui!ding fued, a considerable SIM being still required to clear off the ddr.

div.head: I FUNERAL OF MR. H. H. DUTTON.
div.p: I FUNERAL OF MR. H. H. DUTTON.

Tle funeoal of Mr. H. H. Dutton, whose death occurred on Wednesday week from typhoid fever, took place on Saturday afternoon. The deceased was interred in the Warrington Cemetery in the presence of a large concourse of people. Mr. Wibberley conducted the funeral service. The chief mourners were Mrs. Dutton (wife) and soh, Mr. Dutton (father), Messrs. R. Dutton, John Dutton, and William Dutton (brothers), Mr. and Mrs. E. Stringer (brother-in- law and sister), Mr. and Mrs. N. Cook (brother-in-law and sister), and. Misses H. and M. Dutton (sisters), Mr. and Mrs. Henry Thornton (father and mother-in-law), Mr. and Mrs. W. E. Thornton (brother and sister-in- law), Mr. H. Thornton (brother-in-law). the Misses Thornton (sisters-in-law), and Mr. and Mrs. J. G. Critchley (brother and sister-in-law). There were also present from. the Independent Methodist Chapel, Friars Green, of which denomination the deceased was a member: Messrs. W. Hudson, James Evans, James Gandy, John Critchley, Thomas Barton, A. Jolley, Thomas Shaw, James Mason, John Birch, , Joseph Mounfleld, William Mounfield and others. I Brick-street Mission : Messrs. James Shaw, Edward Roberts, William Barton, William Wright, ti. 'Wright, Benjamin Warburton, and a number of Sunday school teachers and elder scholars in connection 'with Brick-st. and Friars Green Sunday Schools. From the Warrington Debating Society there were present Mr. A. Bennett and Mr. E. J. Hall secretaries, Messrs. J. T. Hulse, John Gandy, C. Lyon, and Harrington. There were also present Messrs. S. B. Stringer, W. Roberts, J. Clayton, Fieldhouee, G. Wallington. Nield and others representing the Warrington Y.M.C.A., Liberal Associa- tion,i-Perfect Thrift Building Society, and Rechabites Order. Wreaths had been sent by. deceased's wife and children, "his heart-broken father and mother," his sisters, Harriet and Marie, Mr. and Mrs. E. Stringer, Mr. and Mrs. N. Cook, Mrs. Thornton and Lillie, Mr. and Mrs. W. E. Thornton, Mr. and Mrs. J. G. Critchley, the teachers of Brick-st. and Friars'-green Sunday Schools ,and members of Friars'-green Chapel choir, Mr. George Gibbons,. Mr. John H. Gittens, Mr. and Mrs. T. Harding, Mr. and Mrs. Wright, Mr. and Mrs. Hodgkinson, Mr. 'and Mrs. Joseph Craik. Mr. and Mrs. E. Lloyd Jones, Mr, T. Braithwaite, and Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Harnin- lett.

At a meeting of the Warringtrm Debating society on Tuesday evening, Mr. John Gandy moved the following vote of condolence: "That this society places on record its deep concern at the death of Mr. H. H. Dutton. the honorary treasurer of the society, and one of its oldest members, and respectfully tenders to his widow, family, and parents, its sincerest sympathy." Mr. Gandy said it was with the deepest regret he moved the resolution. A gloom was spread over their last meeting when it was announced that Mr. Dutton was seriously indisposed, but no one thought his end was so near. The resolution was carried in silence.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC SOLFA CHOIR CONCERT.
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOLFA CHOIR CONCERT.

The Runcorn Tonic Solfa Choir have had a long and honourable career. Musical Societies in Run- corn, have. had as a rule, but spasmodic and evanes- cent existences, but the tonic .aolfa choir appears to gather 'strength and solidity with. age. Each year sees the choir come forward with renewed vigour and earnestneseof purpose in the endeavour to cater for the public in matters musical, and, it is pleasing to record with increasing success. If Runcorn Public Hall was not crowded on Thesday evening, on the occasion of the opening of the pre- sent season, the building yeocontained a large and appreciative audience, who were. fully repaid for thbir support by the excellency of the fare provided. Since they la,st appeared before the Runcorn pub- lic, the choir have been enabled to add the word prize to their title, by reason of a success gained in a choral-com- petition in Maqahester. One of the treats of the evening was the singing of the test piece by which • this proud title-was obtained. It was the quint madrigal of Thos. Morley, written in 1595, and entitled "Fire !. fire ! my heag !" The other items by the choir were the part Bongs The song of the Vikings,' " slumbeit song," " Lochnagaib," and" Three men in a boat." The sing- ing of thechoir manifested all the finish ot former per- formances. Timeand execution were well Marked, and, there was a brightness -and power infused into the several membersthat was highly pleasurable to listen to. Mr. James Holford, the conductor, wielded the baton With his accustomed efficiency. The principals were Misißessie Holt, soprano ; Mr. Stanley Cookson, bari-. tone ; MissGrdon Nunn, solo violin ; and Miss Florence Nunn, solo violoncello; Miss Nunn,. the pianist, was unfortunately unable to be present in consequence of a serious illness. Miss Holt, who has a phasing voice, quickly made herself a favourite with her auditors, and for her first effort" Bid me discourse," she was awarded an encore, and a similar compliment was paid her for her admirable readition-of her other songs..-" Dream stories" and " Sing sweet bird." .Uifted with a robust Voice of good quality,. Mr. Cookson sang with power and expression "Biddy arc*" and " fear no foe' and. arid. for each effort he reeelved an unanknous recall. The performance of the sisters-Nunn were a rich treat, and the audience did not fail to show their appreciation by repeated,rounds of applause. The concert on the whole was highly enjoyable and, success- ful.

div.head: .400 FOR A WIDNES WOMAN.
div.p: .400 FOR A WIDNES WOMAN.

Before Judge ghand and a jury at Widnes County Court, yesterday, Richard Dodd and his wife Mary Elizabeth Dodd, of Halebank, brought an action against the Public Benefit Boot Company to recover damages for injuries sustained through an accident in the shop of the company, at Victoria-road, Widnes, an the 13th May last. Mr. T. Swift (instructed by Mr. J. W. Knowles) represented the plaintiff and Mr. Arthur Browne of W arrington, defended. The evidence for the plaintiff showed that Mrs. Dodd was 23 years of age and up to the time of the accident had enjoyed very good health. On the Saturday night in question she went into the defendant's shop with the intention of purchas- ing a pair of boots for her husband. As she was walking along looking at the boots on the vAll, she fell down a hole, aMich was usually covered with a trap door. The woman had not seen the hole before, and she alleged that she had seen persons walking over the same spot previously. She sustained severe injury to her ribs and her head and knee, and had since been under medical treat- ment and had been unable to do her work. When lifted out of the hole the manager said " Jam very sorry ; I have done the same thing myself."—Dr. Hutchinson said it would probably be years before she COM pletely recovered, if she did at all. She could not walk with comfort. For the defence Mr. Browne denied that his clients were to blame. If there was any negligence they alleged they did not contribute to it. The shop was a small one lighted by eighteen lights, and the front of the building was illuminated with 99 gas jets. The woman was not a customer. On entering, she said she did not want anything,but had come with her friend Mrs. Watkin, who wished to buy a pair of boots. The trap door was opened in her presence for the shop assis- tant to fetch up some boots. The trap door was put in a corner, but this woman " mooning about the shop, went into the corner where no one was expected to go. Evidence was given in support of this statement—ills Honour in directing the jury, said a shopkeeper was bound to use reasonable care towards their cuscomers,so that they should not meet with accidents when they en- tered for the purpose of transacting business or for the purpose of seeing the articles the shopkeeper displayed as wares for purchasers to inspect.—The jury gave a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £5O. Judgment was entered accordingly with costs.

div.head: LATCHFORD GOOD TRMFLARY.
div.p: LATCHFORD GOOD TRMFLARY.

A special session.of the Bonehill Branch Lodge was held in the Temperance Hall on Monday even- ing, under the presidency of Bro. A. Ford, Chief Templar. The programme for the evening consisted of an official visit of the District Chief Templar (Mr. It. H. Drury, of Stockport). It was moved, seconded. and carried that a choir be formed in connection with the Juvenile Temple. Bros. H. Eithardson, A. Ford, H. Blease, and J. Dicchfield, with several sisters, have kindly promised to assist in the training of the young. Bro. Drury who was welcomed by Bro. Ellison, delivered an address dnring the evening, at the conclusion of which he, was heartily thanked on the motion of Bro. Ford. PRESENTATION TO_ MISS SID:II%IONRS.

On Tuesday evening the Sunday school teachers in connection with St. Peter's Church met to say good- bye to one of their number—Miss Simmonds —who is leaving the town. It was felt that, having worked in the school s earnestly and devotedly for the past three years, she should not be allowed to leave without some token of the kindly feelings en- tertained towards her by her fellow teachers. The vicar, the Rev. B. Percival on their behalf pros. ated her with a handsome album, containing the photo- graphs of the vicar and Mrs. Percival, together with a very pretty writing case. In making the presen- tation the vicar said he had not had the pleasure of knowing Miss Simmonds or indeed any of the teachers for more than ten months, but in that time he had been able to observe her devotedness to her class and her interest in the school. He could only say how sorry he felt at parting with so valuable a , teacher, and he hoped what was to them a loss would be to 8017113 one else a gain. He hoped she would take up christian work at the home to which she was going. lie then referred to the harmony and good feeling which prevailed in the school, and looked forward to the time when they should require more teachers as they should have to extend the Sunday school, the present building being too small to accommodate the large numbers attending and seeking admission. Miss Sirumonds accepted the gifts with mach pleasure and expres.sed her regret at having to leave the school.

ELEMENTARY EDUCATION ACT, 1870. SECTION IX.—FINAL NOTICE P.F. • COUNTY OF LANCASTER. SCHOOL DISTRICT OF HAYDOCK. WHEREAS the Education Department, in pursuance Of the Elementary Education Act, 1870, did on the 3rd day of September, 1893 publish a Notice of their decision as to the Public School Accornmodat lin required or the above District: And whereas no public ir.quiry has leen directed to be held, and more thAn a month has elapsed since publication of the said Notice. Now, therefore, the Lords of the Committee of Council on Education HEREBY GIVE FINAL NOTICE as follows I. The School District is the Township of HAY- DOCK. U. The Schools named in the First Schedule to this Notice are considered to be available for such District. 111. Additional Public School accommodation of the amount and description mentioned in the second Schedule to this NAice appears to be required for the District. IV. Their Lordships hereby direct that the Public School accommodation mentioned in the said Second Schedule be supplied within a period • not exceeding two months from the date of the publication of this Notice. V. If at the expiratloa of such period the Public School accommodation mentioned in the said Second Schedule has not been supplied or is not in course of being supplied with due despatch. their Lordships will cause a School Board to be formed for such School District. MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1893. TO THE BURGESSES OF TOWN HALL WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, My term of °flies as one of your representatives in the Town Council having expired, I have decided. in re- sponse to the invitation of a large number of ratepayers, to offer myself for re-election. During the nine years I have been in the Town Connell I have endeavoured to serve you to the best of my ability. I have always, both by my voice and vote, opposed what I be- lieved to be extravagant and unnecessary expenditute, and will not hesitate to do so in the future. At the same time. I hive strongly supported every move- ment whleh irs rpy judgment was conducive to the best interests of the ratepayers. I cordially supported the freeing of our Public Library, the erection of the New Baths, and you will doubtless remember the very active part I took in advocating and completing the purchase of the Water Works. which has proved to be a great advantage to the Borough of Warrington. I therefore appeal to you for your support on Nov ember Ist, believing that I still retain your confidence and approval. I am. Ladies and Gentlemen. Your obedient Servant, 30115 HENDERSON FLEMING. Springfield-st , October 17th, 1893.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, Ma TOWN HALL WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF TUC WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, At the desire of your Ward Committee, an with the unanimous approval aud support of the Council of the Conservative Association, I have much pleasure in offering son my services as one of your representatives in the Town Council. I am a resident in the Ward, your interests and mine are identical, and I shall at all times be at hand and ready to hear the grievances of any of the burgesses, and so fAr as it lies in my power shall endeavour to have such grievances remedied. • The distress whichnow unfortunately exists in the town will be an additional incentive to me to do all I can to secure due economy in all the affairs of the borough and it will ever be my earnest desire to promote the improvement of the town and its trade, so that Lab our and Wages may be created for the Working-classes and business fr the Shopkeepers. I am moderate in my view s g things in general, and I trust I shall never be led to attempt to do an injustice to any sect ion of the ratepayers in order to gratify coy own caprice and crotchets, or the fads of any class of the community. I appeal to the burgesses af the Ward generally for their votes and active support on the polling day. I am. Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOSEPH SRI LLCOCK. Winwick Street, Warrington. October 11111.1893.

ATUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1893. TO THE BURGESSES OF WHITECROSS- WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, My term of office as one of your representati.,es in the Town Council expires on the Ist of November. and at the unanimous request of a large and representative body of the ratepayers. I have consented to offer myself for re-election, I have already addressed a large number of burgesses at a public meeting in the Ward, and I shall esteem it a favour if you will read my ti-hiress upon that occasion, a copy of which I have sent to every elector. During the nine years I have had the honour of a seat in the Town Council I have striven to do my duty without fear or f scour, and if you again elect me as your representa- tive, as I believe you will by a large majority, it will afford me great pleasure to serve you to the best of my ability. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant. HENRY ROBERTS. Rose Cottar, Latchford, October 18th, 1893.

ARRLNGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1893. Writ TMOIZOsS WARD. TO THH BURGBSSIIS THS WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Havirg at the request of a number of Workingmen and other Ratepayers become n Candidate for the represen- tation of the above Ward in the Town Con ncil, I venture to appeal to you to glve me your active support now and your Votes on the Polling Day. I have, as many of you are aware, lived in the Ward for upwards of 20 years, and during that time have gone about amongst you almost every flay. I am thus in touch with your wants and feelings, and my residence amongst you will enable you to readily inform me of any grievances or suggestions in connection with your Ward which you may think require attention. I am myself a Workingman and a Ratepayer in the Ward, and as such an ytltlng that is to the interest of my fellow workingmen will naturally receive my warmest support. The Distress which unfortunatety prevails in thetown de- mands that rigid economy should be practised in the ad- ministration of the Borough Funds, and it will be my aim, if returned, to support only such expenditure of the Public Money as is absolutely necessary for the welfareof the Borough. I appeal to you with the utmost confidence to support the capdidature of one who is anxious to render some service to Town generally, and to this Ward in particular. I hope, therefore, that by your Votes on the Ist of November next, you will enable me to do this. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, ROBERT THURMAN SMITH. r 25, Lovely-lane, Warrington. October 17th, 1893.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1893. To THE BURGESSES OF THE HOWLEY WARD. The term of my services as a Couacillor in the HI Icy Ward (to which position you returned me by a large majority three years ago) will expire on the 31st inst. and I have been asked by burgesses of both political parties, to allow myself to be again nominated for the ward, and after con- sideration I have consented to again, offer my services to you as your representative in the Council. During the term 01 my office I have endeavoured to fulfil my duty to th • best of my ability in furthering and support- ing all claims for the advancement of the town and for the reduction of the rates. I have cons.stently 01 posed the increase of salaries of the officials of the Corporation when I was of the opinion that they were already well enough paid for their services, and on the other band I have never heel_ teed to support an increase of the salaries where I thought the officials deserved it for the onerous dutlea they had to per- form. Three years ago I promised to get remedied the dangerous corldition of Rowley Brook and owing to my persistently raising the:question in the Council and elsewhere, the danger has been entirely removed. I do not know that it is necessary to mention any other of the subje•As that I have endeavoured to carry to a successful issue in the Committee or in the Council as you have bad ample opplrtunity of judging of my merits from the position which I again seek to occupy. If you do me the honour of again returning me I shall not regard any matter that corn Is before me from a party point of view, a., I do not agree with party politics being introduced Into Municipal matters, but I shall endeavour to do my duty in the future as I have done in the past. I ant, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, AETEUR BROWNE. Cloth Hall Yard, Warrington, 19th October,lB93.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1893. TO THE BURGESSES OF ORFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I regret that in consequence of falling hetlth your esteemed representative, Mr. James Walker, is unable to offer himself for re-election. I am desirous of serving the burgesses of Orford Ward,and I rejoice that upon this occasion I have promises of support from both political parties, as I de idedly object to the intro- (Motion of politics in municipal affairs. I have lived nearly the whole of my life in Warrington, and have taken ast active part in public affairs. I have previondy occupied a seat in the Town Council for nine years, and am fully acquainted with the work which, if I am elected. I shall be required to undertake. I believe that healthy recreation is conducive to happiness, and I will endeavour to promote the acquirement of open spaces for playgrounds in crowded areas. I am also of opinion that small free lending libraries and newsrooms, in several parts of the town, could be established with great benefit to Vie localities, and without impairing the efficiency of the present Library and Museum. In conclusion, if you do me the honour of electing me as your representative, I shall appreciate your confidence, and will endeavour to discharge the duties to your satisfaction. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant. WILLIAM PIERPOINT. Latchford, October 17th, 1893.

30,376 10th OctOber. 1893, Investing Rural Sanitary Authority with Urban Powers. RUNCORN UNION. HALTON AND Contributory places, WESTON • • TO THE GUARDIANS OF THE POOR of the RUNCORN UNION, in the Calunty of Chester. being the Sanitary Authority for the Rural Sanitary District of that Uoion And to all others whom it may concern. Whereas. by certain ordrs dated the 17t h day of November, 1883, and the 10th day of Fehru,ry. 1888, issued in pursuance of the Public Health Act, 1875, We the Local Government Board, invested the Guardians of the Poor of the said Run- corn Union as such Sanitary Authority as aforesaid, with certain of the powers, rights, duties, capacities, liabilities, and oh igations of an Urban Sanitary Authority as regards certain p,rtions of their district, including the contributory place of Weston; And whereas, under the provislosts of the Public Health Acts Amendm nt Act, 1890, the said Sanitary Authority have adopted Part Three ot that Act, so far as it is applicable to a Rural Sanitary Authority ; And whereas we have rec iced and duly considered an application nnder Section 276 of the said Public Health Act, 1875, an I under Section 5 of the said Public Health Acts Amendment Act 1891. from the said Sanitary Authority to put in force within the contributory place of Halton and within the said contributory place of Weston within their district certain provisions of such Acts as herein-after men- tioned : Now therefore, in pursuance of the powers given to us by tie statutes in that behalf, we hereby declare and order as follows : ARUOLR I.—Until we by order otherwise direct, the iflider-mentioned provisions of the said Acts sh,ll be in force within the said contributory places of Halton and Weston as herein-after mentioned, and the said Sanitary Authority shall be invested, as regards the said contributory places, will; all the powers, rights, duties, capacities, liabilities, and obligations of an Urban Sanitary Authotity under such pro- visions ; namely— Within the contributory places of Halton and Weston,— The Public Health Act, 1875, bectlon 115. The Public Health Acts Amendment Act. 1890.— Section 23 so mach as is not already in force. Within the contribut ry place of Halton only,— The Public Health Act, 1875,— Sect ion 49. so much as is not already in fume : Section 44, so much as is no. already in force; Sections 112, 113. and 114 ; and Seation 157. so much as is not, already in force. ARTICLE 11.-1 his Order shall come into operation on the Thirteenth day of November, One thousand eight hundred and ninety-three, and the said Sanitary Authority shall cause it to be published once in some newspaper circulated within their district before that date. Given under the Seal of Office of the Local Government Board, this Tenth day of October, in the year One thousand eight hundred and ninety-three. IIENRY H. FOWLER, President. S. B. PROVIS, Assistant Secretary.
